en: In the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā*, Chapter VI, when this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:

"If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the five superknowledges— which are all phenomena whose intrinsic nature is non-existence— "

In that case, Blessed One, since all phenomena have the nature of non-existence, how is the gradual action of a bodhisattva mahāsattva discerned, and how are his gradual training and gradual practice discerned— by means of which gradual action, gradual training, and gradual practice he awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:

"In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva first hears as follows: [the teachings] of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones; of the bodhisattvas mahāsattvas who have attended upon the Buddha-dharma; and of the pratyekabuddhas."

Because of the non-existence of those who abide in the fruit of a *bṛhat*, or of non-returners (*anāgāmin*), or of once-returners (*sakṛdāgāmin*), or of stream-enterers (*srotaāpanna*); because of the non-existence of Buddhas, the Blessed Ones;

because of the non-existence of Pratyekabuddhas; because of the non-existence of Arhats; because of the non-existence of non-returners; because of the non-existence of once-returners; and because of the non-existence of stream-enterers—that is, because of the non-existence of all noble ones (*ārya*)—all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Even down to a space the size of the tip of a single hair, this thought occurs to that bodhisattva mahāsattva:

"The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, the bodhisattvas mahāsattvas, the pratyekabuddhas, the arhats, the anāgāmins, the sakṛdāgāmins, the srotaāpannas, and all noble ones are indeed non-existent, whether I shall awaken to enlightenment or whether I shall not awaken."

"All phenomena are indeed entities; therefore, may I surely awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, having awakened to which I shall establish all sentient beings—who move within the perception of entities—in non-entity, in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Furthermore, that bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment...

Established for the sake of the final nirvāṇa of all sentient beings, he should undertake gradual action, gradual training, and begin with the gradual path. Having trained in this, the former bodhisattva mahāsattvas attained unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening;

they train first of all in the six perfections, namely: the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom.
Thus is the general sequential realization.

Furthermore, Subhūti, from the first production of the thought of awakening onwards, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of generosity gives gifts himself, encourages others in the perfection of generosity, and speaks in praise of generosity.
He speaks in praise of and approves of those others who practice the perfection of generosity;
having acquired a great mass of wealth through that generosity, he gives gifts with a mind free from stinginess—
food to those seeking food, drink to those seeking drink, clothing to those seeking clothing, and ointment to those seeking ointment.

He gives a bed to those seeking a bed, a shelter to those seeking shelter, a lamp to those seeking a lamp, or any other human requisite or accessory; by that gift, he establishes beings in ethical discipline,
and he establishes them in concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.

Endowed with that very aggregate of ethical discipline, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation, he transcends the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Having transcended the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, he enters the fixed course of a bodhisattva; having entered the fixed course of a bodhisattva, he [purifies] a buddhafield.

He purifies the buddha-field; having purified it, he brings sentient beings to maturity; having brought them to maturity, he attains the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*); having attained the knowledge of all modes, he turns the wheel of Dharma; having turned the wheel of Dharma, he establishes sentient beings in the three vehicles; and having established them in the three vehicles, he liberates them from cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*). In this way, Subhūti, the gradual action, gradual training, and gradual practice of a bodhisattva mahāsattva through generosity are made known.
And one does not apprehend any of that. For what reason? Because it has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Thus is the gradual realization (*anupūrvābhisamaya*) by means of the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*).
Furthermore, Subhūti, from the first production of the thought of awakening, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while personally practicing the perfection of ethical discipline, gives gifts;

he establishes others in the perfection of ethical discipline and establishes them in giving; he speaks in praise of the perfection of ethical discipline; and he becomes one who speaks in praise of and approves of those others who practice the perfection of ethical discipline.
By means of that morality, he establishes beings in morality;
he establishes them in concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
By means of that very aggregate of morality, aggregate of concentration, aggregate of wisdom, aggregate of liberation, and aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation, [he establishes them].

Endowed with this, he transcends the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; having transcended the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, he enters the fixed course of a bodhisattva; having entered the fixed course of a bodhisattva, he purifies a buddhafield;
having purified a buddhafield, he brings sentient beings to maturity; and having brought sentient beings to maturity, [he attains] the knowledge of all aspects.

He attains the knowledge of all aspects; having attained it, he turns the wheel of Dharma; having turned the wheel of Dharma, he establishes beings in the three vehicles; having established beings in the three vehicles, he liberates them from cyclic existence. It is in this way, Subhūti, that the gradual practice of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is accomplished through ethical discipline.
Gradual training is discerned, gradual practice is discerned, yet all that is not apprehended. Why is that?
Because it has no intrinsic nature.
Thus is the gradual realization by means of the perfection of ethical discipline.

Furthermore, Subhūti, from the first production of the thought of awakening, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of patience himself, gives gifts and guards his ethical discipline, and he establishes others in the perfection of patience and establishes them in giving and ethical discipline.
He speaks in praise of the perfection of patience; he becomes a speaker of praise and one who approves of others who practice the perfection of patience.
By means of that patience, he establishes sentient beings in ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Endowed with that aggregate of ethical discipline, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation,
he transcends the level of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; having transcended the level of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, he enters the fixed course of a bodhisattva.

He enters the fixed course of a bodhisattva; having entered it, he purifies a buddha-field; having purified a buddha-field, he brings sentient beings to maturity; having brought sentient beings to maturity, he attains the knowledge of all aspects; and having attained the knowledge of all aspects, he turns the wheel of Dharma.
Having turned the wheel of Dharma, he establishes beings in the three vehicles;

having established beings in the three vehicles, he liberates them from cyclic existence. It is in this way, Subhūti, that the gradual activity, gradual training, and gradual practice of a bodhisattva mahāsattva through patience are known, yet all of that is not apprehended. Why is that?
For its intrinsic nature does not exist.
Thus is the successive realization by means of the perfection of patience.

Furthermore, Subhūti, from the first production of the thought of awakening, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of vigor himself, gives gifts, guards morality, and [cultivates] patience.
He establishes others in the perfection of vigor,
establishes them in generosity, ethical discipline, and patience,
and speaks in praise of the perfection of vigor.

He speaks in praise of those others who practice the perfection of vigor and approves of them. By means of that vigor, he establishes beings in ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation. Through that very aggregate of ethical discipline, aggregate of concentration, aggregate of wisdom, aggregate of liberation, and aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation, [he establishes them].

Endowed with this, he transcends the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; having transcended the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, he enters the fixed course of a bodhisattva; having entered the fixed course of a bodhisattva, he purifies a buddha-field;
having purified a buddha-field, he brings sentient beings to maturity; and having brought sentient beings to maturity, he attains the knowledge of all aspects.
Having attained the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), he turns the wheel of Dharma; having turned the wheel of Dharma, he establishes beings in the three vehicles (*triyāna*);

having established beings in the three vehicles, he liberates them from cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*). In this way, Subhūti, the gradual action, gradual training, and gradual practice of a bodhisattva mahāsattva through vigor are discerned, yet none of that is apprehended. Why is that?
For thus its intrinsic nature does not exist.
This is the gradual realization by means of the perfection of vigor.

Furthermore, Subhūti, from the first production of the thought of awakening, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while personally practicing the perfection of meditation, gives gifts, guards morality, and [cultivates] patience.
He accomplishes it, exerts vigor,
and establishes others in the perfection of meditation;
he establishes them in generosity, ethical discipline, patience, and vigor.

He speaks in praise of the perfection of meditation, and he becomes one who speaks in praise of and approves of those others who practice the perfection of meditation. By means of that meditation, he establishes sentient beings in ethical discipline, and he establishes them in concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation. By means of that very aggregate of ethical discipline...

Endowed with the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation, he transcends the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
having transcended the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, he enters the fixed course of a bodhisattva; having entered the fixed course of a bodhisattva, he purifies a buddha-field.

Having purified the buddha-field, he brings sentient beings to maturity; having brought sentient beings to maturity, he attains the knowledge of all aspects; having attained the knowledge of all aspects, he turns the wheel of Dharma; and having turned the wheel of Dharma, he establishes sentient beings in the three vehicles.

Having established beings in the three vehicles, he liberates them from cyclic existence. In this way, Subhūti, the gradual action, gradual training, and gradual practice of a bodhisattva mahāsattva through meditative concentration are known;
yet all of that is not apprehended. Why is that?
Because it has no intrinsic nature.
Thus is the gradual realization by means of the perfection of meditation.

Furthermore, Subhūti, from the first production of the thought of awakening, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom himself, gives gifts, guards morality, accomplishes patience, and exerts vigor.
He enters into meditative absorption and establishes others in the perfection of wisdom;
he establishes them in generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, and meditative concentration.

He speaks in praise of the perfection of wisdom, and he becomes one who speaks in praise of and approves of those others who practice the perfection of wisdom. By means of that wisdom, he establishes sentient beings in ethical discipline, and he establishes them in concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation. Through that very aggregate of ethical discipline and aggregate of concentration...
Endowed with the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation, he transcends the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
having transcended the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, he enters the fixed course of a bodhisattva;
and having entered the fixed course of a bodhisattva, he purifies a buddha-field.
Having purified the buddha-field, he brings sentient beings to maturity;
having brought sentient beings to maturity, he attains the knowledge of all aspects; and having attained the knowledge of all aspects, he turns the wheel of Dharma.
Having turned the wheel of Dharma, he establishes beings in the three vehicles;

having established beings in the three vehicles, he liberates them from cyclic existence. It is in this way, Subhūti, that the gradual activity of a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s wisdom is known, his gradual training is known, and his gradual practice is known.
And all that is not apprehended. Why is that?
Because it has no intrinsic nature.
This is the gradual realization by means of the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in gradual action, in gradual training, and in the gradual practice; starting from the first production of the thought of awakening,

with mental engagements associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he resolves upon all phenomena as having non-existence as their intrinsic nature, and cultivates the recollection of the Buddha, cultivates the recollection of the Dharma, and cultivates the recollection of the Saṅgha.
He cultivates the recollection of ethical discipline,
he cultivates the recollection of generosity,
and he cultivates the recollection of the deities. And how, Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivate the recollection of the Buddha?
In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not bring to mind a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha by way of form;
nor does he bring him to mind by way of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. Why is that?
Because the intrinsic nature of form does not exist.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness have no intrinsic nature;
that which has no intrinsic nature is non-existent. Why is that?
Because mindfulness of the Buddha consists in non-recollection and non-mental engagement—that is, mindfulness of the Buddha through the non-mental engagement with form and the other sense objects.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is not to be attended to by means of the thirty-two marks of a great man, nor is he to be attended to as having a golden body, nor is he to be attended to by means of a fathom-wide radiance, nor is he to be attended to by means of the eighty secondary marks. Why is that?
Because his intrinsic nature does not exist.
That which has no intrinsic nature is non-existence. Why is that?
Because mindfulness of the Buddha is non-recollection and non-mental engagement, by means of mindfulness of the Buddha through the non-mental engagement with [the Buddha's] marks and so forth.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is not to be mentally engaged with as a mass of ethical discipline.

It should not be attended to as the aggregate of concentration, nor as the aggregate of wisdom, nor as the aggregate of liberation, nor as the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation. Why is that?
Because they have no intrinsic nature.
That which has no intrinsic nature is non-existent. Why is that?

Because mindfulness of the Buddha is non-recollection and non-mental engagement; it is mindfulness of the Buddha through the non-mental engagement with the aggregates of ethical discipline and the rest. Furthermore, Subhūti, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha does not [exist] by means of the ten powers of a Tathāgata.
It should not be brought to mind by means of the four grounds of self-confidence, nor should it be brought to mind by means of the four analytical knowledges;
it should not be brought to mind by means of great compassion, nor by great loving-kindness, nor by the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. Why is that?
Because they have no intrinsic nature.
That which has no intrinsic nature is non-existence. Why is that?
Because mindfulness of the Buddha is mindfulness without recollection and without mental engagement, by way of not mentally engaging with the ten powers and so forth.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is not to be mentally engaged as dependent origination. Why is that?
For thus it has no intrinsic nature;
that which has no intrinsic nature is non-existent. Why is that?
Because mindfulness of the Buddha is non-recollection and non-mental engagement, through mindfulness of the Buddha by way of non-mental engagement with dependent origination.

In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should bring to mind the recollection of the Buddhas. In this way, indeed, his gradual action is made known; his gradual training and gradual practice are made known. Training himself in this gradual action, gradual training, and gradual practice, by means of these gradual undertakings, he...
He fulfills the four foundations of mindfulness;

he fulfills the four right endeavors, the four bases of miraculous power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path, the concentration of emptiness, the signless concentration, and the wishless concentration.
He fulfills the immeasurables, the dhyānas, the formless attainments, the liberations, the concentrations, the meditative absorptions, and the gateways of dhāraṇī;
he fulfills all the perfections, all the emptinesses, the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique buddha-qualities;
he fulfills great compassion.
He fulfills great loving-kindness;
he fulfills the knowledge of all aspects.
By means of the application to the nature of non-existence, he will fully awaken to all phenomena as having the nature of non-existence, wherein even the notion of "nature" does not exist.
Thus is the recollection of the Buddha.

And how, Subhūti, should the recollection of the Dharma be cultivated by a bodhisattva mahāsattva? Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should not direct the mind toward wholesome dharmas.
Unwholesome phenomena are not to be attended to; neither are indeterminate phenomena nor neutral phenomena to be attended to.

Neither worldly nor supramundane, neither carnal nor spiritual, neither noble nor ignoble, neither with outflows nor without outflows, neither included within the realm of desire nor the realm of form nor the formless realm are they to be attended to.
Conditioned and unconditioned phenomena are to be brought to mind. Why is that? Because those phenomena have no intrinsic nature; that which has no intrinsic nature is a non-entity. Why is that?

Because the recollection of phenomena is non-recollection and non-mental-attention. Having trained in this recollection of phenomena through the application of the intrinsic nature of non-existence...
Until he attains the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), he will fully awaken to all phenomena as having non-existence as their intrinsic nature (*abhāvasvabhāva*),

wherein even the notion of an intrinsic nature does not exist. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should cultivate the recollection of phenomena (*dharmānusmṛti*), in which there is not even a particle of the activity of recollection.
How much more so, then, the loss of mindfulness!
Thus is the recollection of the Dharma.
And how, Subhūti, should a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivate the recollection of the Saṅgha? Here, Subhūti:
A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should recollect the Saṅgha as having the nature of non-existence—
that is, the Blessed One’s community of disciples, consisting of the four pairs of persons and the eight great individuals. Why is that?

For thus they have no intrinsic nature; those which have no intrinsic nature are non-existent entities, and they are said to be manifested through the intrinsic nature of non-existence—namely, the four pairs of persons and the eight great individuals.
Why is that?

Because it is non-recollection and non-mental engagement that constitutes the recollection of the Saṅgha. Having trained here in this recollection of the Saṅgha by way of the yoga of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, up to...

He will attain the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). He will fully awaken to all phenomena as having the nature of non-existence (*abhāvasvabhāva*), wherein even the notion of "own-nature" (*svabhāva*) does not exist. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should cultivate the recollection of the Saṅgha, in which there is not even a particle of the activity of recollection.
How much more so, then, the loss of mindfulness!
This is the recollection of the Sangha.
And how, Subhūti, should a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivate the recollection of ethical discipline? Here, Subhūti,

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom is established in ethical discipline that is unbroken, flawless, unspotted, untarnished, unadulterated, independent, praised by the wise, well-undertaken, and conducive to meditative concentration,
he should not attend to that ethical discipline as having the nature of non-existence, wherein there is not even an atom of the activity of mindfulness.

How much more so, then, the disappearance of mindfulness? For what reason? Because they have no intrinsic nature; that which has no intrinsic nature is non-existent. Contemplating in this way, he will gradually attain even the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). Why is that?

Non-mindfulness and non-mental engagement constitute the recollection of ethical discipline (*śīlānusmṛti*). Subhūti, it is in this manner that a bodhisattva mahāsattva should attend to the recollection of ethical discipline.
Where even the perception of intrinsic nature does not exist, how much less so the perception of non-existence?
Thus is the recollection of ethical discipline.

And how, Subhūti, should a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom cultivate the recollection of generosity? Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should recollect generosity through the application of the nature of non-existence—whether it be the gift of material things or the gift of the Dharma. Why is that?

The mind does not arise in this way: "I give" or "I do not give," "I relinquish" or "I do not relinquish. When relinquishing the limbs and members [of the body], one should not give rise to such a thought in which there is not even an atom of mindful action, let alone the loss of mindfulness. Why is that?

For indeed, those things have no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); and those which have no intrinsic nature are non-existent (*abhāva*). Contemplating in this way, he will gradually attain even the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). Why is that?

Because non-recollection and non-mental-attention (*amanasikāra*) constitute the recollection of renunciation (*tyāgānusmṛti*). Thus, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) should attend to the recollection of renunciation in such a way that even the notion of intrinsic nature does not exist therein.
How much less, then, can there be the perception of non-existence?
Thus is the recollection of relinquishment.
And how, Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom practice the recollection of the deities?

They should be brought to mind. Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should bring to mind those gods who are stream-enterers, born among the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Trayastriṃśa gods, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, and the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, as being of the nature of non-existence. Why is that?

For indeed, they have no intrinsic nature; those which have no intrinsic nature are simply non-existent. Contemplating in this way, he will gradually attain even the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). Why is that?

Because the recollection of the deities is non-recollection and non-mental-attention (*amanasikāra*). Thus, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should attend to the recollection of the deities in such a way that even the notion of intrinsic nature does not exist, let alone the notion of non-existence.
Thus is the recollection of the deities.
In this way, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who attends to these six recollections, a gradual practice is discerned, a gradual training, and a gradual path are discerned.
Thus are the six recollections.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom who wishes to fulfill the gradual performance, who wishes to fulfill the gradual training and the gradual practice, should train in internal emptiness and should train in external emptiness by means of the yoga of the nature of non-existence.

One should train in internal and external emptiness, up to training in the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature. One should train in the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path;

one should train in the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the liberations, the samādhis, the meditative absorptions, and the gateways of the dhāraṇīs.

One should train in emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha by way of the yoga of the nature of non-existence. One should train in the ten perfections and in the ten great compassions;
training thus in the path to enlightenment, one will fully awaken to all phenomena as having the nature of non-existence.
Where there is not even an atom of the activity of mindfulness, how much less could there be form, or feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness?
Likewise, [where there is no such activity], there can be no aggregates, elements, sense-bases, dependent origination, or the factors of dependent origination; no perfections, or emptiness;

no factors conducive to awakening, noble truths, immeasurables, meditative absorptions, or formless attainments; no liberations, concentrations, attainments, or doors of dhāraṇī; and no emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, superknowledges, the ten powers, fearlessnesses, analytical knowledges, or the unique qualities of a Buddha.

Or omniscience—this is not possible. In this way, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, a gradual action is discerned, a gradual training is discerned, and a gradual practice is discerned;
therein proceed the action, the mind, the conduct, the practice, and the training.
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:

"If, Blessed One, all dharmas have non-existence as their intrinsic nature, then there is no form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; there are no aggregates, elements, sense-fields, or dependent origination, nor are there any factors of dependent origination."
There is no perfection; there is no emptiness; there are no applications of mindfulness, right efforts, bases of miraculous power, faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, or paths;

there are no noble truths, immeasurables, meditative absorptions, formless attainments, liberations, concentrations, meditative attainments, or doors of dhāraṇī; there are no emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, or superknowledges; there are no ten powers, intrepidities, analytical knowledges, or unique buddha-qualities; there is no knowledge of all aspects; there is nothing.

“There is no Buddha, there is no Dharma, there is no Saṅgha; there is no path, there is no fruit, there is no affliction, there is no purification, there is no attainment, there is no realization, and so on, up to: there are no phenomena at all.
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
"Subhūti, in all dharmas which have non-existence as their intrinsic nature, is either existence or non-existence apprehended?
Subhūti replied: "No, Blessed One; in all dharmas which are non-existent, neither existence nor non-existence is apprehended."
The Blessed One said:
"In that case, Subhūti, how can this be so?
If all dharmas have non-existence as their intrinsic nature, then form, feeling, perception, and mental formations do not exist."
There is no consciousness;

there are no aggregates, elements, sense bases, or dependent originations, nor are there the factors of dependent origination; there are no perfections, emptinesses, factors of enlightenment, noble truths, immeasurables, meditative absorptions, formless attainments, liberations, concentrations, meditative equipoises, or doors of dhāraṇī; and there are no [the three gates of] emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, nor the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, or the unique qualities of a Buddha.

"There is no omniscience; there is no fruit of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha; there is no path, no affliction, no purification, no attainment, and no clear realization, up to and including the non-existence of all dharmas. When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:
“Blessed One, I have no doubt and no uncertainty regarding these teachings.

However, Blessed One, in a future time there will be monks belonging to the vehicle of the disciples, the vehicle of the solitary buddhas, and the vehicle of the bodhisattvas who will say: ‘All phenomena have non-existence as their intrinsic nature; who here is defiled or purified? There is neither defilement nor purification. Knowing this, they will become fallen in morality and fallen in view.”
And they will be corrupted in conduct; for those who are corrupted in morality, corrupted in view, and corrupted in conduct, one of three destinies is to be expected:
either the destiny of hell, the destiny of the animal realm, or the destiny of the world of Yama.
"Lord, seeing this future danger as well, I ask the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha about this matter. Nevertheless, Lord, I have no doubt and no uncertainty regarding these teachings.
The Blessed One said:
"Excellent, excellent, Subhūti! It is just as you say; it is indeed so.
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One:

"If, Blessed One, all dharmas have non-existence as their intrinsic nature, for what purpose do bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, perceiving what benefit, seek to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment for the sake of sentient beings?"
The Blessed One said:

"Subhūti, it is precisely because all dharmas have non-existence as their intrinsic nature that bodhisattva mahāsattvas have set out to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Why is that?

For, Subhūti, in the exhaustion of suffering there is no apprehension for one who possesses the notion of apprehension; there is no attainment, no realization, and no unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
Subhūti said:
"But, Blessed One, is there an attainment or a clear realization of non-apprehension, or even unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
The Blessed One replied:
Subhūti, non-apprehension itself is attainment; non-apprehension itself is clear realization; non-apprehension itself is unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
This is because of the unshakeability of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). One who would wish to disturb the realm of phenomena would be wishing to disturb the attainment of non-apprehension.
or the realization, or the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
Subhūti said:
"If, Blessed One, for that which is non-apprehensible there is neither attainment, nor realization, nor unsurpassed perfect enlightenment,"
Non-apprehension itself is attainment; non-apprehension itself is clear realization; non-apprehension itself is unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Therefore, Blessed One, from where could there be a first bhūmi for a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
From where a second? From where a third? And so on, up to: from where a tenth bhūmi?
From where does unexcelled, perfect enlightenment come?
From where does the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena come? From where do the superknowledges born of maturation come? From where does the gift born of maturation come?
Whence is morality born of maturation? Whence is patience born of maturation? Whence is vigor born of maturation?
Whence comes the concentration born of maturation,
and whence the wisdom born of maturation, by abiding in which maturation one matures sentient beings through dharmas born of maturation and takes hold of a buddha-field?
And he attends upon the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, with food and drink, vehicles, clothing, articles, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners,
and flags, with beds, seats, and lodgings, with lamps, or with various other human prosperities.
And these [roots of merit] of his are not cut off; rather, they ripen within his body and among his disciples even after he has attained final nirvāṇa, and they do not perish.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
"Subhūti, it is precisely because of non-apprehension that there is the first stage, the second stage, and the third stage."

Up to the tenth stage, there are for him the five superknowledges born of maturation; and from that very source, there is the gift, morality, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom born of maturation; and from that very source, there are the roots of merit born of maturation by which he effects the welfare of all sentient beings and takes hold of a Buddha-field.
He attends upon the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, with food, drink, vehicles, bedding, seats, clothing, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, flags, and excellent dwellings,

as well as lamps and various other human requisites and accomplishments; and these offerings do not cease for him until his final nirvana, when they continue as worship toward the relics and ripen among the disciples.
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:

"Blessed One, what is the distinction between non-apprehension and generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, wisdom, and the superknowledges? What is the difference between them?"
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
"Subhūti, there is no distinction whatsoever between non-apprehension and the generosity, morality, patience, vigor, meditation, wisdom, and supernormal knowledges.
Furthermore, Subhūti, for those whose generosity, morality, patience, vigor, meditation, wisdom, and supernormal knowledges are indeed unstained..."
And their distinction has been pointed out.
Subhūti said:

"But how, Blessed One, is no distinction whatsoever pointed out among generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, wisdom, and the superknowledges, when they are all unstained?"
The Blessed One said:
"In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom gives a gift without apprehending the gift and without apprehending the recipient;
he guards his morality without apprehending it."
Without apprehension, one accomplishes patience; without apprehension, one exerts vigor;
without apprehension, one enters meditative absorption.
He cultivates wisdom without apprehension;
he courses in the superknowledges without apprehension; he cultivates the foundations of mindfulness without apprehension.
In this way, not apprehending the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, and the factors of enlightenment, he cultivates the path;
not apprehending the three gateways to liberation, he cultivates them.
Without apprehending them, he cultivates the noble truths, the immeasurables, the dhyānas, the formless attainments, the meditative concentrations, and the gateways of dhāraṇī;
without apprehending them, he cultivates the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a buddha;
and without apprehending them, he brings sentient beings to maturity.
Without apprehending a buddha-field, he purifies it;

without apprehending the buddha-qualities, he awakens to supreme enlightenment. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom by means of non-apprehension. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva...
The Mahāsattva, practicing in the perfection of wisdom, becomes invincible to Māras or to the deities belonging to the host of Māra.
Thus, through the knowledge of the non-existence of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, there is the gradual realization.

Thus concludes the sixth chapter, the "Gradual Training," which is the section on the gradual realization (*anupūrvābhisamaya*) in the Noble *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Bhagavatī Prajñāpāramitā*, as revised according to the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*.
The Perfection of Wisdom in Twenty-Five Thousand Lines, Chapter Seven.
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, embrace the six perfections with a single mind?"

The four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment,
the noble eightfold path, the three gateways to liberation, the four noble truths, the eight liberations, and the nine successive meditative attainments.
He grasps the five superknowledges, from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence; the ten powers, the four grounds of self-confidence,
the four analytical knowledges, great compassion, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, the eighty minor marks, and the thirty-two marks of a great man.
Thus, regarding the realization in a single moment of mind, the Blessed One spoke in general terms:
"In this regard, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom gives a gift, that gift is not [given] otherwise than being embraced by the perfection of wisdom."
The ethical discipline which he guards, the patience with which he accomplishes,
and the vigor which he exerts—
Whatever meditative absorption he enters and whatever wisdom he cultivates,
that is not apart from being embraced by the perfection of wisdom.
Whatever immeasurable he attains,
whatever formless attainments,
whatever application of mindfulness, and whatever right exertion, basis of psychic power, faculty, power, factor of enlightenment, and path he cultivates—
When he cultivates the noble truths, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the superknowledges, the liberations, the meditative concentrations, the attainments, and the gateways of the dhāraṇīs;
when he cultivates inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature;
and when he cultivates the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, the unique buddha-qualities, and great compassion—
Those thirty-two marks of a great man and eighty minor characteristics that he assumes are not assumed by anything other than the perfection of wisdom.
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, embraced by the perfection of wisdom, embrace the six perfections with a single mind?

How does he embrace all the modes of emptiness, all the factors of enlightenment, the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the liberations, the samādhis, the meditative absorptions, the gateways of dhāraṇī, the emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, the unique buddha-qualities, great compassion, the thirty-two marks of a great man, and the eighty minor marks?"
The Blessed One said:

"In this regard, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, sustained by the perfection of wisdom, gives a gift, he does not form a dualistic perception regarding it; and when he guards his ethical discipline,"
The patience by which he accomplishes, the vigor which he exerts, and the meditative concentration into which he enters.
Whatever wisdom he cultivates, regarding that he does not form a dualistic perception;

even as far as he cultivates the factors conducive to enlightenment, regarding those he does not form a dualistic perception. It is the same for the noble truths, the immeasurables, the dhyānas, the formless attainments, the liberations, the meditative concentrations, the meditative absorptions, and the gateways of the dhāraṇīs.
the dharmas of a Buddha—emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities;
that which is great compassion;
and those which are the thirty-two marks of a great man.
He grasps the eighty secondary marks,
yet therein he does not form a dualistic perception.
Subhūti said:
And how, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, give a gift and not form a dualistic perception?
Likewise, he cultivates ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom, and yet does not form a dualistic perception.
He cultivates everything from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence,
yet he does not form dualistic perceptions;

likewise [he cultivates] the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment, the noble truths, the immeasurables, the dhyānas, the formless attainments, the liberations, the meditative concentrations, the meditative absorptions, and the gateways of dhāraṇī.

He brings forth emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, the unique qualities of a Buddha, great compassion, the thirty-two marks of a great man, and the eighty minor marks,
yet he does not conceive of them as a duality.
The Blessed One said:
"In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom fulfills the perfection of giving;
therein, having included all six perfections within that perfection of giving, he bestows gifts."

To the extent that he gives a gift having included all the factors conducive to enlightenment within it. Furthermore, Subhūti, at the time when that bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, gives a gift, he gives the gift while abiding in an untainted mind; abiding there in that untainted mind, he does not perceive any sign. "To whom do I give? he thinks.
"What shall I give? or "With what shall I give?"—
he gives a gift with a mind free from signs.
With a mind that is untainted, free from craving, and free from becoming, he does not perceive that gift, nor does he perceive that mind.
He does not perceive that recipient,
nor indeed does he perceive any phenomena at all.
Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he observes ethical discipline with a mind that has entered into signs.
He does not perceive that morality;
he does not perceive that mind;
indeed, he does not perceive any of the qualities of a Buddha.
Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he accomplishes patience with a mind that has entered into signs;
yet he does not perceive that patience,
nor does he perceive that mind.
...up to the point that he does not perceive any of the qualities of a Buddha.
Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom exerts vigor with a mind that has approached signs,
he does not perceive that vigor.
He does not perceive that mind,
nor does he perceive anything up to all the buddha-qualities.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom enters into meditative absorption with a mind free from signs.
He does not perceive that dhyāna;
he does not perceive that mind;
indeed, he does not perceive anything up to and including all the qualities of a Buddha.
Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he cultivates wisdom with a mind free from signs;
while cultivating that wisdom, he does not perceive it,
nor does he perceive that mind.

...until he no longer perceives any of the Buddha-qualities. Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom cultivates, with a mind free from signs, the applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the path, the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the liberations, the meditative absorptions, and the gateways of dhāraṇī.
He cultivates the emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness of the superknowledges and all the modes of emptiness;
he cultivates the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, the unique buddha-qualities, and great compassion;
and he brings to fulfillment the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary characteristics.
He does not perceive those phenomena; he does not perceive that mind;
indeed, he does not perceive anything up to and including all the qualities of a Buddha.
Subhūti said:
“How, Blessed One, does the perfection of generosity become fulfilled for dharmas that are signless and without volitional construction?
Likewise, how do the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom become fulfilled?”

There is the fulfillment of the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path;
there is the fulfillment of emptiness, the signless, and the wishless.

There comes to be the fulfillment of the noble truths, the immeasurables, the dhyānas, the formless attainments, the liberations, the meditative concentrations, the meditative absorptions, and the gateways of the dhāraṇīs; there is the fulfillment of all the emptinesses, the five superknowledges, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:

In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom gives gifts with a mind free from signs (*animitta*), giving food, drink, clothing, vehicles, beds, seats, gold, silver, jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, crystals, coral, raw gold, and wrought silver; flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, flags, and dwellings;
and all other various human requisites and appurtenances, whether internal or external, including wives, sons, daughters, and kingdoms.
Having adorned it, he gives it as a gift to beggars. Then someone might come and say to him:
"What is the use of this gift you have given, which is so unbeneficial? To that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, it occurs thus:
"Even though these beings revile me..."
"What is the use of this gift, or of giving in such a vast manner? A gift must simply be given by me;
it is not that I should not give. Having made that gift common to all sentient beings, he dedicates it toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
He dedicates it in such a way that, while dedicating it, he does not perceive any sign.
What shall I give? To whom shall I give? Or who is it that gives here?
Or rather, what does he transform, or into what does he transform? He does not perceive that object which, having given it away, he transforms into unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
For what reason?
Because it is empty by way of internal emptiness, empty by way of external emptiness, and so on, up to empty by way of the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence.
He thus perceives: who will dedicate, or where will one dedicate, or what will one dedicate?

For one who dedicates in this way, the dedication becomes free from poison; it is a dedication to the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). It brings all sentient beings to maturity, takes hold of a Buddha-field, and fulfills the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*).
He fulfills the perfection of ethical discipline,
fulfills the perfection of patience,
and fulfills the perfection of vigor.
He fulfills the perfection of meditation,
he fulfills the perfection of wisdom,
and he fulfills the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment.

He fulfills the concentrations of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, the formless attainments, the liberations, the concentrations, the meditative equipoises, and the gateways of the dhāraṇīs; he fulfills internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence;
he fulfills the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha;
and in that very same way, he fulfills the perfection of generosity.
And just as he does not grasp at the ripening [of karma],
Subhūti, it is just as, for example, all the requisites of the gods who Control the Creations of Others appear by mere thought;
even so, Subhūti, all the requisites of a bodhisattva mahāsattva are fulfilled by mere thought.

By means of that gift, he serves the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and satisfies the world with its gods, humans, and asuras. Having embraced those beings through that perfection of giving, he establishes them in the three vehicles by means of skillful means. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva [practices] in the perfection of wisdom.
Practicing with a mind free from signs, he fulfills the perfection of generosity.
Subhūti said:
"And how, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline?"
The Blessed One said:

"In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom attains that noble, untainted morality which is included within the path and acquired through the very nature of phenomena."
And this aggregate of his ethical discipline is unbroken, flawless, unspotted, untarnished, unblemished, unfettered, well-mastered, and praised by the wise;
yet by means of that ethical discipline, he does not grasp at any dharma— whether form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness— nor even the thirty-two marks of a great man.
Or the eighty secondary marks; or a great kshatriya clan, or a great brahmin clan, or a great householder clan;
or the gods of the Four Great Kings, or the Trayastrimsha, Yama, Tushita, Nirmanarati, or Paranirmita-vasavartin gods; or the Brahmaparisadyas, Brahmapurohitas, or Mahabrahmas.

or the gods of Limited Light, or Immeasurable Light, or Luminous Radiance; or the gods of Limited Purity, or Immeasurable Purity, or Universal Purity; or the Cloudless gods, or those Born of Merit, or Vast Fruit; or the Non-percipient Beings, or the Pure Abodes; or the gods Free from Desire, or Untroubled, or Clearly Visible, or Good to Behold, or the Highest Gods (Akaniṣṭha); or the Sphere of Infinite Space.

Nor does he grasp at the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, or the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; nor does he grasp at the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, arhatship, or the state of a pratyekabuddha, or even the sovereignty of a universal monarch.
Rather, having shared these with all sentient beings, he dedicates them toward omniscience in all its aspects.
One dedicates [the merit] through the signless, the non-apprehensible, and the non-dual; this is by way of worldly convention and not by way of the ultimate truth.
And with that perfection of ethical discipline fully perfected, through skillful means, one generates the four meditative concentrations without attachment and brings forth the divine eye.

With that divine eye born of karmic maturation, he sees the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who reside, remain, and maintain themselves in the world systems of the eastern direction, teaching the Dharma; and that vision of theirs does not perish until he awakens to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.

In this way, he sees those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who reside, remain, and maintain themselves in the world-systems of the southern direction, the western direction, the northern direction, above, below, and in the intermediate directions,
and who teach the Dharma; his vision of them does not fail.

...until he awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. With his purified divine ear, which transcends that of humans, he hears the voices of those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones; and what he has heard does not perish until, by means of what he has heard, he accomplishes the welfare of both himself and others.

By means of the knowledge of the movements of the minds of others, he understands with his own mind the minds of those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones; by that knowledge of the movements of the minds of others, he effects the welfare of all sentient beings.
By means of the knowledge of the recollection of past lives, he points out past karma—that karma which, having been performed, does not perish.
And by means of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows, he [understands] sentient beings.
He establishes them in the fruit of stream-entry,
he establishes them in the fruit of once-returning,
and he establishes them in the fruit of non-returning.
He establishes them in arhatship,
he establishes them in pratyekabodhi, and he establishes them in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

In this way, wherever sentient beings have the capacity for wholesome qualities, there he establishes them. It is in this manner, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom with a mind free from signs, fulfills the perfection of ethical discipline.
Subhūti said:
"How does one fulfill the perfection of patience regarding phenomena that are signless, effortless, unapprehendable, non-manifesting, and unconditioned?
The Blessed One replied:

In this regard, Subhūti, from the first production of the thought of awakening until the time he is seated at the seat of awakening, even if all sentient beings were to come and strike him with clods of earth, sticks, or blows, the bodhisattva mahāsattva must not allow even a single moment of agitation accompanied by mental disturbance; and in that situation, the bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice two types of patience.
There are two things that must be cultivated. Which two? That which is the patience toward all sentient beings regarding abuse, punishment, clods of earth, blows, and so forth;

and that which is the patience regarding non-arising phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) that must be produced. In this regard, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva is being abused, reviled, or struck with clods of earth, sticks, or weapons, he should reflect thus: "Who is abusing me?"

Or reviles them, or strikes them with clods, sticks, or weapons—one should, by that very act, contemplate the intrinsic nature of phenomena (*dharmasvabhāva*). While contemplating the intrinsic nature of phenomena, one does not perceive even the phenomena themselves; how much less, then, the intrinsic nature of phenomena? As he thus contemplates the intrinsic nature of phenomena, it occurs to him:

"Who cuts me, or who breaks me? Examining in this way, he attains the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) regarding the intrinsic nature of phenomena. In that regard, what is patient acceptance toward the non-arising of phenomena? It is the state of being uncuttable by the knowledge of the non-arising of afflictions. Endowed with these two types of patience, he fulfills the four meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*).

He fulfills the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of miraculous power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path, the three gateways to liberation, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
abiding here in these noble, untainted, supramundane dharmas, which are common to all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
He fulfills the supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), and by means of these fulfilled supernormal knowledges and the six perfections (*pāramitā*), he fully attains them.

Abiding here in these supernormal knowledges, with his divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*) he beholds those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, in the eastern direction; having seen them, he attains the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*).
That recollection of the Buddha shall not be interrupted for him until he awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

In this way, having seen the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, in the southern direction, the western, the northern, above, below, and in the intermediate directions, he attains the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*);
that recollection of the Buddha shall not be interrupted until he awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi*).

With the divine ear-element, purified and surpassing that of humans, he will grasp everything that those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, shall speak; having grasped it, he will teach the Dharma to sentient beings in accordance with suchness.
And he will know with his own mind the mental deliberations of those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, as well as those of all noble ones—of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

When he will know the mental deliberations of all sentient beings with his own mind, he— having known the mental states of sentient beings with his own mind through that knowledge of the course of minds— will teach the Dharma for the sake of suchness.

Through his knowledge of the recollection of past abodes, having known the roots of merit of those sentient beings, he will demonstrate, inspire, and encourage them by means of those former roots of merit.

With the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna*), he will lead those beings into the three vehicles and establish them therein. Furthermore, that bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) through skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*), matures sentient beings, purifies the buddha-field, and, while practicing for the sake of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), [attains] the knowledge of all aspects.
Having fulfilled [the perfections], he will realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening and turn the wheel of Dharma.
In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom fulfills the perfection of patience.
Subhūti said:

“Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing in the perfection of wisdom, fulfill the perfection of vigor while [dwelling] in the signless, the untainted, the effortless, the non-apprehensible, and the non-manifest? The Blessed One said:
In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, endowed with physical vigor, attains and dwells in the first dhyāna;
he attains and dwells in the second, third, and fourth dhyānas.
Having entered the fourth dhyāna, he experiences manifold kinds of supernatural power (ṛddhi).

As long as he touches and strokes the sun and moon with his hand, being endowed with such physical vigor, he goes by means of his supernatural power to the worlds in the ten directions where the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, reside and teach the Dharma to sentient beings;
having gone to hundreds of thousands of world-systems, he attends upon those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, with robes, alms-food, bedding, seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
His robes and alms-food will not be exhausted until he awakens to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment;
and once he has awakened to enlightenment, the world with its gods, humans, and asuras shall become happy;
and even after he has entered final nirvana, worship of his physical remains shall continue through the offering of robes and alms-food.
By that very same miraculous power, having gone there, he hears the Dharma from those Blessed Buddhas,
and it never fails him until he awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
He brings sentient beings to maturity and purifies the Buddha-field;

while coursing in the knowledge of all aspects, he fulfills the knowledge of all aspects, and having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, he will turn the wheel of Dharma. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva [proceeds].
Practicing the perfection of wisdom, endowed with physical vigor, he fulfills the perfection of vigor.

And how, Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, endowed with mental vigor that is noble, untainted, a factor of the path, and included within the path, fulfill the perfection of vigor? Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva...
Practicing in the perfection of wisdom, endowed with mental vigor, he allows no opportunity for unwholesome bodily action,
nor does he allow an opportunity for unwholesome vocal action or unwholesome mental action;
he does not grasp at them as "permanent" or "impermanent," nor as "pleasure" or "suffering," nor as "self" or "non-self."
or as conditioned or unconditioned; or as the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm;
or as the realm with outflows or the realm without outflows;
or as the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, or the fourth dhyāna; or as loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, or equanimity; or as the sphere of infinite space.
or the sphere of infinite consciousness, or the sphere of nothingness, or the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;

or the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, or the noble eightfold path; or emptiness, signlessness, or wishlessness;
or the noble truths, the superknowledges, or the liberations.

Nor does he grasp at the nine successive meditative attainments, or the concentrations, or the gateways of mnemonic formulas, or the powers of a Tathāgata, or the grounds of self-confidence, or the analytical knowledges, or the unique qualities of a Buddha— whether as permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, peaceful or unpeaceful;
nor does he grasp at the fruit of stream-entry, or the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning, or arhatship, or even individual enlightenment.

He does not grasp at unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, nor a stream-enterer, a once-returner, a non-returner, an arhat, a pratyekabuddha, a bodhisattva, or a Buddha, the Blessed One; he perceives that these beings are distinguished by the stage of vision.
"These beings are characterized by the stage of the body; these are characterized by the lower portion;

these are characterized by the higher portion; these are characterized by omniscience; these are characterized by the knowledge of the path; these are characterized by the knowledge of all aspects"—even in this way, he does not grasp at them.
For such is the case because their intrinsic nature does not exist.
By whatever intrinsic nature they might be manifested,

being endowed with that mental vigor, even while abiding in the happiness of death, he acts for the benefit of sentient beings; yet he does not apprehend those sentient beings, he fulfills the perfection of vigor,
and he does not apprehend that perfection of vigor.
He fulfills the qualities of a Buddha,
yet he does not apprehend those qualities of a Buddha;
he purifies the Buddha-field, yet...
And he does not apprehend that buddha-field;
endowed with that physical and mental vigor, he grasps those wholesome qualities and yet does not become attached to them.
Moving unhindered from buddha-field to buddha-field and from world-system to world-system, he works for the benefit of sentient beings;
while working for the benefit of sentient beings, he performs whatever miraculous manifestation he desires by means of whichever miraculous power.

Whether by means of a rain of flowers, or by the emission of fragrance, or by the accompaniment of song, or by an earthquake, or by the manifestation of world-systems consisting of the seven precious gems, or by manifesting himself for the sake of sentient beings made of luminous jewels, or by emitting fragrance, or by performing a great sacrifice—
Wherein no taking of life occurs, or where one leads infinite sentient beings onto the path, even to the extent of liberating them from the taking of life.
He liberates them from taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, slanderous speech, harsh speech, frivolous chatter, covetousness, malice, and wrong view; he favors some with gifts,
others with moral discipline, and for the sake of some, he relinquishes his major and minor limbs.
For some he bestows favor through his son and wife; for others he offers himself as a noble gift; in this way, by whatever means the welfare of sentient beings must be accomplished, [he acts].
By those various means he acts for the benefit of sentient beings;
in this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom, endowed with mental vigor regarding signless phenomena, fulfills the perfection of vigor.
Subhūti said:
"And how, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, abide in signless phenomena and fulfill the perfection of meditation?
The Blessed One said:
"In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom fulfills all meditative absorptions, with the exception of the Tathāgata-samādhi."

Secluded from sensual desires and secluded from evil, unwholesome states, he, with directed thought and evaluation, attains and dwells in the first dhyāna, which is born of seclusion and possesses rapture and pleasure; he attains and dwells in the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, and the fourth dhyāna.

With a mind accompanied by loving-kindness, a mind accompanied by compassion, a mind accompanied by sympathetic joy, and a mind accompanied by equanimity, he dwells having pervaded the entire world-system;
he dwells having attained the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Abiding there in the perfection of meditation, he dwells having attained the eight liberations in forward and reverse order.
He dwells having attained the nine successive meditative attainments;
he dwells having attained the concentration on emptiness;
he dwells having attained the signless concentration and the wishless concentration.
He dwells having attained even the uninterrupted concentrations; he dwells having attained the concentration resembling lightning;
and he dwells having attained right and perfect enlightenment and the diamond-like concentration.
Having attained the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening, he dwells therein;

established in the perfection of meditative concentration, he attains and dwells in the knowledge of all aspects, by means of which knowledge of all aspects [he realizes] that all meditative concentrations are like space.
Having established the stage of pure vision and transcended the stage of the spiritual lineage, the stage of the eighth, the stage of refinement, the stage of vision,

the stage of freedom from passion, the stage of one who has completed what was to be done, the stage of the śrāvaka, and the stage of the pratyekabuddha, he enters the fixed course of a bodhisattva and fulfills the stage of a buddha.
He courses in these stages,
yet he does not attain the fruit of meditative concentration in the interim until he reaches the knowledge of all aspects.
Abiding here in this perfection of meditation, he travels from buddha-field to buddha-field,
attending upon the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones; he attends upon those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, plants roots of merit in the presence of those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and purifies a buddha-field.
He passes from world-system to world-system,
performing the welfare of sentient beings;
therein, he [benefits] some...
He gathers some beings through generosity, some through ethical discipline, some through patience, some through diligence,
some through meditative concentration, and some through wisdom.

He establishes some in liberation, some in the knowledge and vision of liberation; he establishes some in the fruit of stream-entry, some in the fruit of once-returning, some in the fruit of non-returning, and some in arhatship; he establishes some in pratyekabuddha-enlightenment and some in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

By whatever wholesome dharmas sentient beings emerge, he establishes those sentient beings therein; remaining here in this perfection of meditation, he brings forth all the gateways of samādhi, attains the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), and becomes a possessor of the superknowledges born of maturation (*vipākaja*). He is never again reborn in a mother’s womb.
He never indulges in sensual desires; there is no rebirth that he does not take on, yet he is never defiled by the faults of birth. Why is that?

Because he has seen all phenomena as like an illusion and has fully awakened to them. Having understood that the entire range of conditioned formations is like an illusion, he embraces great compassion and acts for the benefit of all sentient beings.
And therein he does not perceive beings or the designation "being.
Not perceiving beings or the designation "being," he establishes beings in the very non-perception of all phenomena,
by resorting to worldly convention, yet not by way of ultimate truth in this perfection of meditation.

Abiding in all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), samādhis, and attainments (*samāpatti*), he courses [in them] and is never deprived of the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*) until he awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi*).
Coursing here in this omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), he brings omniscience to fulfillment.
Abiding therein, one abandons the continuity of all latent predispositions (*vāsanā*).
Having abandoned the continuity of all latent predispositions and accomplished one’s own welfare, one accomplishes the welfare of others.
While accomplishing the welfare of both oneself and others, one becomes worthy of offerings (*dakṣiṇīya*) by the world with its gods, humans, and asuras. Thus...
Indeed, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom fulfills the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*) regarding signless phenomena.

Thus, by means of any one of the [perfections] beginning with generosity, this first momentary realization (*ekacittakṣaṇābhisamaya*) is characterized by the inclusion of all the undefiled (*anāsrava*) factors within a single characteristic.
Subhūti said:
"Lord, how does the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom reach fulfillment for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom regarding signless phenomena?
The Blessed One said:
In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom does not perceive any dharma as truly existent or as fully accomplished.
He perceives the non-existence and the lack of full accomplishment of form;
he perceives the non-existence and the lack of full accomplishment of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
He does not perceive the arising of form;
he does not perceive the arising of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
Not perceiving the arising of form, and not perceiving the arising of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, he does not perceive the gateway for the arrival of form.
He does not perceive even an accumulation;
likewise, he does not perceive an entrance for the arising of any phenomena, whether they be with outflows or without outflows,
but perceives them as truly empty.

Contemplating in this way, he does not perceive the intrinsic nature of form, nor does he perceive the intrinsic nature of any phenomena, whether they be with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*).
Practicing in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), he resolves that all phenomena have non-existence as their intrinsic nature.

Having thus resolved, while practicing in internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*), external emptiness (*bahirdhā-śūnyatā*), and so on up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence (*abhāvasvabhāva-śūnyatā*), he does not adhere to any phenomena whatsoever.
Whether in form, or feeling, or perception, or mental formations, or consciousness; or in the aggregates, elements, sense bases, or dependent origination;

or in the factors of dependent origination; or in the perfections, or the emptinesses, or the factors conducive to awakening; or in the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the liberations, the meditative absorptions, the meditative attainments, or the doors of dhāraṇī.

He does not become attached to emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, or the unique qualities of a Buddha, nor to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Practicing the perfection of wisdom, which has non-existence as its intrinsic nature, he fulfills the path to awakening;

that is to say, the six perfections up to the thirty-seven factors of awakening, the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the liberations, the meditative absorptions, the meditative attainments, the doors of dhāraṇī, the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha.
He fulfills everything from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, as well as the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary characteristics.

Abiding on the path of a bodhisattva consisting of dharmas born of maturation, when the six perfections are fulfilled, and likewise when the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are fulfilled, and finally when he stands in the five superknowledges born of maturation, those beings who are to be assisted by means of giving [are so assisted].
He favors them with generosity;

those who are to be favored by ethical discipline, those by meditative concentration, those by wisdom, those by liberation, and those by the knowledge and vision of liberation—he favors them with those.
Those who are to be established in the fruit of stream-entry, those in the fruit of once-returning, those in the fruit of non-returning, and those in arhatship—he establishes them therein.

Those who are to be established in individual enlightenment and those who are to be established in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, he establishes them in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
in this manner, it should be applied in detail. Performing various kinds of miraculous powers, he does not go to world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges.
Desiring those world-systems, he miraculously creates them with whatever kinds of jewels he desires; fulfilling the intentions of sentient beings, he travels through those world-systems,
and having seen them, he takes hold of a buddha-field as his own.

It was just as, for example, the enjoyments and luxuries of the gods who wield power over the creations of others; even in other world-systems that were free from evil, such were the enjoyments and luxuries they possessed— [all] by virtue of that perfection of generosity, perfection of ethical discipline, perfection of patience, and perfection of vigor born of karmic maturation.
By means of the perfection of meditation and the perfection of wisdom, through superknowledges born of maturation and the path of a bodhisattva born of maturation,

while practicing in the knowledge of paths, he will attain all the perfections and subsequently realize the knowledge of all aspects; for all form is indeed ungrasped, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are ungrasped.

To whatever extent all phenomena— whether wholesome or unwholesome, worldly or supramundane, with outflows or without outflows, conditioned or unconditioned, blameworthy or blameless— are unappropriated, therefore, Subhūti, for one who has fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, every enjoyment in that buddha-field will be unappropriated. Why is that?

For all dharmas are ungraspable by way of non-apprehension. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom through the yoga of signlessness [realizes] the perfection of wisdom.
