consciousness itself is the dharma-realm, and the dharma-realm itself is consciousness.
"Just as it was done in the middle chapter, so should all dharmas be understood.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
"So it is, Subhūti; so it is, just as you say."
Form itself is the dharma-realm, and the dharma-realm itself is form;
likewise, feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness itself are the dharma-realm, and the dharma-realm itself is consciousness.

Furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, were to perceive any phenomenon as being separate from the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), he would not be established for the sake of awakening to unsurpassed,
perfect, and complete enlightenment within the perfection of wisdom. Thus, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in this way [realizes] the realm of phenomena of all phenomena.
He understands them as they truly are;

therefore, the bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing in the perfection of wisdom, having realized that all phenomena are indeed the dharma-realm, teaches all phenomena through names and conventions from that which is nameless, saying: "This is form; these are feeling, perception, and mental formations."
This is consciousness; these are the aggregates, elements, sense bases, and dependent originations—both the dependent originations themselves and the factors of dependent origination;
these are the perfections;
and these are the gateways to emptiness.
These are the factors conducive to awakening;

these are the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the liberations, the meditative absorptions, the meditative attainments, and the gateways of the dhāraṇīs;
these are emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
These are the superknowledges;
these are the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha;
this is unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Thus is the activity of establishing the knowledge of affliction and purification.

Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, a skilled illusionist or an apprentice of an illusionist, having empowered some material substance, were to display various forms— either the body of a woman, the body of a man, the body of an elephant, the body of a horse, or the body of an ox.
Whether it be gardens or cities, delightful groves, delightful rivers, or delightful lotus ponds,
he would display there various kinds of rugs and coverlets;
he would show clusters of flowers, incense, perfumes, and garlands, as well as food for chewing and food for eating, and would delight the people with great singing and instrumental music.

Whether giving a gift, guarding ethical discipline, cultivating patience, exerting vigor, entering meditative absorption, or developing wisdom— he, by means of these modes, might manifest there great kṣatriya families,
or great brahmin families, or great householder families; or he might manifest the gods belonging to the retinue of the Four Great Kings.
He might show Mount Sumeru, or he might show the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods,

the Brahmā’s Retinue gods, the Brahmā’s Ministers gods, the Great Brahmās, the Limited Radiance gods, the Immeasurable Radiance gods, the Utmost Radiance gods, the Limited Purity gods, the Immeasurable Purity gods, the All-pervading Purity gods, the Cloudless gods, the Merit-born gods, the Vast Fruit gods, the Pure Abodes, the Untroubled gods, and so forth.
He might show him the Ātapa, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, or Akaniṣṭha gods;

or he might show him the gods of the Sphere of Infinite Space, the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, the Sphere of Nothingness, or the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception; or he might show him form-possessing Stream-enterers, Once-returners, Non-returners, Arhats, or Pratyekabuddhas; or those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who, from the first production of the thought of awakening, [have practiced] in the perfection of generosity...
They practice the perfection of ethical discipline,
they practice the perfection of patience,
and they practice the perfection of vigor.
They practice the perfection of meditative concentration, they practice the perfection of wisdom, and so on, up to practicing in the tenth stage.
They enter the fixed course of the bodhisattvas,
they bring forth the superknowledges,
they sport with them, and they bring sentient beings to maturity.
They purify the buddha-field, sport with the meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments,
and bring to fulfillment the powers of a Tathāgata.

He should also manifest those who are accomplishing the grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*), the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*), or great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*);
or he should manifest the form of a Buddha complete in all its major and minor limbs. Therein, ordinary foolish beings (*bālapṛthagjana*) would perceive it thus:

"Aha! How well-trained indeed is this man; he acts with such beauty, namely, that he delights people in this way and displays various forms, even up to the form of a Buddha in detail. Now, those among the people there who were wise, intelligent, and skillful, and who possessed such analytical investigation, thought to themselves:
This is a marvel, a wonderful phenomenon: no phenomenon whatsoever is apprehended here,
yet this man delights this country in phenomena that do not exist in such a way.

And that knowledge of his is this: that people perceive a notion of substantiality regarding this very non-substantiality. In the same way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive anything as being separate from the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) while practicing the perfection of wisdom through skillful means.
He perceives neither a sentient being nor the designation "sentient being.
Thus, performing the deed of establishing beings in the true nature of reality, he himself gives gifts and encourages others to give.
He speaks in praise of giving,
and he is one who commends and approves of others who also give gifts.
He himself maintains ethical discipline, establishes others in ethical discipline, and speaks in praise of ethical discipline.
Furthermore, those others who guard their ethical discipline, he speaks in praise of them and approves of them.
He himself accomplishes patience and encourages others to apply themselves to patience.
He speaks in praise of patience,
and he also commends and approves of others who cultivate patience.
He himself exerts vigor and encourages others to exert vigor;
he speaks in praise of vigor,
and for those others who also exert vigor, he becomes a speaker of their praise and one who approves of them.
He himself enters into meditative absorption,
establishes others in meditative absorption,
and speaks in praise of meditative absorption.
Furthermore, he speaks in praise of and approves of others who enter into meditative absorption;
he himself cultivates wisdom and also encourages others to apply themselves to wisdom.
He speaks in praise of wisdom,
and he is one who speaks in praise of and approves of others who also cultivate wisdom.
This is the activity of establishing [beings] in the six perfections.
He himself undertakes and abides in the ten paths of wholesome action, encourages others to undertake the ten paths of wholesome action,
and speaks in praise of the ten paths of wholesome action.
Furthermore, he adopts and abides by the other ten paths of wholesome action, speaks in praise of them, and approves of them;
he himself undertakes the five precepts of training, and he encourages others to undertake the five precepts of training.

He speaks in praise of the five precepts; he is one who speaks in praise of and approves of others who abide in the undertaking of the five precepts. And he himself observes the *poṣadha* endowed with the eight limbs of the noble ones.
He encourages others to undertake the *poṣadha* endowed with the eightfold noble limbs and speaks in praise of the *poṣadha* endowed with the eightfold noble limbs;
he also commends and approves of others who observe the *poṣadha* endowed with the eightfold noble limbs.

Furthermore, he himself enters into the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the formless attainments (*ārūpya*), the liberations (*vimokṣa*), the meditative absorptions (*samādhi*), the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), and the gateways of the dhāraṇīs.

He encourages others in the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the liberations, the meditative absorptions, the meditative attainments, and the gateways of the dhāraṇīs; he speaks in praise of the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the liberations, the meditative absorptions, the meditative attainments, and the gateways of the dhāraṇīs, and he approves of those others who likewise enter into the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the liberations, the meditative absorptions, the meditative attainments, and the gateways of the dhāraṇīs.
Furthermore, he himself cultivates the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment.
He also establishes others in the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening,
speaks in praise of the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening,
and is one who commends and approves of others who likewise engage in the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening.
He himself cultivates emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness,
he encourages others to apply themselves to emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness,
and he speaks in praise of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
He speaks [of them], and he also praises and approves of others who cultivate emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
He himself cultivates the four noble truths and establishes others in the four noble truths.
He speaks in praise of the four noble truths,
and he is one who commends and approves of others who cultivate the four noble truths.
He himself accomplishes the five superknowledges.
He encourages others to attain the five superknowledges,
speaks in praise of the five superknowledges,
and is one who commends and approves of others who also accomplish the five superknowledges.

He himself cultivates the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; he establishes others in the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; and he speaks in praise of the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Furthermore, he praises and approves of others who cultivate the other qualities of a Buddha— the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique buddha-dharmas—
and he himself cultivates great compassion.
He encourages others toward great compassion,
proclaims the praise of great compassion,
and speaks in praise of and approves of those others who cultivate great compassion.
He himself accomplishes the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary characteristics,
he encourages others toward the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary characteristics,
and he speaks in praise of the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary characteristics.
Furthermore, he speaks in praise of and approves of others who accomplish the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor characteristics.
This is the activity of establishing [beings] on the path of the Buddha.

Subhūti, if the dharma-realm were not such that it is the same in the beginning, the same in the end, and the same in the middle, then a bodhisattva mahāsattva would not purify the dharma-realm through skill in means.
Nor would he bring sentient beings to maturity. For this reason, Subhūti, because the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) is exactly the same before,
after, and in the middle, therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom engages in the conduct of a bodhisattva for the sake of sentient beings.
Subhūti said:

"If, Blessed One, a sentient being is ultimately not apprehended, nor even the designation 'sentient being,' for whose sake does a bodhisattva mahāsattva course in the perfection of wisdom? When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
Subhūti, it is by taking the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) as his standard that a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti, if the limit of reality were one thing and the limit of sentient beings (*sattvakoṭi*) another, then a bodhisattva mahāsattva would not course in the perfection of wisdom.

But since, Subhūti, the limit of reality is not one thing and the limit of sentient beings another, therefore a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom for the sake of sentient beings.
"Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in the perfection of wisdom, he establishes beings in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) without disturbing the limit of reality.
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Blessed One, if the limit of reality is the limit of beings (*sattvakoṭi*),"
But further, Blessed One, could the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) be established within the limit of reality?
If, Blessed One, the limit of reality were established within the limit of reality, then intrinsic nature (svabhāva) would be established within this intrinsic nature.
"Moreover, Blessed One, intrinsic nature does not abide within this intrinsic nature;
how then, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva establish beings in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi)?
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
Subhūti, the limit of reality does not abide within the limit of reality,
nor does intrinsic nature abide within this intrinsic nature;
nevertheless, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom establishes sentient beings in the limit of reality through skill in means.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) is not one thing and the limit of sentient beings (*sattvakoṭi*) another; for the limit of reality and the limit of sentient beings are non-dual and indivisible.
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Blessed One, what is the skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*) of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, by which skill in means they are endowed?"
"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he establishes beings at the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) and yet does not disturb the limit of reality?
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:

In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, from the first production of the thought of awakening, establishes beings in generosity. Having established them in generosity, he explains to them the prior limit and the subsequent limit of that generosity: "Just as that generosity is empty of a prior limit, empty of a subsequent limit, and empty of a middle, so too is the fruit of that generosity empty."
The gift is empty, the donor is empty,
and the giver is also empty of the intrinsic nature of a giver.
The recipient, too, is empty of the intrinsic nature of a recipient.
Thus, noble son, all these phenomena do not exist within the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*);
do not think that there is any other gift.
You will conceive of the donor as one thing, the fruit of the gift as another, and the recipient as yet another.
you will regard it as another limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*),
since you, noble son, will not regard the gift as something other [than that limit], nor will you regard the donor as something other [than that limit].
You shall not conceive of the fruit of giving as something else, you shall not conceive of the recipient as something else,
and you shall not conceive of the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) as something else.
Then this gift of yours will bring about immortality, have immortality as its fruit, and culminate in immortality;
and by means of this gift, you shall not grasp at form, nor feeling, nor perception, nor mental formations.
Do not grasp at consciousness. Why is that?
Because this gift of yours is empty of the intrinsic nature of a gift, and the fruit is also empty of the intrinsic nature of a fruit.
The recipient as well is empty of the intrinsic nature of a recipient;
and within emptiness, neither the gift nor the fruit of the gift is perceived.
No recipient is apprehended. Why is that?
Because, in this way, all these phenomena are ultimately empty of intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom establishes beings in ethical discipline through skill in means.
"Come, son of good family, having abandoned the taking of life, abstain from the taking of life; likewise,

having abandoned taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, slanderous speech, harsh speech, idle chatter, covetousness, and malice— come, son of good family, having abandoned wrong view, abstain from wrong view."
"Noble son, no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) exists in these phenomena as you have conceptualized it. Therefore, noble son, examine their intrinsic nature:
what is this phenomenon called 'life' that is deprived of its vitality, or what is that by which it is deprived?
Likewise, [examine] taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, slander, harsh speech, idle chatter, covetousness, and malice."
"What is this phenomenon called 'wrong view,' or who is it that views wrongly?

Subhūti, it is by being endowed with such skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*) that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), brings sentient beings to maturity; yet he does not desire the fruit of that giving or of that morality.
Furthermore, that fruit of giving and fruit of ethical discipline are empty of intrinsic nature;
therefore, having understood that the fruit of giving and the fruit of ethical discipline are empty of intrinsic nature, that son of good family does not become attached to them.
Not becoming attached, he gives rise to non-distraction and produces wisdom.

By means of that wisdom, having severed all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and active obsessions (*paryutthāna*), one attains final nirvana (*parinirvāti*) in the realm of nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*). This is according to worldly convention (*lokavyavahāra*), but not in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*). Why is that?
Because within emptiness (*śūnyatā*), no phenomenon (*dharma*) is apprehended that could attain final nirvana, nor by which one would attain it;
rather, this very final nirvana is indeed absolute emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*).
Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees other beings, other persons, who are hungry and possess malevolent thoughts, he instructs and exhorts them thus:

"Come, son of good family, cultivate patience and be forbearing. Be brave, have a mind intent on giving, and be of a nature that endures. All these phenomena for which you feel malice are empty by their very nature; come now, examine this!"
Noble son, where am I to be provoked to anger? Or who is provoked to anger? Or toward what is one provoked to anger?
All these phenomena are empty by nature;
and that which is emptiness by nature is never not emptiness,
nor is it created by the Tathāgatas.

It was not by Pratyekabuddhas, nor by Śrāvakas, nor by Bodhisattvas, nor by gods, nor by Nāgas, nor by Yakṣas, nor by Gandharvas, nor by Asuras, nor by Garuḍas, nor by Kiṃnaras, nor by Mahoragas, nor by the four Great Kings,
nor by Śakra, the lord of the gods, nor by the divine son Yāma, nor by the divine son Tuṣita, nor by Nirmāṇarati.
Neither by the sons of gods of the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations, nor by the sons of gods of the Retinue of Brahmā, nor by the Ministers of Brahmā,

nor by the Great Brahmas, nor by those of Limited Light, nor by those of Immeasurable Light, nor by those of Radiant Purity, nor by those of Limited Beauty, nor by those of Immeasurable Beauty, nor by those of Universal Beauty, nor by those of Cloudless, nor by those of Merit-Born, nor by those of Vast Fruit, nor by those of the Pure Abodes, nor by those of No-Heat.

It was not made by the Sudṛśa gods, nor by the Sudarśana gods, nor by the Akaniṣṭha sons of the gods, nor by those in the sphere of infinite space, nor by those in the sphere of infinite consciousness, nor by those in the sphere of nothingness, nor by those in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Come now, noble son, examine this: where am I to become angry?
Or who is it that becomes angry?
Or toward whom could malice arise?
All these phenomena are empty by nature, and emptiness does not harbor malice toward anyone.
In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom [establishes] sentient beings in the emptiness of intrinsic nature.

This cause applies [beings] to this fruit; by applying them to the emptiness of intrinsic nature, it gradually demonstrates, inspires, settles, and establishes them in everything up to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Yet that is, moreover, according to worldly convention, not [in ultimate reality].
Furthermore, from the perspective of ultimate truth. For what reason?
Because in intrinsic emptiness there is nothing whatsoever that could attain, nothing by which one could attain, nor anything in which one could attain.
Subhūti, this is the limit of reality, namely intrinsic emptiness, wherein the bodhisattva mahāsattva [practices] the perfection of wisdom.
He acts for the sake of sentient beings, yet herein no sentient being is apprehended, nor is there any designation of a "sentient being. Why is that?
Because all phenomena are by nature devoid of a sentient being.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom and endowed with skillful means, seeing sentient beings who are deficient in vigor, [observes] both their physical and mental...
And he encourages [others] in vigor.
Noble son, in intrinsic emptiness there exists no sinking of any dharma whatsoever—neither that in which one might sink, nor that by which one might sink, nor he who might sink;
all these dharmas are empty by nature and do not transcend emptiness. Come now, [apply this] to both the physical and the mental!
And having generated vigor and cast off laziness, exert yourself in wholesome action—whether it be in generosity, or ethical discipline, or patience, or vigor, or meditative concentration, or wisdom;

or in the gateways of the meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, attainments, and dhāraṇīs; or in the applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of miraculous power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of awakening, and the path.

Whether it be in the emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; or in the noble truths; or in internal emptiness; or in external emptiness; or in internal-external emptiness; or up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature; or in the superknowledges; or in the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique buddha-dharmas; or in [the state of]...
"O son of good family, observe all these phenomena among all phenomena as being without obstruction by virtue of their emptiness of intrinsic characteristics;
for in phenomena that are unobstructed, there is no sinking whatsoever.
In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom encourages, introduces, and establishes beings in the emptiness of intrinsic nature."
And he establishes them in such a way that duality does not exist. Why is that?
Because the emptiness of intrinsic nature is non-dual and free from division;
for a non-dual phenomenon never falls into indolence anywhere.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, by means of the emptiness of intrinsic nature, introduces beings to vigor and instructs them:

"Come, son of good family, exert vigor! Whether it be in generosity, or in ethical discipline, or in patience, or in vigor, or in meditative concentration, or in wisdom; or whether it be in the applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of miraculous power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, or the path."
Whether it be regarding the gates of the liberations, concentrations, attainments, and dhāraṇīs; or the ten powers of a Tathāgata;

or the four grounds of self-confidence; or the four analytical knowledges; or great compassion; or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—do not attend to these dharmas as dual, nor as non-dual. Why is that?
For these phenomena are empty by nature; indeed, the emptiness of nature should not be mentally engaged as dualistic, nor as non-dual.
In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom and engaging in the conduct of a bodhisattva through skillful means brings sentient beings to maturity.
Having brought sentient beings to maturity, he gradually establishes them in the fruit of stream-entry.
He establishes them in the fruit of once-returning,

he establishes them in the fruit of non-returning, he establishes them in arhatship, he establishes them in pratyekabuddha-enlightenment, and he establishes them in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom acts for the benefit of sentient beings through skill in means; he introduces them specifically to the cultivation of meditative concentration, saying:
"Come, son of good family, cultivate meditative concentration and do not harbor perceptions of distraction. Why is that?
Because these phenomena are empty by nature, and within the emptiness of nature no phenomenon is found that is either distracted or one-pointed."

Abiding in this meditative concentration, whatever wholesome action you shall perform— whether by body, speech, or mind; whether you give gifts, or maintain ethical discipline, or cultivate patience, or exert vigor, or produce meditative concentration, or develop wisdom— [all that will be so].
Whether you will cultivate the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path;

or whether [you will cultivate] the doors of liberation, meditative concentrations, attainments, and dhāraṇīs; or whether [you will cultivate] the noble truths, the immeasurables, the dhyānas, the formless attainments, the meditative concentrations, and the absorptions; or whether [you will cultivate] the superknowledges; or whether [you will cultivate] the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the analytical knowledges.
Whether it be great loving-kindness, or great compassion, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, or the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, or the eighty minor marks, or the path of the śrāvaka,
or the path of the pratyekabuddha, or the path of the bodhisattva, or the path of the Buddha, or the fruit of stream-entry.

Whether it be the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning, or arhatship, or solitary enlightenment, or omniscience; whether you will bring sentient beings to maturity, or purify a buddha-field— [in all these, you must rely on skillful means].
For you who course in the emptiness of intrinsic nature, these wholesome qualities will manifest with little difficulty.
In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva coursing in the perfection of wisdom performs the welfare of sentient beings through skill in means;
from the first production of the thought of awakening, he has never been inactive.
Seeking what is wholesome and acting for the benefit of sentient beings, he constantly and continuously travels from buddhafield to buddhafield,
attending upon the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones;
and whatever Dharma he hears in the presence of those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones—

Even when he has passed away from that birth, he will never lose it until he has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment; and having attained the dhāraṇīs, his faculties will always and continuously remain unimpaired—
whether by the faculty of the body, the faculty of speech, or the faculty of the mind.
For what reason?

Because he constantly and continuously cultivates the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*); by means of this well-cultivated knowledge of all aspects, all paths become well-cultivated—whether it be the path of the śrāvaka, the path of the pratyekabuddha, or the path of the bodhisattva—and the superknowledges (*abhijñā*) of that bodhisattva mahāsattva become constantly and continuously beneficial to him.
They will exist through the principle of non-perishing;
established in those superknowledges born of maturation, he works for the benefit of sentient beings and does not fall away while wandering in the saṃsāra of the five destinies.
In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, remaining in essential emptiness, works for the benefit of sentient beings through skill in means.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, abiding in the emptiness of intrinsic nature, benefits sentient beings through skillful means.
Having well-cultivated that perfection of wisdom, he thus advises and instructs sentient beings:
"Come, noble son, whatever action you perform by way of body, speech, or mind, all of that..."
Dedicate these toward the attainment of the deathless; thus, all these phenomena will lead you to the attainment of the deathless and culminate in the deathless.
Furthermore, within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, there is no phenomenon whatsoever that could become attached or fall away. Why is that?
Because emptiness itself does not fall away.
And no one falls away from the emptiness of intrinsic nature. Why is that?
Because the emptiness of intrinsic nature is neither an entity nor a non-entity. How then could a non-entity fall away from a dharma that is a non-entity?
It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva [trains].
The Mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, instructs and exhorts sentient beings in this way;
while thus instructing and exhorting them, he was never inactive himself,
and he himself constantly and continuously abided in the ten paths of wholesome action.

He encourages others to undertake the ten paths of wholesome action, as well as the five precepts and the eightfold noble *upoṣadha*. He himself enters the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), and he encourages others to enter the meditative absorptions and the formless attainments. He himself dwells constantly and continuously in loving-kindness (*maitrī*), and he encourages others to dwell constantly and continuously in loving-kindness.
He himself dwells constantly and continuously in compassion, and he also encourages others to dwell constantly and continuously in compassion;
he himself dwells constantly and continuously in sympathetic joy,
and he also encourages others to dwell constantly and continuously in sympathetic joy.
They themselves dwell constantly and continuously in equanimity and also encourage others to dwell constantly and continuously in equanimity;

they themselves cultivate the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of awakening, and the path, and also encourage others in the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of awakening, and the path;
they themselves cultivate emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and also encourage others in emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
He himself trains in all the perfections and all the emptinesses, and he encourages others to take up all the emptinesses and all the perfections;

he himself trains in the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and he encourages others to take up the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;

he himself fulfills the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor marks, and he encourages others to achieve the perfection of the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor marks.
He himself produces the knowledge of the fruit of stream-entry and yet does not abide therein, and he establishes others in the fruit of stream-entry;
he himself produces the knowledge of the fruit of once-returning and yet does not abide therein, and he establishes others in the fruit of once-returning.

He himself produces the knowledge of the fruit of non-returning, yet he does not abide therein, and he establishes others in the fruit of non-returning; he himself produces the knowledge of arhatship, yet he does not abide therein, and he establishes others in arhatship;
he himself produces the knowledge of individual enlightenment, yet he does not abide therein, and he establishes others in individual enlightenment.

He himself generates the path toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and he instructs, exhorts, and establishes others in that same path. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, through skill in means never remains inactive.
Then, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
If, Blessed One, all phenomena are empty by nature, and within this emptiness of nature neither sentient beings,
nor dharma, nor non-dharma are apprehended,
how, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva become firmly established in the perfection of wisdom?
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
"So it is, Subhūti, so it is. It is just as you say: all phenomena are empty by nature, and within the emptiness of nature neither sentient beings, nor dharma, nor non-dharma are apprehended."
Furthermore, Subhūti, if all phenomena were not empty by nature, then a bodhisattva mahāsattva would not have set out toward the emptiness of nature,
nor, having thus awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, would he have taught the phenomenon that is empty by nature.
Subhūti, form is empty by nature.
Feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness are empty by nature; thus, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he teaches the Dharma that the five aggregates are empty by nature,
and he teaches the Dharma that the twelve sense bases and the eighteen elements are empty by nature.

He teaches the Dharma that the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path are empty by nature.

He teaches the Dharma that the three gates of liberation, the eight liberations, the nine successive meditative attainments, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, the thirty-two marks of a great man, and the eighty minor marks are all empty by nature.

He teaches the Dharma that the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, arhatship, pratyekabuddha-enlightenment, and the knowledge of all aspects— the abandonment of all afflictions along with their habitual tendencies— is natural emptiness (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*). Furthermore, Subhūti, if internal emptiness were not natural emptiness, then a bodhisattva mahāsattva would not teach the Dharma within natural emptiness.

In this way, if external emptiness, internal-external emptiness, and so on up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence were not empty by their very nature (*prakṛtiśūnya*), then the bodhisattva mahāsattva would not teach the Dharma within the emptiness of intrinsic nature;
nor would that emptiness of intrinsic nature perish, nor would it be immutable, nor would it ever depart. Why is that?
For it does not abide in a place, nor does it abide in a location, nor does it go anywhere, nor does it come from anywhere;
this is that stability of phenomena (*dharmasthititā*).

Wherein no accumulation or diminution, no increase or decrease, no arising or cessation, and no defilement or purification of any dharma whatsoever is perceived— this is the intrinsic nature of dharmas. Abiding in this, the bodhisattva mahāsattva sets out for the realization of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, yet he perceives no setting out of any dharma whatsoever.
All phenomena are non-proceeding;
this is the established nature of phenomena (*dharmasthititā*).

In this regard, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, seeing that all phenomena are empty by nature, he does not turn back from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment. That...
For what reason?
Because he does not perceive the obscuration of any dharma, nor does he perceive its lack of obscuration.

How then could one have doubt regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, wherein— in the emptiness of intrinsic nature— neither a sentient being is apprehended nor the designation of a sentient being, neither a self, nor a sentient being,
nor a living soul, nor a creature, nor a nourisher, nor a person, nor an individual, nor a human, nor a youth, nor an agent, nor an experiencer?
Neither a knower nor a seer is apprehended;

neither form, nor feeling, nor perception, nor mental formations, nor consciousness is apprehended; indeed, all phenomena are not apprehended as internal, nor as external, nor as both internal and external, up to and including the eighty minor marks, which are not apprehended.
Thus is the practice of entering into the emptiness of intrinsic nature.

Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, a monk, a nun, a layman, a laywoman, or a bodhisattva were to continuously teach the Dharma for a hundred thousand eons to a magically created being of a Tathāgata—
what do you think about that?
Subhūti, would those emanations be capable of attaining the fruit of stream-entry, or attaining the fruit of once-returning, or attaining the fruit of non-returning, or attaining arhatship?
"To attain pratyekabodhi; to attain unexcelled, perfect, complete enlightenment.
Subhūti said: "No, Blessed One. For what reason?"
For indeed, Blessed One, they have no objective basis.
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti, so it is."

Since all dharmas are without substance, who is that being whom a bodhisattva mahāsattva establishes and settles in the fruit of stream-entry, or the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning, or in arhatship,
or in pratyekabuddha-enlightenment, or in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
Apart from this, he establishes and settles one who has fallen into perverted perception within non-perversion;
and that which is perversion is itself non-perversion, for it is non-conceptual when based on the drying up of conceptual construction,
and where there is no conceptual construction, there is no perversion, nor is there a self, a sentient being, a living soul, a creature, or a person.
There is no person, no individual, no human being, no youth, no agent, no experiencer, no knower, and no seer;

therein there is no form, no sensation, no perception, no mental formations, and no consciousness; there are no aggregates, elements, sense bases, or dependent origination, nor the factors of dependent origination; therein there are no perfections, no gateways to emptiness, and no factors conducive to enlightenment.

Therein are not the noble truths, the immeasurables, the dhyānas, the formless attainments, the liberations, the meditative concentrations, the meditative absorptions, the gateways of dhāraṇī, or the superknowledges; there are not the emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
therein are not the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, or the unique qualities of a Buddha; nor is there therein unexcelled perfect enlightenment.

This is that intrinsic emptiness wherein the bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells while practicing the perfection of wisdom, and while practicing, he liberates those perverted beings from their perception of a "being."
In this way, he liberates [beings] from the perception of form and the perception of the formless;
in this way, he liberates them from the perception of all phenomena,
including even those untainted phenomena such as the four foundations of mindfulness and the four right efforts.

The four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path— even these do not belong to it, just as the ultimate truth does not; that is to say, the unconditioned, non-arising, non-manifestation, and non-existence— this is that emptiness of intrinsic nature.

This is that awakening of all the Blessed Buddhas, wherein there is no life-principle, no being, no nourisher, no person, no individual, no human, no youth, no agent, no experiencer, no knower, no seer; and wherein there is no form, no sensation, no perception, no mental formations, no consciousness; and no aggregates, elements, sense-bases, or dependent origination.

There are no factors of dependent origination, no perfections, no gateways to emptiness, no factors conducive to enlightenment, no noble truths, no immeasurables, meditative absorptions, formless attainments, liberations, concentrations, meditative equipoises, or gateways to the dhāraṇīs;

there are no [the three doors of] emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, no supernormal knowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, or the unique qualities of a Buddha;
there is no great compassion, no thirty-two marks of a great man, and no eighty minor marks—for indeed, the bodhisattva [is not these].

The great being, for the sake of the path, has set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; yet this is solely for the purpose of fully understanding intrinsic emptiness. That intrinsic emptiness is never at any time—whether before, after, or in the middle—not intrinsically empty.
Abiding in that perfection of intrinsic emptiness, the bodhisattva mahāsattva...

For the sake of liberating beings who possess the notion of a "being" from that very notion of a being, he courses in the knowledge of the paths; while coursing in that knowledge of the paths, he courses in all paths—namely, in the paths of the śrāvakas, the paths of the pratyekabuddhas, and the paths of the bodhisattvas.

Furthermore, Subhūti, that bodhisattva mahāsattva, having fulfilled all paths, having ripened sentient beings, and having purified a buddha-field, exercises mastery over the formative forces of his lifespan and [proceeds toward] unsurpassed...
One awakens to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment;
having awakened to that unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, one does not sever the lineage of the Buddhas,
namely, intrinsic emptiness.
This is that guide of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, namely, the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*).
Those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who existed in the past, for those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, this alone was the guide of the Buddhas, namely, the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
Those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who will exist in the future, for those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, this alone will be the guide of the Buddhas, namely, the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who currently reside, remain, and maintain themselves in the world-systems of the ten directions,

teaching the Dharma— even for those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, this very same guidance of a Buddha is suchness, namely, intrinsic emptiness; for apart from intrinsic emptiness, there is no manifestation in the world.

In the presence of those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should likewise practice the perfection of the emptiness of intrinsic nature in such a way that, while practicing, he does not fall away from omniscience. Subhūti said:
It is marvelous, O Blessed One, this regarding the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, that they course in these phenomena which are empty by nature,

yet they do not disturb that emptiness of nature— [thinking] that form is one thing and the emptiness of nature another, or that feeling is another, perception is another, and mental formations are others.
Consciousness is one thing and the emptiness of intrinsic nature is another;
the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, dependent origination, and the factors of dependent origination are one thing, while the emptiness of intrinsic nature is another;
the perfections are one thing, the gateways to emptiness are another, and the factors conducive to awakening are one thing, while the emptiness of intrinsic nature is another.

The noble truths, the immeasurables, the dhyānas, the formless attainments, the liberations, the concentrations, the meditative absorptions, and the gateways of dhāraṇī are one thing, while intrinsic emptiness is another;

the emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and the superknowledges are one thing, while intrinsic emptiness is another; the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the specific understandings, and the unique qualities of a buddha are one thing, while intrinsic emptiness is another.
"Is unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening one thing, and intrinsic emptiness another?
Is intrinsic emptiness itself unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, and is unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening itself intrinsic emptiness?
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:

If, Subhūti, form were one thing and the emptiness of intrinsic nature another, or if feeling were one thing, perception another, formations another, and consciousness another, while the emptiness of intrinsic nature were yet another;
The aggregates, elements, and sense-fields, as well as dependent origination and the factors of dependent origination, are one thing; emptiness of intrinsic nature is another;
the perfections are another;
and the gateways to emptiness are another.
The factors conducive to enlightenment are one thing,

and the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, the formless attainments, the liberations, the concentrations, the doors of dhāraṇī, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the specific understandings, and the unique qualities of a buddha are another; and intrinsic emptiness is yet another.
Unsurpassed perfect enlightenment is one thing, and intrinsic emptiness is another.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva will not realize form in all-aspect omniscience;
a bodhisattva mahāsattva will not realize feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness in all-aspect omniscience. For this reason, Subhūti, form is intrinsically empty.
Feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness are empty by nature;
the aggregates, elements, sense bases, dependent origination, and the factors of dependent origination are empty by nature.

All the perfections, all the emptinesses, all the factors of enlightenment, all the concentrations, all the doors of dhāraṇī, all the liberations, all the meditative attainments, all the superknowledges, all the dhyānas, all the immeasurables, all the formless attainments, all the powers of the Tathāgatas, all the bodhisattva stages, and the four grounds of self-confidence.
The four analytical knowledges and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are emptiness by nature;
unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is emptiness by nature.
Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should fully awaken to form within omniscience.

One would fully awaken to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness within the knowledge of all aspects; one would fully awaken to everything up to awakening itself within the knowledge of all aspects. This is because, Subhūti, intrinsic emptiness itself is form, and form itself is intrinsic emptiness.
Feeling, perception, and mental formations are the emptiness of intrinsic nature;
consciousness itself is the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of intrinsic nature is consciousness.
The emptiness of intrinsic nature is awakening, and awakening itself is the emptiness of intrinsic nature.

Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having understood that all phenomena are empty by nature, should set out to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Why is that?

Because therein no phenomenon whatsoever perishes, nor is it immutable, nor does it transmigrate; yet the world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, and this generation with its śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, including gods, humans, and asuras, do not know form as it truly is.
They do not understand feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as they really are.
Not understanding, they adhere to form;
they adhere to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Having adhered to them, they engage in the notions of "I" and "mine."
Adhering to the notions of "I" and "mine," they engage with internal and external entities;
adhering to them, they perceive them, and having perceived them, they grasp form as form, feeling as feeling, perception as perception, and mental formations as mental formations.

Those who grasp at consciousness as being consciousness are not liberated from birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, dejection, and despair; they are not liberated from the cycle of existence consisting of the five destinies.

In that regard, the bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of the emptiness of intrinsic nature, does not disturb form by thinking it is "empty" or "not empty"; nor does he disturb feeling, perception, mental formations,
or consciousness by thinking they are "empty" or "not empty."
In this way, [he trains in] all samādhis, all dhāraṇī-doors, and all liberations;

the noble truths, the immeasurables, the dhyānas, and the formless attainments; emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; the superknowledges; the ten bodhisattva stages, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
One does not disturb [the mind] by thinking "it is empty" or "it is not empty. Why is that?

For emptiness does not disturb this form, this feeling, this perception, these formations, this consciousness; nor does it disturb these aggregates, elements, sense bases, dependent origination, or these factors of dependent origination.

This is emptiness; these are the factors conducive to enlightenment; these are the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the liberations, the meditative absorptions, the meditative attainments, and the gateways of mnemonic formulas;

these are emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and the superknowledges; these are the ten powers, the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha; this is unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Subhūti, it is just as, for example, space does not disturb space.
Whether internal or external, internal space does not disturb external space,
nor does external space disturb internal space;
in the same way, Subhūti, form does not disturb emptiness.
And emptiness does not disturb form. Why is that?
Because it has no intrinsic nature (svabhāva) by which it could thus disturb [it], thinking, "This is empty; this is not empty.
In this way, the same should be applied in detail to all phenomena.
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:

"If, Blessed One, there is no differentiation among all phenomena, from where, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva set out to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment? For, Blessed One, enlightenment is not a duality."
"By practicing duality, it is not possible to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti; so it is."
Enlightenment does not belong to one who courses in duality, nor is enlightenment characterized by duality;
for, Subhūti, enlightenment is non-dual and free from duality.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not course toward enlightenment by means of duality.
Furthermore, the awakening of a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not course in form,
nor does it course in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
He does not course in the aggregates, elements, or sense-fields; he does not course in dependent origination;
he does not course in the factors of dependent origination;
nor does he course in dependently originated phenomena.

He does not course in the emptinesses; he does not course in the factors conducive to awakening; nor does he course in the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, the formless attainments, the liberations, the concentrations, the meditative equipoises, or the gateways to the dhāraṇīs.
He does not course in emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, or the superknowledges;
he does not course in the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, or the unique qualities of a Buddha;
he does not course in perfect enlightenment. Why is that?
For the expression "I am awakening" does not operate upon form, nor upon feeling, perception, or mental formations;
the expression "I am awakening" does not operate upon consciousness.

In this way, up until the point where there is no sound of "I am enlightenment" coursing in perfect complete enlightenment, nor does the perfect complete enlightenment of the bodhisattva mahāsattva course in grasping.
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:
“Blessed One, if the unexcelled, perfect enlightenment of a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not course in grasping, then where does the enlightenment of a bodhisattva mahāsattva course?
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Where does the cognition of a Tathāgata’s emanation operate—upon grasping or upon non-grasping?
Subhūti replied:
"No, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think?"
"Subhūti, when an Arhat has entered into a dream, where does his cognition operate—either in grasping or in non-grasping?
Subhūti replied: "No, Blessed One."
“Blessed One, since an arhat who has reached the ultimate does not sleep, how could consciousness function in a dream, whether toward grasping or non-grasping?
The Blessed One said:
“In just this way, Subhūti, the awakening of a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not function toward grasping or non-grasping.”

When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows: "If, Blessed One, the awakening of a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not proceed in grasping or non-grasping, nor does it proceed in form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;..."

It is not in the aggregates, elements, or sense-fields; nor in dependent origination, nor in the factors of dependent origination; nor in the perfections, nor in the emptinesses, nor in the factors conducive to awakening; nor in the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, the formless attainments, the liberations, the concentrations, the meditative equipoises, or the gateways of dhāraṇī;
nor in emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, or the superknowledges; nor in the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, or the unique qualities of a buddha.

He does not course in the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). How, then, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having coursed in the ten bodhisattva stages, in the six perfections, in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, in all the modes of emptiness, in the meditative concentrations,
in the immeasurables and the formless attainments, in the doors of liberation, in the nine successive attainments, and in the noble truths?
Abiding in the superknowledges, in emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, in the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha,

in great compassion, in the thirty-two marks of a great man, in the eighty minor marks, and in the five superknowledges, he enters the fixed course of a bodhisattva, purifies a buddha-field, and [matures] sentient beings.

And having brought [beings] to maturity, he will fully awaken to omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). Yet, Blessed One, it is not possible to do so without abiding in the ten bodhisattva stages, the six perfections, all the modes of emptiness, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the liberations, the meditative absorptions, the meditative attainments, and the doors of dhāraṇī;

nor without abiding in emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; nor without abiding in the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, the unique buddha-qualities, and great compassion.

"Without abiding in the five superknowledges, without entering the fixed course of a bodhisattva, and without purifying a buddhafield and ripening sentient beings, it is not possible to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti, so it is,
just as you say. It is not possible, without having fulfilled the ten bodhisattva stages, the ten perfections, all the emptinesses, and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment..."

Without having fully perfected the dharmas— the noble truths, the immeasurables, the dhyānas, the formless attainments, the liberations, the meditative concentrations, the meditative absorptions, the gateways of the dhāraṇīs, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, the thirty-two marks of a great man, and the eighty minor characteristics— one cannot [attain] unsurpassed...
Subhūti, having fulfilled [the path] in order to realize full and perfect awakening, one is then able [to fulfill] the ten stages, the ten perfections, all the emptinesses, the four dhyānas,
the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the four foundations of mindfulness, and so on, up to the noble eightfold path, as well as emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.

Having fulfilled the three gates of liberation, up to the eighty minor marks, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity, in order to attain the knowledge of all aspects— furthermore, Subhūti, this is by remaining in the intrinsic nature of form, as well as feeling, perception, and mental formations.

Abiding in the intrinsic nature of consciousness, and so on, up to abiding in the intrinsic nature of awakening— that intrinsic nature is quiescent; it effects neither the increase nor the decrease of any dharma, nor its arising or cessation, nor its annihilation or eternity, nor its affliction or purification, nor its attainment or realization.

Thus, Subhūti, regarding the activity of establishing the non-dual Dharma, it is indeed by relying on the phenomena of worldly convention and designation that a bodhisattva mahāsattva awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; yet herein, in the ultimate sense, there is nothing whatsoever— neither form, nor feeling, nor perception, nor mental formations.

Whether it be consciousness, or the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields, or dependent origination, or the factors of dependent origination, or the perfections, or emptiness, or the factors conducive to enlightenment, or the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, the formless attainments, the liberations, the concentrations, the meditative equipoises, the doors of dhāraṇī,
or the doors of liberation, or the superknowledges, or the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha.
Unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, or whoever would course toward unsurpassed perfect enlightenment—

all these phenomena are designated based upon worldly convention, but not in the ultimate sense. Furthermore, Subhūti, that bodhisattva mahāsattva, from the first production of the thought of awakening, courses toward awakening.
Furthermore, one does not perceive that mind, nor a sentient being, nor awakening.
What do you think, Subhūti, at the time when Subhūti abandoned the afflictions and attained the faculties?

When the immediate concentration has been attained, or the fruit of stream-entry has been reached, or the fruit of once-returning has been reached, or the fruit of non-returning has been reached, or arhatship has been reached— at that time, is a dream perceived, or the path of the mind, or the fruit of the path?
Subhūti said: "No, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"In that case, how did you, the Elder named Subhūti, designate that you have attained arhatship?
Subhūti replied:
"By relying upon worldly convention."

The Blessed One said: "So it is, Subhūti. It is by way of worldly convention that a bodhisattva is designated; it is by way of worldly convention that form is designated, and feeling, perception, and mental formations [are designated] by way of worldly convention."

Consciousness is designated by way of worldly convention; the aggregates, elements, sense bases, dependent origination, and the factors of dependent origination are also designated by way of worldly convention. All the perfections, all the emptinesses, all the factors conducive to enlightenment, the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the liberations, the meditative absorptions, the meditative equipoises, and the doors of the dhāraṇīs are designated by way of worldly convention.

Emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha are designated by way of worldly convention; omniscience is likewise designated.
Yet, by a bodhisattva mahāsattva, no dharma whatsoever has been apprehended in relation to perfect enlightenment.

One might effect an increase or decrease of the Dharma, or perform a benefit or harm; yet, taking the intrinsic nature of phenomena as the basis, even that intrinsic nature of phenomena is not apprehended—
how much less could one apprehend the first production of the thought of awakening?
He will apprehend the ten bodhisattva stages, the ten perfections, all the modes of emptiness,
the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening,

the concentrations of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, the formless attainments, the liberations, the concentrations, the meditative absorptions, the doors of dhāraṇī, the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a buddha.
As long as one perceives any phenomena, this is impossible;

it is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having practiced the six perfections and awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, acts for the benefit of sentient beings.
Thus is the activity of establishing conventional knowledge.
Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:

"If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva [practices] in all the perfections, in all the emptinesses, in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, in the ten powers of a Tathāgata, in the four grounds of self-confidence, and in the four analytical knowledges..."
While practicing in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha and purifying the path to enlightenment, one would be incapable of awakening to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
how then, Blessed One, will a bodhisattva mahāsattva awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, practices the perfection of giving through skill in means,
yet does not apprehend that gift,"
When he does not perceive a giver, a recipient, nor does he course in any phenomena other than these,
then the bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to course on the path to awakening.
In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva coursing in the perfection of wisdom will, through skill in means, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Thus, while practicing the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom, he does not apprehend wisdom;
nor does he apprehend that which would practice it, or that which is practiced, nor does he practice apart from these dharmas.
When this is so, the bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to persevere in practicing the path to enlightenment. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva...

The Mahāsattva, practicing in the perfection of wisdom through skill in means, will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; likewise, even while practicing in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, he does not perceive those Buddha-qualities,
nor does he perceive that which meditates or that which is being cultivated.
Nor does he course elsewhere than in these dharmas;
at that time, the bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to course on the path to enlightenment.
In this way, Subhūti, the bodhisattva mahāsattva will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment through skill in means within the perfection of wisdom.
Then the venerable Śāriputra said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, apply himself to the practice of giving?
When this was said, the Blessed One said this to the venerable Śāriputra:
In this regard, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not, through skill in means, join form nor disjoin it. Why is that?
Because form has no intrinsic nature that could either join or disjoin; and the same applies to feeling, perception, and mental formations.
Consciousness neither joins nor disjoins. Why is that?
Because consciousness has no intrinsic nature that could either join or disjoin.

Likewise, the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom neither join nor disjoin. Why is that?
For its intrinsic nature does not exist that which either joins together or disjoins;
likewise, the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields are not dependent origination, nor the factors of dependent origination, nor the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment,
nor internal emptiness, nor external emptiness, nor internal-external emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.

The immeasurables, the dhyānas, and the formless attainments do not join nor disjoin; the noble truths do not join nor disjoin; emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness do not join nor disjoin; the doors of liberation, concentrations, attainments, and dhāraṇīs do not join nor disjoin; and the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a buddha do not join nor disjoin. Why is that?
For indeed, there is no intrinsic nature of the Buddha-qualities that could either join them together or separate them.
Śāriputra said:
"If, Blessed One, no intrinsic nature of any dharma exists that could either join it together or separate it,"
How does the accomplishment of the perfection of wisdom come about, wherein a bodhisattva mahāsattva must train?
For without training in the perfection of wisdom, it is not possible for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Blessed One said: "So it is, Śāriputra, so it is;
just as you say, it is not possible for a bodhisattva mahāsattva, without having trained in the perfection of wisdom, to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
If, indeed, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom through skillful means perceives or grasps the intrinsic nature of any dharma,

then how could he not grasp this as "this is the perfection of wisdom," "this is the perfection of meditation," "this is the perfection of vigor," "this is the perfection of patience," "this is the perfection of ethical discipline," or "this is the perfection of generosity"?

This is form, this is feeling, this is perception, these are mental formations, this is consciousness; these are the aggregates, elements, sense bases, and dependent origination; these are the members of dependent origination; these are the perfections; these are the emptinesses; these are the factors of enlightenment; these are the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, the formless attainments, the liberations, the concentrations, the meditative equipoises, and the doors of dhāraṇī;
these are the emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and the superknowledges.

"These are the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha; this is unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment"—a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not apprehend these dharmas.
Why then would he grasp them, Śāriputra? For the perfection of wisdom is ungraspable.
The perfection of meditation is ungraspable;
the perfection of vigor is ungraspable;
the perfection of patience is ungraspable.
The perfection of ethical discipline is ungraspable;
the perfection of generosity is ungraspable;
all forms of emptiness are ungraspable.
The factors conducive to enlightenment are ungraspable;

the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the liberations, the samādhis, the meditative absorptions, and the gateways of the dhāraṇīs are ungraspable; emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and the superknowledges are ungraspable; the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a buddha are ungraspable.
Śāriputra, this perfection of wisdom is the perfection that is non-apprehendable, namely, the perfection of wisdom;

herein a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train. While training therein, the bodhisattva mahāsattva will not even find a training, let alone enlightenment, let alone the perfection of wisdom, let alone the qualities of a bodhisattva. Why is that?

Furthermore, from where would there be the qualities of a pratyekabuddha, from where the qualities of a śrāvaka, and from where the qualities of an ordinary person? For what reason? Because, Śāriputra, no dharma whatsoever has an intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
Thus, among all dharmas which have non-existence as their intrinsic nature, what is the quality of an ordinary person, and what is a stream-enterer?
Who is the once-returner, who is the non-returner, who is the arhat, who is the pratyekabuddha, who is the bodhisattva, and who is the perfectly awakened one?
If these persons are not apprehended, [how can they exist]?
"In that case, from where will these dharmas arise,

among which dharmas one is designated as an ordinary person, or a stream-enterer, or a once-returner, or a non-returner, or an arhat, or a pratyekabuddha, or a bodhisattva, or a perfectly awakened buddha? Śāriputra said:

“Blessed One, since all phenomena are without substance, from where does their coming forth become known— such that one says, ‘This is an ordinary person,’ ‘this is a stream-enterer,’ ‘this is a once-returner,’ ‘this is a non-returner,’ ‘this is an arhat,’ ‘this is a pratyekabuddha,’ ‘this is a bodhisattva,’ or ‘this is a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha’? When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Śāriputra:
"Śāriputra, does there exist any real entity in form— past or future— such as that upon which a foolish common person is fixated?
Śāriputra replied, "No, Blessed One."
“O Sugata, this is not so; rather, it is the ordinary person with a perverted mind who is attached to the notion that ‘form is [the self],' as well as to feeling, perception, and mental formations.
The Blessed One said:
"Śāriputra, does consciousness have any real entity, past or future, such as that in which a foolish worldling is attached?
Śāriputra replied: "No, Blessed One."
"This is not so, O Sugata; it is only the ordinary person with a perverted mind who is attached to the notion that there is consciousness.
The Blessed One said:
"But then, Śāriputra, does any real entity—past or future—exist for all phenomena in the way that the foolish ordinary person is attached?"
Śāriputra said: "No, Blessed One; this is not so, Sugata, except for the ordinary person with a perverted mind who is attached to the notion that 'all dharmas' exist.
The Blessed One said:

In the same way, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom, seeing through skillful means that all phenomena are without substance, sets out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
This is the activity of establishing the knowledge of non-apprehension.
When this had been said, the venerable Śāriputra addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Blessed One, what is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, seeing all phenomena as being without substance through skill in means, has set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
When this had been said, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Śāriputra as follows:

In this regard, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive the substantial entity of any dharma wherein he might encounter resistance; nor, encountering resistance therein, would he become attached, nor, becoming attached, would he sink or fall into indolence.
Therefore, Śāriputra, all dharmas are without substance, without life, devoid of a living soul, having non-existence as their intrinsic nature, and empty by their very essence.
Elsewhere, beings are attached due to delusion to the aggregates, or the elements, or the sense bases, or to dependent origination,

or to the factors of dependent origination; yet the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, practicing in the perfection of wisdom, perceives all phenomena as having the nature of non-existence, seeing them as empty by nature and empty of their own specific characteristics while practicing in the perfection of wisdom.
Having established himself as being like a magician, he teaches the Dharma to sentient beings;
for those beings who are stingy, he gives discourses on generosity,
and for those of immoral conduct, he gives discourses on ethical discipline.
He gives a discourse on patience to those with malicious minds, a discourse on vigor to those who are indolent,
and a discourse on meditation to those with distracted minds.
He gives discourse on wisdom to those of poor wisdom;
when those beings become established in generosity, and become established in ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
Then he delivers to those beings an instructive discourse that is noble and leads to liberation—
a discourse by which they attain the fruit of stream-entry,
the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and arhatship.
They attain individual enlightenment and they reach the knowledge of all aspects. Then, the venerable Śāriputra said this to the Blessed One:
"Bhagavān, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is characterized by apprehension urge beings— who do not exist— to practice generosity, to practice ethical discipline,
and to practice patience?"
He enjoins them to diligence,
enjoins them to meditative concentration,
and enjoins them to wisdom; furthermore, the teacher delivers a discourse that leads to definitive liberation.
By means of that discourse, they attain the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and arhatship;
they attain pratyekabuddhahood and reach the knowledge of all aspects.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Śāriputra:
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, there is no apprehension whatsoever. Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not apprehend any sentient being at all; he employs speech only by means of conventional designations."
Therefore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the two truths, teaches the Dharma to sentient beings.
For, Śāriputra, neither a sentient being nor the designation "sentient being" is apprehended through the two truths;
rather, it is by means of skillful means that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, teaches the Dharma to sentient beings.
Therefore, those beings do not perceive a self even in this very life,
let alone one who will cause [them] to attain [it], or that by which they will cause [them] to attain it.
"In this way, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom teaches the Dharma to sentient beings through skill in means.
When this had been said, the venerable Śāriputra addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"It is indeed a great marvel, O Blessed One, that this bodhisattva mahāsattva neither perceives the oneness, nor the manifoldness, nor the distinctness of any dharma whatsoever."
And he dons such armor that, having donned this armor, he is not seen in the realm of desire,
nor is he seen in the realm of form, nor is he seen in the formless realm.
It is not seen in the realm of conditioned phenomena, nor is it seen in the realm of the unconditioned;
yet it liberates sentient beings from the three realms.
Furthermore, one does not perceive a sentient being or the designation "sentient being.

Because there is no designation of a sentient being, there is neither bondage nor liberation for a sentient being; because there is neither bondage nor liberation, there is neither affliction nor purification; because there is neither affliction nor purification, no differentiation of realms of existence is discerned.
Due to the non-differentiation of realms of existence, there is neither karma nor affliction.
"How could there be a maturation for that which is non-action and non-affliction, by means of which maturation beings might be seen by themselves in the fivefold cycle of existence?
