When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Śāriputra:
"So it is, Śāriputra, so it is, just as you have spoken.
If there were first an existence of a sentient being and later a non-existence, then this fault would follow;
if the Bodhisattva and the Tathāgata likewise had first been existent and later became non-existent, then this fault would follow."
If the saṃsāra of the five destinies were to exist previously and then later cease to exist, then this fault would follow;

however, Śāriputra, whether Tathāgatas arise or whether Tathāgatas do not arise, this nature of phenomena remains constant—the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), the stability of phenomena (dharma-sthititā), and the fixed order of phenomena (dharma-niyāmatā).
In that regard, there is no self, no sentient being, no life-force, and no person.
There is no nourisher, no person, no individual, no human being, no youth, no agent, no experiencer, no knower, and no seer;
so how could there be form? How could there be feeling? How could there be perception? How could there be mental formations?
Whence will there be consciousness?

Whence will there be the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases? Whence will there be dependent origination? Whence will there be dependently originated phenomena? Whence will there be the members of dependent origination? Since these phenomena do not exist, whence will there be the saṃsāra of the five destinies?
Since, Śāriputra, these dharmas are thus empty of intrinsic nature— that is, since those sentient beings who are to be liberated [do not exist]—
therefore, having heard this from the presence of the former Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, the bodhisattva mahāsattva has set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

And herein there is no intrinsic nature of any dharma that one perceives, nor anything that can be the object of resolute conviction, other than the perversions in which foolish ordinary people are attached;
nevertheless, the bodhisattva mahāsattva dons the armor, and having donned that armor, he does not turn back from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
I must not fail to awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; indeed, I must awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
and having awakened, I shall accomplish the welfare of beings through the Dharma.
By whatever means I shall liberate sentient beings from their perversion—

just as, Śāriputra, a man created by a magician might manifest many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of living beings, and having manifested them, might satisfy them with abundant food, drink, and delicacies— so too [should it be understood].
Having thus satisfied them, he should utter this inspired utterance: "Great merit has been produced by me. What do you think, Śāriputra? Would anyone there have been fed or satisfied?
Śāriputra said:
"No, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"In this very way, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, from the first production of the thought of awakening, [practices] in the six perfections..."

Practicing in the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the formless attainments, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment,
the noble eightfold path, all the emptinesses, emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and in the nine doors of liberation...
Practicing within the five successive meditative attainments, the five superknowledges, all samādhis, all doors of dhāraṇī,

the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the ten bodhisattva stages, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, as well as great loving-kindness and great compassion, he fulfills the path to awakening and purifies the buddha-field.
He brings sentient beings to maturity, yet he does not apprehend any sentient being whom he might apprehend and then discipline.
This is the activity of establishing the maturation of sentient beings.
Then, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, what is the path to enlightenment of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon which a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing should bring sentient beings to maturity and purify a buddhafield?
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:

In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, from the first production of the thought of awakening onwards, while practicing the perfection of generosity, practicing the perfection of ethical discipline, practicing the perfection of patience, practicing the perfection of vigor, practicing the perfection of meditative concentration, and practicing the perfection of wisdom,

Practicing in internal emptiness, practicing in external emptiness, practicing in internal-external emptiness, up to practicing in the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence; practicing in the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path; practicing in the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the liberations, the meditative absorptions, the meditative attainments, and the gateways of dhāraṇī;
practicing in emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and the superknowledges; [and practicing] in the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a buddha.
While practicing, he brings sentient beings to maturity and purifies the buddha-field.
Subhūti asked: "Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of generosity, bring sentient beings to maturity?"
The Blessed One said:
"In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom gives gifts to sentient beings; having given the gift, he instructs them thus:
'O sons of good family, do not grasp at the gift as something to be clung to.'"
Do not, gripped by the grasping of giving, bring forth a personal existence through which, once brought forth, you will experience many sufferings;
for here, O sons of good family, in the ultimate sense, there is no gift, no giver, and no recipient.
All these three factors are empty;

for emptiness is ungraspable, and one does not grasp at phenomena that are empty by nature. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of generosity gives gifts to sentient beings, yet he does not perceive therein the gift, nor the giver, nor the recipient. This is the perfection of non-apprehension.
That is to say, the perfection of generosity: not perceiving the gift, the giver, or the recipient, he establishes beings in the fruit of stream-entry,
establishes them in the fruit of once-returning, and establishes them in the fruit of non-returning.
He establishes them in arhatship, he establishes them in pratyekabuddha awakening,

and he establishes them in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of generosity, brings sentient beings to maturity.
He gives gifts himself,
encourages others to give gifts,
speaks in praise of giving, and also [rejoices] in those others who give gifts.
And he speaks in praise of them and approves of them;
having given such a gift as this, the bodhisattva mahāsattva is reborn into the company of great kṣatriya clans or into the company of great brahmin clans.
He is reborn to share the vows with great wealthy householders, or he becomes a regional king, or he attains the sovereignty of a universal monarch.
There he gathers sentient beings by means of the four bases of sympathy;
by which four?
By generosity and by pleasant speech.

Through beneficial conduct and consistency of purpose, having thus gathered those beings through generosity, he gradually establishes them in ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom; [he establishes them] in the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the four foundations of mindfulness,
the four right efforts, the four bases of miraculous power, the five faculties, the five powers, and the seven factors of enlightenment.
He establishes them in the noble eightfold path,
leads them to enter the correct determination regarding emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness,
and causes them to attain the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and arhatship.
He causes them to attain individual enlightenment and inspires them toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, saying:
"O men, realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment!
For therein, not a single phenomenon exists by way of its own intrinsic nature."
Since sentient beings do not understand this due to their various misconceptions,
therefore you should not grasp at any misconceptions;
liberate yourselves from saṃsāra.

"And you will liberate others; in this way, you will accomplish a great purpose for yourselves and establish others in a great purpose. Subhūti, it is in this manner that a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the perfection of generosity."

Just as, by practicing from the first production of the thought of enlightenment onward, one never falls into an evil rebirth and never fails to exercise the sovereignty of a universal monarch— why is that?
For as is the seed, so is the fruit that results.
When beggars come to that universal monarch, it occurs to that king, the universal monarch:
"I have undertaken the fruit of a universal monarch for no other purpose than for the sake of sentient beings; therefore, let this be given to you."

Therefore, in this regard, I have no need for this sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch, much less for anything else; rather, I have taken up cyclic existence solely for the sake of sentient beings. Feeling compassion, he fulfills great compassion;
and having fulfilled great compassion, he acts for the benefit of sentient beings.
Yet those sentient beings who might be established as real are not to be apprehended; it is nothing other than a designation, a convention, and a worldly usage.

And that conventional discourse should be understood as being like an echo, devoid of verbal expression. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the perfection of generosity, such that while practicing, there is nothing whatsoever that he does not relinquish for the sake of sentient beings,
even unto his own flesh.
How much more so external requisites—those requisites by which sentient beings are to be liberated from saṃsāra;
what, then, are those requisites? Namely, the requisite of the perfection of generosity, and so forth.

The equipment for the perfection of ethical discipline, the equipment for the perfection of patience, the equipment for the perfection of vigor, the equipment for the perfection of meditative concentration, and the equipment for the perfection of wisdom;
the equipment for internal emptiness, the equipment for external emptiness,
the equipment for internal and external emptiness, up to the equipment for the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence.

The foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of miraculous power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path are the requisites; the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the liberations, the samādhis, the meditative absorptions, and the doors of dhāraṇī are the requisites; emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a buddha are the requisites—these are those requisites by which beings, being sustained by them, will be liberated from saṃsāra.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of generosity, while giving gifts to all, should speak these words:

"O noble sons, you must guard your ethical discipline; I shall provide for you without deficiency, whether with food or drink, clothing or bedding and seats, vehicles, or with gold, silver, gems, pearls, diamonds, lapis lazuli, conch shells, crystals, or coral."
Whether with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, or robes;
or with medicinal requisites for the sick; or with any other human necessities and utensils—by means of which you, being in want, commit immoral conduct.
Therefore, I shall provide for you without deficiency, whether with food and drink or with the seven precious gems;
whatever you desire, I will bring all of that to fulfillment.

Thus, remaining established in the morality of restraint, you shall gradually bring an end to suffering by means of the three vehicles—whether by the vehicle of the disciples, the vehicle of the solitary buddhas, or [the Great Vehicle].
Or by means of the Mahāyāna.
And how, Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of giving, establish beings in patience and gentleness?
Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, to those beings who are angry or who harbor malice, should speak these words:
"For what reason, sons of good family, are you harboring malice and giving rise to anger?
I shall provide you with everything;
whatever it is for the sake of which you are agitated and resentful, take that from me."

"By means of this, I shall provide for the Blessed Ones' lack of deficiency with food or drink, clothing or bedding and seats, flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, and powders; or with gold, fine gold, silver, conch-shells, crystals, and coral;
or with various precious gems, or with whatever other human requisites and appurtenances there may be."

By means of that through which you do not become angry or malicious—established in the perfection of generosity, the bodhisattva mahāsattva enjoins sentient beings to patience and gentleness, [teaching them]:
"In this regard, there is no entity whatsoever, no existing thing, by which anger would arise in you; it is merely an unreal conceptualization."
This is anger; there is no object whatsoever belonging to it for the sake of which you become attached, become angry, or harbor ill will.
Having become attached, having become angry, and having harbored ill will, you strike one another with sticks or weapons, or deprive one another of life.
Therefore, agitated by unreal imaginings, you will fall into hell, or into the animal realm, or into the world of Yama;
you will also experience painful sensations in whatever other destinies there may be.
O men, do not, for the sake of base and unsubstantial phenomena, undertake such actions that, once undertaken, you shall no longer obtain rebirth as a human being.

The appearance of a Buddha is difficult to encounter even more so than that. Indeed, O man, the appearance of a Buddha is difficult to encounter; the attainment of human birth is difficult to encounter; the perfection of the opportune moment is difficult to encounter. Do not let this moment pass you by in the midst of saṃsāra; do not fall into doubt now that you have attained this moment. Therefore, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva himself accomplishes patience, and he also establishes others in patience and gentleness.
He speaks in praise of patience;
he also becomes one who speaks in praise of and approves of those others who cultivate patience.
Having thus established those beings in patience and having settled them in patience, he gradually [establishes them] by means of the three vehicles.

He brings them to final nirvāṇa by means of either the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, or the Mahāyāna. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of generosity, establishes beings in patience and gentleness.
And how, Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of generosity, [establish beings]?
He establishes beings in the perfection of vigor.
Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having recognized beings who are indolent, lacking in vigor, and lazy, instructs them thus: "For whose sake are you falling into indolence?"
He spoke to them thus:
"Due to a deficiency of conditions," that bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of generosity, said this to those beings:

"O men, I shall provide you with all the necessary conditions—whether it be generosity, or ethical discipline, or patience, or whatever forms and characteristics by which you may exert vigor; I shall provide those for you.
Then, through the requisites provided by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, those beings exert vigor, whether physical or mental.
By means of that physical or mental vigor, they fulfill all wholesome qualities (*kuśaladharma*);
by those wholesome qualities, they cultivate the noble, untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas,

cultivating which they will attain the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*), the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*), the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*), and arhatship (*arhattva*).

They will attain individual enlightenment and they will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of generosity enjoins beings toward the perfection of vigor.

And how, Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of generosity instruct beings in the perfection of meditative concentration? Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva [instructs] beings...
He instructs them thus:
"O beings, why do you not enter into meditative absorption?
They reply to him as follows:
Regarding the phrase "due to a deficiency of conditions," the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva said this to them: "O men, I shall provide those conditions."
By whatever conditions you will not conceptualize thoughts—
whether as "this," or as "external," or as "internal," or as "both internal and external"—
the bodhisattva mahāsattva provides those very conditions for those beings by which [they may attain such states].
They do not engage in discursive thoughts because of those [qualities] being withdrawn; then, with discursive thoughts cut off, those beings enter the first dhyāna,
they enter the second dhyāna,
and they enter the third dhyāna.
They enter the fourth dhyāna;
they enter loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
By means of those dhyānas and those immeasurables, up to—
Cultivating the eightfold path, they attain final nirvāṇa through the three vehicles;

therein, others do not fall away from the path to awakening until they reach unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of generosity, instructs beings regarding the perfection of meditation.
And how, Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of generosity, embrace sentient beings with the perfection of wisdom?
Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of generosity, instructs sentient beings thus:
"O sentient beings, why do you not cultivate the perfection of wisdom?"
They said,
"It is due to a deficiency of conditions.
To those beings, the bodhisattva mahāsattva spoke thus:

"Take up the requisites for my sake; having taken up the requisites for my sake, give gifts, guard your ethical discipline, accomplish patience, exert vigor, and accomplish meditative concentration. Having fulfilled these aspects, investigate thus."
Is there anyone who is apprehended in the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom—
whether it be a self, a sentient being, a living soul, a creature, a nourisher, a person, an individual,
a human, a man, an agent, an experiencer, a knower, or a seer; or whether it be the realm of desire, the realm of form, or the formless realm?

Or the six perfections, or all the modes of emptiness, or the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening, or the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, and the formless attainments;

or emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; or the eight liberations, or the nine successive meditative attainments; or the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha;
or the fruit of stream-entry, or the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning, or arhatship, or pratyekabuddha-awakening.
Or even up to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—

while practicing the perfection of wisdom, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not apprehend any dharma such that, having apprehended it, he might become attached to it; and because he is without attachment, he does not perceive the arising or the cessation of any dharma whatsoever.

He does not perceive either affliction or purification; not perceiving them, he does not conceptualize: "This one belongs to the realm of hell-beings, this one to the animal realm, this one to the world of Yama, this one is an asura, this one is a deva, this one is a human, this one is a non-human;
this one is virtuous, this one is immoral; this one is a stream-enterer, this one is a once-returner, this one is a non-returner, this one is an arhat."
"This is a pratyekabuddha; this is a bodhisattva; this is a tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly awakened one.
In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of generosity embraces sentient beings through the perfection of wisdom.
And how, Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while established in the perfection of generosity, [establish them] in the perfection of ethical discipline?

Abiding in the perfection of patience, abiding in the perfection of vigor, abiding in the perfection of meditation, and abiding in the perfection of wisdom, he embraces sentient beings by means of the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment.
In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva provides sentient beings with the necessary requisites; embraced by those requisites, sentient beings cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness.
They cultivate the four right efforts, the four bases of miraculous power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path;

by cultivating this path, they are completely liberated from cyclic existence. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva embraces sentient beings through the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of generosity, matures sentient beings in this manner.

"O noble sons, take from me food, drink, vehicles, clothing, garlands, perfumes, ointments, flowers, incense, powders, and indeed all human necessities and utensils, and by means of the seven jewels, provide for the welfare of sentient beings."
That will be for your long-term welfare, benefit, and happiness;
do not think,
"This matter belongs to him, it does not belong to us."
"Since you have for a long time acquired this wealth for the sake of sentient beings, take it as being your own and give gifts to those beings;

and by means of that giving, establish them in ethical discipline, establish them in patience, establish them in vigor, establish them in meditative concentration, establish them in wisdom, and establish them in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment."
Enjoin them to the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditations, the formless attainments, the liberations, the concentrations, the meditative absorptions, and the doors of the dhāraṇīs;
enjoin them to emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
yet do not find satisfaction with merely this much.

"Until you establish them in the unsurpassed, noble, and untainted dharmas; establish them in the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, arhatship, pratyekabuddhahood, and in unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should bring sentient beings to maturity."
Just as they are ripened so that they are liberated from the three evils,
and even liberated from the entire cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), [established] in the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*)...
Abiding in the perfection of vigor, abiding in the perfection of meditative concentration, and abiding in the perfection of wisdom, he brings sentient beings to maturity, saying:
"O sentient beings, since these conditions do not exist, you fall into immorality; you fall into malice, laziness, distraction, and faulty wisdom. I shall provide those conditions for you."
Whether it be food, drink, clothing, or bedding and seats— indeed, all human requisites and appurtenances—
he favors those beings with such assistance that, being thus favored,
they undertake and abide in the ten paths of wholesome action.

Abiding in the morality of restraint that is unbroken, flawless, unspotted, untarnished, and unblemished, and abiding in the six perfections, in all the emptinesses, in emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and in the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening,
they attain the knowledge of all modes.
Then, this thought occurred to the venerable Subhūti:
"What is the path to enlightenment of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established upon which a bodhisattva mahāsattva must don such armor?
Then the Blessed One, knowing with his own mind the reflection in the mind of the venerable Subhūti, said this to the venerable Subhūti:
Subhūti, the six perfections are the path to awakening for a bodhisattva mahāsattva;
the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening are the path to awakening for a bodhisattva mahāsattva;

and all forms of emptiness, the eight liberations, the nine successive meditative attainments, the noble truths, the immeasurables, the dhyānas, and the formless attainments [are the path to awakening].
The gateways of all dhāraṇīs, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the superknowledges, the ten bodhisattva stages, the ten powers of a Tathāgata,

the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha constitute the path to enlightenment for the bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti, even all dharmas whatsoever constitute the path to enlightenment for the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
What do you think, Subhūti?

Is there any dharma in which a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not train, such that by not training in it he would attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening? There is no such dharma, Subhūti, in which a bodhisattva [should not train].
A great being must train; for without training, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is unable to attain the knowledge of all aspects. Then, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"If, Blessed One, all dharmas are empty,"
How, Blessed One, will a bodhisattva mahāsattva train in all dharmas?
For he does not conceptualize that which is non-conceptual,
thinking "they are this many" or "they are not this many."

"This dharma is either worldly or supramundane, with outflows or without outflows, conditioned or unconditioned, the dharma of an ordinary person, the dharma of an Arhat, the dharma of a Pratyekabuddha, or the dharma of a Buddha. When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
"So it is, Subhūti; so it is. All dharmas are empty.
Furthermore, Subhūti, if all dharmas were not empty, a bodhisattva mahāsattva would not realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Because, Subhūti, all dharmas are empty, therefore a bodhisattva mahāsattva will realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
Moreover, Subhūti, as to what you have said: "If all dharmas are empty,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva create a differentiation among dharmas?"
"Whether they are so many or not so many;

whether this phenomenon is mundane or supramundane, with outflows or without outflows, conditioned or unconditioned, the dharma of an ordinary person, the dharma of an Arhat, the dharma of a Pratyekabuddha, or the dharma of a Buddha. What more [is there to say]?

Subhūti, if these beings knew that all phenomena are empty, then these bodhisattva mahāsattvas would not, after training in all phenomena, attain the knowledge of all aspects; but because, Subhūti, they do not know that all phenomena are empty, [they train and attain it].

Therefore, having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and established the systematic arrangement of all phenomena, the bodhisattva mahāsattva teaches the Dharma to sentient beings.
Thus is the activity of establishing [beings] on the bodhisattva path;
therein, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the path to enlightenment must first investigate in this way:
There is no dharma here whatsoever that is apprehended by way of its own intrinsic nature, except through conditioned formation; indeed,

I should examine the intrinsic nature of dharmas, and while examining them, I would not become attached to any dharma— whether to the perfections, or to the emptinesses, or to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.

Whether it be regarding the dharmas, or the fruit of stream-entry, or the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning, or arhatship, or pratyekabuddha-enlightenment, or unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. For what reason?
Because all dharmas are empty by their very nature; indeed, emptiness does not adhere to emptiness.
First of all, emptiness itself is not apprehended; how much less could one be attached to emptiness? In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells without attachment to any phenomena;
remaining established in this training, he surveys sentient beings.
"What beings are these who move within non-apprehension?"—this is what occurs to the bodhisattva mahāsattva: "Alas, these beings are to be well-liberated from non-apprehension!
Therein, the bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of wisdom through skill in means, instructs them in this way.
"O beings, give gifts! Then there will be no deficiency for you regarding enjoyments;

yet do not become conceited on account of those enjoyments, for there is nothing substantial in them. Thus he instructs them in ethical discipline, and by means of that ethical discipline, he says: 'Do not become conceited, for there is nothing substantial in it. Thus he instructs them in patience and gentleness."

And regarding that patience, he instructs: "Do not be conceited on account of it; there is no essence whatsoever in it. Likewise, he instructs regarding vigor: "Do not be conceited on account of that vigor; there is no essence whatsoever in it. Likewise, he instructs regarding meditative concentration:
"Do not be conceited on account of that meditative concentration; there is no essence whatsoever in it. Likewise, he instructs regarding the perfection of wisdom.

And do not be conceited on account of that wisdom, for there is no essence whatsoever in it. Thus he instructs regarding the fruit of stream-entry; and do not be conceited on account of that fruit of stream-entry, for there is no essence whatsoever in it. Likewise regarding the fruit of once-returning and the fruit of non-returning.
Thus he instructs regarding arhatship; do not be conceited on account of that arhatship, for therein there is no essence whatsoever.

Thus he instructs regarding pratyekabodhi; do not be conceited on account of that pratyekabodhi. Thus he instructs regarding the buddha-dharmas; do not be conceited on account of those buddha-dharmas, for therein there is no essence whatsoever. He, in this way...
Instructing others, he courses in the path to enlightenment and does not become attached to any phenomenon. Why is that? Because they are unattached.

And all phenomena are likewise, for they have no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) such that one could become attached to them, by virtue of their having emptiness as their intrinsic nature. Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing on the path does not abide anywhere; through the yoga of non-abiding, he practices the perfection of generosity and does not abide therein either.
He practices the perfection of ethical discipline and yet does not abide therein;
he practices the perfection of patience and yet does not abide therein;
he practices the perfection of vigor and yet does not abide therein.
He practices the perfection of meditation and yet does not abide therein;
he practices the perfection of wisdom and yet does not abide therein.
He enters the first dhyāna and yet does not abide therein. Why is that?
For in this way, meditative absorption is empty of intrinsic nature; that which one enters is also empty; and those aspects by which one enters are also empty.
Thus one enters the second meditative absorption, and thus one enters the third meditative absorption.

In this way he enters the fourth dhyāna; in this way he enters loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; in this way he enters the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; in this way he enters the eight liberations and the nine successive meditative attainments.
In this way, he enters into the meditative attainments of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; he realizes the fruit of stream-entry and yet does not abide therein,
and he realizes the fruit of once-returning and yet does not abide therein.
He attains the fruit of non-returning and yet does not abide therein; he attains arhatship and yet does not abide therein; he attains the stage of a pratyekabuddha and yet does not abide therein.
Subhūti said:
"For what reason, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva not abide?
The Blessed One replied:
Subhūti, it does not abide for two reasons. Which two?
Because those fruits have no intrinsic nature (svabhāva) in which one might abide, by means of which one might abide, or who might abide;
and yet, one does not find satisfaction with merely that much.
And it is not that the fruit of stream-entry is not to be attained by me; the fruit of stream-entry is to be attained by me, yet I must not abide therein.
Likewise for the fruit of once-returning and the fruit of non-returning.
It is not that arhatship is not to be attained by me; arhatship is to be attained by me, yet I must not abide therein.
"It is not that I should not attain the stage of a pratyekabuddha; indeed, I must attain the stage of a pratyekabuddha, yet I must not abide there.
For when I shall fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, I do not abide [in those stages] for two reasons. Why is that?"

For it is thus: from the first production of the thought of awakening (prathamacittotpāda) onward, that bodhisattva mahāsattva has obtained no mind other than that which is directed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening (anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhiḥ). Why is that?

Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva, even while abiding in the first stage (bhūmi), does not produce any thought other than that which is directed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening; and so it continues up to the tenth stage.
Abiding in reliance [upon the Dharma], he does not give rise to any thought other than unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening;

until he has entered the bodhisattva’s certainty, he has not produced any thought other than unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, his mind never being satiated. Subhūti, that bodhisattva mahāsattva, for as long as he is with the body...

or exerts himself, whether by speech or by mind, he does so nowhere other than in the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*). Abiding in that thought of awakening with an undistracted mind, that bodhisattva mahāsattva generates the path to awakening. Then, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
“Blessed One, if all dharmas are unarisen, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva generate the path to awakening?
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
“So it is, Subhūti; so it is.”
"All dharmas are unarisen; how then is it that for those who perform volitional formations, all dharmas are unarisen?
When this was said, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Furthermore, Blessed One, whether Tathāgatas arise or whether Tathāgatas do not arise, this stability of the nature of phenomena (dharmasthititā) remains constant for these phenomena.
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti; so it is."
Whether Tathāgatas arise or whether Tathāgatas do not arise, this stability of the nature of phenomena (dharmasthititā) remains constant for these phenomena.

Furthermore, for the sake of those who do not know this stability of the nature of phenomena, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva generates the path to enlightenment, by which path he liberates sentient beings from saṃsāra.
Thus is the activity of establishing the relinquishing of all attachments.
Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"But, Blessed One, is awakening attained by means of a path that has not arisen, or rather by one that has arisen?
The Blessed One replied: "No, Subhūti."
Subhūti said:
"But then, Blessed One, is awakening attained by means of a path that is neither unarisen nor arisen?
The Blessed One said: "No, Subhūti."
Subhūti said:
"But then, Blessed One, is awakening not attained by a path that is neither unarisen nor not arisen?
The Blessed One said: "No, Subhūti."
Subhūti said:
"In that case, Blessed One, how then is awakening attained?
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
Subhūti, awakening is not attained by means of a path, nor by means of what is not a path;
rather, Subhūti, awakening itself is the path,
and the path itself is awakening.
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"If, Blessed One, awakening itself is the path and the path itself is awakening, such that awakening has already been attained by the bodhisattva mahāsattva,
then how is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, designated?"

By means of the thirty-two marks of a great man, the eighty secondary characteristics, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the four immeasurables, the four meditative absorptions, the four formless attainments, the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening, the four noble truths, and [the three doors of liberation, namely] emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
[It is endowed] with the five superknowledges, the eight liberations, the nine successive meditative attainments, all the doors of dhāraṇī,
the ten bodhisattva stages, the ten perfections, the twenty kinds of emptiness, and the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Does a Buddha attain awakening? Is the Buddha himself awakening, and is awakening itself the Buddha?"
Subhūti said: "No, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
Furthermore, as for what Subhūti says— that a bodhisattva mahāsattva has indeed attained awakening— here, Subhūti, it is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva,
having fulfilled the six perfections and the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening, [and] all the modes of emptiness...

The four noble truths, emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the eight liberations, the nine successive meditative attainments, the five superknowledges, all the gateways of samādhi and dhāraṇī, the ten bodhisattva stages, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, and the fearlessnesses.

Having fulfilled the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), and remaining in the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*), he awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment through wisdom conjoined with a single moment of mind.
At that time, he is designated as a "Tathāgata" because he knows all phenomena; therefore, he is called the "All-Seeing One" (*sarvadarśin*) and the "Omniscient One" (*sarvajña*).
Thus ends the section on the activity of entering into the attainment of perfect enlightenment.
Then, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva purify a buddha-field?"
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:

"In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, from the first production of the thought of awakening, purifies for himself and for others bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct; and by means of those [purifications], he purifies the buddhafield."
Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
“Blessed One, what is a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s immorality of body, immorality of speech, and immorality of mind?
When this was said, the Blessed One said this to the venerable Subhūti:
Whatever bodily action is unwholesome, whether it consists in taking life, taking what is not given, or engaging in sexual misconduct;
This is called bodily misconduct; as for verbal action that is unwholesome, it consists in engaging in false speech and engaging in slanderous speech.
Engaging in harsh speech and engaging in idle chatter— this is called verbal misconduct.
Whatever unwholesome mental action exists that operates within covetousness, operates within ill will,
and operates within wrong view.
This is called mental immorality.

Furthermore, Subhūti, that which is a mind of stinginess is the mental immorality of a bodhisattva mahāsattva; likewise, a mind of immorality, a mind of agitation, a mind of laziness, a mind of distraction, a mind lacking concentration, and a mind of faulty wisdom [are all mental immorality].
This too is a mind of immorality for a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti, whatever morality is impure—this too is an impure mind of immorality for a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti, [one who is] devoid of the four foundations of mindfulness and the four right efforts...
To be devoid of the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment,
the noble eightfold path, the concentration on emptiness, the concentration on the signless, and the concentration on the wishless—
this too is a mind of immorality for a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Furthermore, Subhūti, whatever constitutes the realization of the fruit of stream-entry and the longing for it—this too is a corruption of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Whatever constitutes the realization of the fruit of once-returning and the longing for it—this too is a corruption of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Whatever constitutes the realization of the fruit of non-returning and the longing for it—[this too is a corruption].

This too is a corruption for a bodhisattva mahāsattva: namely, the realization of arhatship and the longing for it—this too is a corruption for a bodhisattva mahāsattva. The realization of pratyekabuddhahood and the longing for it—this too is a corruption for a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the perception of form is a state of corruption; the perception of feeling, the perception of perception, the perception of mental formations, and the perception of consciousness are states of corruption;
the perception of the eye is a state of corruption.

The perception of the ear, the perception of the nose, the perception of the tongue, the perception of the body, and the perception of the mind are coarseness; the perception of forms, the perception of sounds, the perception of odors, the perception of tastes, the perception of tangibles, and the perception of mental phenomena are coarseness.
The perception of eye-consciousness is a state of corruption;

the perception of ear-consciousness, the perception of nose-consciousness, the perception of tongue-consciousness, the perception of body-consciousness, and the perception of mind-consciousness are states of corruption;
the perception of eye-contact is a state of corruption.
The perception of ear-contact, the perception of nose-contact, the perception of tongue-contact, the perception of body-contact, and the perception of mind-contact are depravity;
the perception of feeling conditioned by eye-contact is depravity;

the perception of feeling conditioned by ear-contact, the perception of feeling conditioned by nose-contact, the perception of feeling conditioned by tongue-contact, and the perception of feeling conditioned by body-contact [are depravity].
The perception of feeling conditioned by mental contact is a state of corruption; the perception of the earth element is a state of corruption;
the perception of the water element and the perception of the fire element are states of corruption.
The perception of the wind element,
the perception of the space element, and the perception of the consciousness element are corruption;
the perception of the aggregates is corruption.
The perception of the elements is a state of corruption; the perception of the sense bases is a state of corruption; the perception of dependent origination is a state of corruption;
and the perception of dependently originated phenomena is a state of corruption.
The perception of the factors of dependent origination is a state of corruption; the perception of ignorance is a state of corruption;

the perception of formative forces, the perception of consciousness, the perception of name-and-form, the perception of the six sense bases, the perception of contact, and the perception of feeling are states of corruption.

The notion of craving, the notion of grasping, the notion of becoming, the notion of birth, the notion of old age and death, the notion of sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair—these are depravity.
The notion of woman, the notion of man, the notion of the desire realm, the notion of the form realm, and the notion of the formless realm—these are depravity.

The notion of the wholesome, the notion of the unwholesome, the notion of the mundane, the notion of the supramundane, the notion of the contaminated, the notion of the uncontaminated, the notion of the conditioned, and the notion of the unconditioned—these are depravity.
This is the corruption of body, the corruption of speech, and the corruption of mind;
having abandoned these, one gives gifts oneself and encourages others to give gifts as well.

He gives food to those seeking food, drink to those seeking drink, clothing to those seeking clothing, and so on, up to all other various human necessities and utensils; furthermore, he encourages others to likewise undertake the giving of all such various human necessities and utensils.
And having made that root of merit common to all sentient beings, he dedicates it for the purification of the Buddha-field;
he himself guards morality and encourages others to undertake morality;
he himself accomplishes patience and encourages others in patience.

He himself exerts vigor and encourages others to exert vigor; he himself enters into meditative concentration and encourages others to enter into meditative concentration; and he himself cultivates wisdom.
He encourages others to take up wisdom,

and having made that root of merit common to all sentient beings, he dedicates it for the purification of the Buddha-field; and he himself, having filled the triple-thousand great-thousand world-system with the seven precious jewels, gives a gift to the Three Jewels and makes that root of merit common to all sentient beings.
It occurs to him: "By this root of virtue, may my buddha-field consist of the seven precious jewels.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva plays divine musical instruments before the Buddhas or before the shrines of the Buddhas.

And he makes that root of merit common to all sentient beings, thinking: "By this root of merit, may divine sounds—delightful and pleasing to the ear—be constantly and perpetually produced as music in my buddha-field. Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having filled the trichiliocosm with divine fragrances, [offers them] to the Buddhas or to the shrines of the Buddhas.
And he makes that root of merit common to all sentient beings;
it occurs to him: "By this root of merit, may there be divine fragrances, pleasant to the nose and delightful, in my buddha-field.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives foods of a hundred flavors to the Tathāgatas.

Or he shares that root of merit in common with all sentient beings among the disciples of the Tathāgata, and it occurs to him: "By this root of merit, when I have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in my Buddha-field, may food of a hundred flavors be provided for the community of my disciples.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives divine ointments.
Whether toward the Tathāgatas, or the disciples of the Tathāgatas, or the reliquaries of the Tathāgatas,
he makes that root of merit common to all sentient beings,
and it occurs to him: "By this root of merit, may there be divine tangibles and physical pleasures in my Buddha-field that are agreeable to the mind."
May all sentient beings attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment once I have realized it.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, through his mental intentions, together with himself and all sentient beings, offers the five strands of sensual pleasure to the Buddhas, or to the disciples of the Buddhas, or to all sentient beings; and he makes that root of merit common to all sentient beings.

It occurs to him: "By this root of virtue, when I have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, may there be delightful objects of the five sensory pleasures for my entire community of disciples and for all sentient beings. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva purifies a buddhafield.

Furthermore, Subhūti, as a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, it occurs to him: "What if I were now to enter the first dhyāna myself and establish all sentient beings in the first dhyāna; and likewise in the second and third dhyānas?"
May I myself enter the fourth dhyāna and establish all sentient beings in the fourth dhyāna;
may I myself cultivate loving-kindness and establish all sentient beings in the cultivation of loving-kindness.
In this way, I would cultivate compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity myself, and I would establish all sentient beings in the cultivation of equanimity;
I would personally attain the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space and establish all sentient beings in the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space,
as well as the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite consciousness and the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness.

May I myself enter the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and establish all sentient beings in the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; may I myself cultivate the foundations of mindfulness and establish all sentient beings in the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness;
and likewise for the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, and the factors of enlightenment.

May I myself cultivate the noble eightfold path and establish all sentient beings in the cultivation of the noble eightfold path; may I myself cultivate the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—and establish all sentient beings in the cultivation of the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
and when I have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, [may it be so for me].
May all sentient beings never be separated from the four dhyānas; may they cultivate them without being separated from the four formless attainments, never be separated from the four divine abodes,
never be separated from the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and may they never be separated from the gateways to liberation— emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva purifies a buddhafield;
he courses toward awakening until all these aspirations are fulfilled,
and he himself becomes endowed with all wholesome qualities.
He causes others to be endowed with all wholesome dharmas;
his own physical form becomes handsome, pleasing, beautiful, and adorned with the marks of a great man (mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa);
and for those beings who have been ripened by that bodhisattva mahāsattva, their physical forms likewise become handsome, pleasing, beautiful, and adorned with the marks of a great man.
It comes about, namely, through the acquisition of merit;
in this way indeed, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should purify a buddhafield such that even the designation of the three lower realms will no longer exist.
There will be no designation even for all types of views,
and there will be no designation even for passion, hatred, and delusion.

Until even the designation of duality no longer exists, until even the designation of impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity no longer exists, and until even the designation of an appropriator no longer exists.

There will be no designation of "I-making" or "mine-making," nor will there be any designation of the establishment of fruits; rather, only the sound of the concentrations of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness will circulate.

From the mere desire of all sentient beings for the aspiration toward renunciation up to the aspiration toward wisdom, sounds will issue forth from trees stirred by the wind; likewise, sounds will issue forth from all internal and external phenomena—
whether as "emptiness," or "signlessness," or "wishlessness."
The sound "neither arising nor ceasing" will issue forth;
just as all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature, so too will the sound issue forth:
"all phenomena are empty of all phenomena."
Just as is the intrinsic nature of these phenomena, so shall the sound issue forth: whether Tathāgatas arise or whether Tathāgatas do not arise, all phenomena are empty of all phenomena.

That which is empty has no sign therein; that is the wishless. This very teaching of the Dharma, of such a form, shall issue forth—whether by night or by day, whether standing or sitting, lying down or walking—such is the teaching of all phenomena.
They will emerge. When that bodhisattva mahāsattva has awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in that buddha-field,
then for that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, it shall be [the result] of that very bodhisattva mahāsattva.
All those Buddhas, Blessed Ones, who currently reside, remain, and maintain themselves in the world-systems of the ten directions, will all speak his praise;
and whatever beings hear his praise or his name, they shall all become destined for unsurpassed [enlightenment].

Regarding perfect enlightenment: furthermore, when that Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha teaches the Dharma, no sentient being will have any doubt as to whether "this is the Dharma" or "this is not the Dharma. For what reason?
Furthermore, that which is the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena—therein there is no phenomenon that is not a phenomenon; it is entirely a phenomenon.

In this regard, those beings who are seized by unwholesome roots, or who have not planted wholesome roots, or who are not sustained by spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), whether toward the Buddhas or the disciples of the Buddhas...
They adhere to the view of a self, up to and including the view of a beholder; they abide in extremes, whether in annihilationism or eternalism.

Seized by their own false grasping, they perceive those who are not perfectly enlightened ones as being perfectly enlightened ones, or perceive those who are perfectly enlightened ones as being not perfectly enlightened ones; they declare what is not Dharma to be Dharma, and they reject the true Dharma.
Having rejected the Dharma, at the breaking up of the body after death, they fall into states of woe, miserable destinies, and perdition, and are reborn in the hells.

Having awakened to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, separate from that state of evil views those beings who are involved in saṃsāra; having separated them, they establish them in the fixed group [of those destined for enlightenment]. Once established there, they are never again reborn in the miserable states. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva...
He purifies a buddha-field such that,
once it is purified, there will be no deficiency for sentient beings regarding any phenomena— whether mundane or supramundane, with outflows or without outflows, conditioned or unconditioned.
or regarding phenomena, until all shall become fixed in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
This is the activity of establishing the purification of the buddha-field.
Then, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"But, Blessed One, is a bodhisattva mahāsattva fixed?
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is fixed; he is indeed fixed."
Subhūti asked:
"In which group is he fixed: in the group of the śrāvakas or in the group of the pratyekabuddhas?
The Blessed One replied:

“Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not fixed in the category of the śrāvakas, nor is he fixed in the category of the pratyekabuddhas; rather, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is fixed in the category of the Buddhas.
Subhūti asked:
“But is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has first produced the thought of awakening [already] fixed?”
"Or is it the irreversible [bodhisattva], or the one in his final existence?
The Blessed One said:

"Subhūti, it is not that the bodhisattva mahāsattva is fixed as irreversible, nor is he fixed as being in his final existence; rather, it is the one who has first produced the thought of awakening who is fixed."
Subhūti said:
"But, Blessed One, will a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is fixed [in the path] ever be reborn in the lower realms?
The Blessed One said:
“Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is fixed and irreversible will not be reborn in the lower realms. What do you think, Subhūti?
Would an eighth-rank person, or a stream-enterer, or a once-returner, or a non-returner, or an arhat, or a pratyekabuddha—who are all fixed—be reborn in the lower realms?
Subhūti replied:
"No, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"In the same way, Subhūti, it is impossible for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to be reborn in the states of woe; such a thing cannot occur. For what reason?"
For instance, Subhūti, any bodhisattva mahāsattva who, from the first production of the thought of awakening, practices giving, guards morality, accomplishes patience, exerts vigor,
enters meditative concentration, cultivates wisdom,
and cultivates loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity toward sentient beings—
Having abandoned all unwholesome states, he remains [in them]; that he would be reborn in the lower realms—this is impossible;
or that he would be reborn among the long-lived gods—this is impossible.
It is impossible that he should be reborn where there is a lack of wholesome qualities, or in border regions;
it is impossible that he should be reborn among families with wrong views;
and it is impossible that he should be reborn where the sound of "Buddha," the sound of "Dharma," or the sound of "Saṅgha" is not heard.
It is impossible that he would be reborn in families with wrong views of non-action;

indeed, Subhūti, it is impossible for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has first resolved upon and set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening to commit the ten unwholesome paths of action through his resolute intention.
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is thus endowed with wholesome dharmas— namely, that he will not be reborn in unfavorable states—
then why has the Tathāgata himself described his own birth stories (jātakas)?"
"But where have these wholesome dharmas gone? When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not take up a physical existence without deliberate intention."
He takes on whatever physical form is necessary for the benefit of sentient beings; he assumes that very form for the sake of sentient beings.
Subhūti, does an Arhat or a Pratyekabuddha possess such skillful means by which, endowed with that skillful means, they might be reborn among the animals?
Subhūti replied:
"No, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"The Tathāgata possesses that skill in means by which he might be reborn there."

And those who there strive for their destruction, he encourages them toward supreme patience and establishes them in discipline; for their sake alone he sacrifices himself, yet no harm comes to those beings. Therefore, Subhūti, by this method it should be understood that in such a way a bodhisattva mahāsattva, fulfilling great compassion for the sake of beings, [strives] for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
"He exists among the animal realm.
When this was said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"In which wholesome dharmas, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva abide when he assumes such a physical form as this?"
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti: "Subhūti, all that wholesome karma which is to be fulfilled by a bodhisattva mahāsattva—
the fulfillment of all wholesome dharmas— is, for that bodhisattva mahāsattva, unexcelled perfect enlightenment."

From the first production of the thought of awakening until sitting at the seat of enlightenment, there is no dharma whatsoever that should not be fulfilled, by the fulfillment of which one awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.

Therefore, from the first production of the thought of awakening, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train for the sake of fulfilling all wholesome dharmas; having trained therein, he will attain the knowledge of all aspects.
"He will abandon the continuity of all habitual tendencies.
When this was said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"But how, Blessed One, can a bodhisattva mahāsattva, being endowed with such pure qualities and the noble, untainted dharma, be reborn in the states of woe or among the animals?"
The Blessed One said:
"Furthermore, Subhūti, is the Tathāgata noble and free from outflows?
Subhūti replied:
“Noble one, the Blessed One is without outflows.
The Blessed One said:
“But does the Tathāgata manifest himself as a living being born of the animal realm?”
"Having manifested what would one perform the work of a Buddha?
Subhūti said: "One would perform it, Blessed One; one would perform it, Sugata."
The Blessed One asked:
"But does the Tathāgata become an animal?
Subhūti replied:
"No, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"What then, does one experience the suffering of the animal realm?"
Subhūti said: "No, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti, so it is.
Endowed with the noble, untainted Dharma, a bodhisattva mahāsattva intentionally assumes such a physical form that, possessing that body, he brings others to maturity just as a Tathāgata does."
Subhūti said:
"But, Blessed One, does the Tathāgata create an emanation, and having created it, cause it to perform an action?"
"By what action does joy arise in others?
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti; so it is."
The bodhisattva mahāsattva, endowed with the noble, untainted dharma, assumes such a physical form that, possessed of that body, he accomplishes the welfare of sentient beings,
yet he does not experience any corresponding sensation.
Subhūti said:
"Are not the states of woe, Blessed One, indeed suffering?
The Blessed One said:

What do you think, Subhūti? When a magician displays an illusion— whether the form of an elephant, the form of a horse, the form of an ox, or various other kinds of living beings— does that [illusion] actually become an elephant, or [the other things it represents]?
They become horses, or oxen, or various other kinds of living beings.
Subhūti said: "No, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti, so it is.

A bodhisattva mahāsattva, endowed with the noble, untainted dharma, intentionally assumes such a physical form that, being endowed with that physical form, he [acts] for the sake of sentient beings..."
He performs his duty,
yet he does not experience such a sensation.
Subhūti said:
O Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is skilled in great skillful means is one who, being endowed with the noble, untainted dharma,
assumes whatever form of existence by which he is able to accomplish the welfare of sentient beings.
This is the activity of establishing [beings] in the determination of perfect enlightenment.
“Blessed One, abiding in which pure dharmas does he perform such skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*) by which he is not defiled by them?
The Blessed One said:
“Subhūti, it is by abiding in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) that a bodhisattva [performs this].”

A mahāsattva is endowed with such skillful means that, through this skillful means, he performs the welfare of sentient beings in world systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā in the east, south, west, north, below, above, and in the intermediate directions, yet he is not touched by anything therein. Why is that?

For in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not apprehend phenomena in any way whatsoever—neither that which might be touched, nor that by which one might touch, nor he who might touch. Why is that?
Because all these three phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*); therein, emptiness is not touched by emptiness, nor does anyone touch emptiness at all.
Nor is emptiness contacted. Why is that?
Because, by virtue of the emptiness of intrinsic nature, emptiness itself is not apprehended.
This is that non-apprehension emptiness (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*), abiding in which the bodhisattva mahāsattva awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Subhūti said:
"But, Blessed One, does he abide only in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) and not in other dharmas?"
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, what dharma is there that is not included within the perfection of wisdom?
Subhūti replied:
Blessed One, since the perfection of wisdom is empty of intrinsic nature,
how can all phenomena be included within the perfection of wisdom?
For, Blessed One, no phenomenon whatsoever is included within emptiness.
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti, so it is. Yet, Subhūti, it is not that all phenomena are empty by means of all phenomena."
Nor are all phenomena included within emptiness.
This is the activity of establishing immeasurable sentient beings in the welfare [of others].
Then, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
How, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing in the perfection of wisdom and abiding in the emptiness of all phenomena, bring forth the perfection of the superknowledges (*abhijñā*),
by means of which superknowledges he goes to world-systems in the eastern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā,
and to those world-systems where the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, currently reside, remain, and maintain themselves?

He attends upon them and hears the Dharma from them, and in those Blessed Buddhas he plants roots of merit; likewise, he goes to world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges in the south, west, north, below, above, and in the intermediate directions, and in those world-systems, he sees the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who are staying, remaining, and maintaining themselves.
He attends upon them and hears the Dharma from those Blessed Buddhas, and he plants roots of merit under those Blessed Buddhas.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:

"In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom perceives all those world-systems in the eastern direction, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, as empty."
Those Buddhas, those Blessed Ones who dwell there, remain, and maintain themselves—they too, those Buddhas, those Blessed Ones, are empty of intrinsic nature;

they are designated only by way of names, conventions, and designations, and all such designations are empty of intrinsic nature. If those world-systems were not empty of intrinsic nature, [the Tathāgata would not have attained unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment].
If those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, were not empty of intrinsic nature,
and if even those conventional designations and activities were not empty of intrinsic nature,
then emptiness would be merely partial; however, since a partial emptiness is not found, therefore all phenomena are empty of all phenomena.
In this regard, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom through skill in means brings forth the perfection of the superknowledges (*abhijñā*).

Abiding in these superknowledges, he brings forth the divine eye, the divine ear, the knowledge of the modes of psychic power, the recollection of former abodes, and the knowledge of death and rebirth. By means of these superknowledges, it is possible for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Since this awakening of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is included within the perfection of the superknowledges,

and awakening is to be sought as being included within the superknowledges, while seeking it, he— by means of the purified divine eye, which transcends that of humans— sees for himself those wholesome qualities and establishes others in wholesome qualities.
Nor will one be attached to wholesome dharmas. Why is that?
Because all those wholesome dharmas are empty by their very nature;
and emptiness does not become attached to anything such that it would relish attachment, for emptiness is devoid of intrinsic nature.
Therefore, the bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing in the perfection of wisdom, brings forth the divine eye, by which eye he sees that all phenomena are empty.

Furthermore, the bodhisattva mahāsattva, relying on those phenomena, discerns that activity; through that discernment of activity, he teaches the Dharma to sentient beings, yet he does not perceive the designation "sentient being."
Thus, by means of the yoga of non-apprehension, the bodhisattva mahāsattva brings forth the superknowledges (*abhijñā*) within the perfection of wisdom;
through those superknowledges, he performs those deeds of compassion and dharma that are to be performed.
Then, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, the bodhisattva mahāsattva [beholds] in the eastern direction...
In the southern direction, in the western direction, in the northern direction, in the downward and upward world-systems,
and as far as the intermediate directions in the world-systems, he beholds sentient beings; having gone there by means of his miraculous power, he works for the benefit of those beings.

Whether by means of generosity, or morality, or patience, or vigor, or meditation, or wisdom; whether by means of the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening, or the immeasurables, the meditations, the formless attainments, the liberations, the concentrations, the meditative absorptions, and the gateways of dhāraṇī; whether by means of the qualities of śrāvakas, or the qualities of pratyekabuddhas, or the qualities of bodhisattvas, or the qualities of buddhas.
He performs the welfare of those beings.

Therein, to those beings who are miserly, he teaches the Dharma in this way: "Give gifts, O men! For poverty is suffering; indeed, it is not possible through poverty to accomplish one's own purpose, let alone that of another."
Therefore, you shall be happy yourselves and you shall bring happiness to others; do not, while being impoverished, eat the flesh of others, lest you fail to be liberated from the three lower realms.
To those beings who are immoral, he teaches the Dharma in this way:
"O men, immorality is indeed suffering; one cannot achieve one's own welfare through immorality, much less that of another."

Furthermore, as for the ripening of immorality— whether it be hell, the animal realm, or the world of Yama— you would fall into those three lower realms and not even be able to rescue yourselves, let alone allow even a single moment of an immoral thought to arise; do this lest you suffer for a long time hereafter.

To those beings who have hostile minds and who, toward another, become angry, harbor malice, and give rise to hatred, he teaches the Dharma in this way: "Sirs, do not agitate one another; do not harbor malice toward one another; do not give rise to hatred. For in one whose mind is agitated, no wholesome quality whatsoever can manifest.
Therefore, sirs, it is possible that by being thus agitated in mind and harboring malice toward one another, you will fall into hell, or into the animal realm, or into the world of Yama."
Therefore, you must not be disturbed even by a single thought, much less give any opportunity for other thoughts to arise.
Those beings who are indolent, he establishes in vigor and teaches them the Dharma thus:
"Sirs, do not fall into indolence; for those who are indolent and of inferior vigor, there is no auspicious activity whatsoever."

It is possible that for those who are indolent there may be rebirth in hell, or in the animal realm, or in the world of Yama; therefore, you must not allow even a single moment of an indolent thought to arise, much less other such thoughts.
As for those beings whose minds are distracted, he establishes them all in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). In this way, for them... (PSP_6-8:137)
He teaches the Dharma, saying:
"Sirs, do not be of muddled mindfulness or distracted mind; for those of muddled mindfulness or distracted mind, it is possible that wholesome qualities will not arise.

It is possible that for those of muddled mindfulness or distracted mind, there may be rebirth in hell, the animal realm, or the world of Yama. Therefore, you must not allow even a single moment of distraction to occur."
How much more so for other states of mind?
Those beings who are of poor wisdom, he establishes them all in wisdom; to them he teaches the Dharma in this way:

"Do not give rise to thoughts of poor wisdom; for those lacking wisdom there is no going to a happy rebirth. It is possible that for those of poor wisdom there will be rebirth in hell, the animal realm, or the world of Yama.
Therefore, you must not give rise to even a single thought devoid of wisdom, much less provide an opportunity for other such thoughts to arise.
As for those beings whose conduct is dominated by passion, he establishes them in the cultivation of the beautiful."

Those beings who are not established on the path, he establishes them on the path— whether he establishes them on the path of the śrāvaka or the path of the pratyekabuddha— and he teaches them the Dharma in this way:
"Venerable sirs, those dharmas to which you are attached are empty of intrinsic nature."
It is not possible to become attached to phenomena that are empty of intrinsic nature, and emptiness itself is non-attached.
In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, while established in the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), brings benefit to sentient beings.
Subhūti, there is no bodhisattva mahāsattva who is able to teach the Dharma to sentient beings without being established in the superknowledges.

Nor is it possible for one to lead beings who have set out upon wrong paths back onto the right path. Subhūti, just as a bird without wings cannot traverse the sky, even so, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has not attained the superknowledges (*abhijñā*) is unable to teach the Dharma to beings.
Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) must bring forth the superknowledges.
Having brought these superknowledges to perfection, he will accomplish whatever he desires for the benefit of sentient beings;
with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he will see world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges,
and he will see the sentient beings born therein.
Having seen those beings, he will go by means of his supernormal power and discern their minds with his own mind;
having known their minds, he will teach them the Dharma accordingly, whether it be a discourse on giving, or [other teachings].
Whether it be a discourse on ethical discipline, a discourse on patience, a discourse on diligence, a discourse on meditative concentration, a discourse on wisdom, or even a discourse on nirvana—

by means of the divine ear-element, purified and surpassing that of humans, he will hear both sounds, human and non-human; therein, he will hear the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, teaching the Dharma in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges.

Having heard it with the divine ear-element, he will grasp it exactly as it is; having grasped it exactly as it is, he teaches the Dharma to sentient beings—whether a discourse on generosity, or a discourse on ethical discipline, or a discourse on patience, or a discourse on diligence, or a discourse on meditative concentration, or a discourse on wisdom, up to a discourse on nirvāṇa.
His knowledge of the movements of others' minds will become perfectly pure; by means of that perfectly pure knowledge of the movements of others' minds, he will discern the minds of sentient beings.
Having understood their minds, he will teach them the Dharma accordingly—

whether it be a discourse on generosity, or a discourse on ethical discipline, or a discourse on patience, or a discourse on diligence, or a discourse on meditative concentration, or a discourse on wisdom, up to a discourse on nirvana.
He will recollect his manifold former abodes.
By means of that knowledge of recollecting former abodes, he will know thus for himself and for others:
"Those previous Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly enlightened Buddhas, together with their assemblies of disciples, had such names.
Furthermore, to those beings who will have an inclination toward the recollection of former abodes, he will teach the Dharma in exactly that way.
He will preach discourses on generosity, or on ethical discipline, or on patience, or on diligence, or on meditative concentration, or on wisdom, up to discourses on nirvāṇa.
Endowed with manifold and diverse supernormal powers, he will go to world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges and [visit] the Buddhas.
He will attend upon those Blessed Ones and plant roots of merit under those Blessed Buddhas; having planted those roots of merit, he will return again to that very same buddha-field,
and having arrived, he will teach the Dharma to those sentient beings.

Whether it be a discourse on giving, or a discourse on ethical discipline, or a discourse on patience, or a discourse on vigor, or a discourse on meditative concentration, or a discourse on wisdom, or even a discourse on nirvāṇa—
