his superknowledge consisting in the realization of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows will become perfectly pure.
With that superknowledge consisting in the realization of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows, being thoroughly purified, he will teach the Dharma to sentient beings.

Whether it be a discourse on generosity, or a discourse on ethical discipline, or a discourse on patience, or a discourse on diligence, or a discourse on meditative concentration, or a discourse on wisdom,
up to and including a discourse on nirvāṇa— Subhūti,
it is in this way that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should bring forth the superknowledges.

With these supernormal powers brought forth, whatever kind of personal existence he may desire to assume, that very kind of personal existence he will assume; yet he will not be affected by pleasure or pain, nor will he be elated or dejected, nor will there be in him either attachment or aversion. Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, a person created by a Buddha were to perform all his tasks.
And he is not stained by that pleasure or by that suffering.

In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should sport with the superknowledges; sporting thus, he will purify the buddha-field and bring sentient beings to maturity.

In this way, Subhūti, when the buddha-fields have been purified and sentient beings have been brought to maturity by a bodhisattva mahāsattva, it is possible for him to awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, there is no deficiency in any factor for this bodhisattva mahāsattva regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Thus ends the section on the practice of approaching, attending upon, and dwelling near the Buddhas.
Then, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, what are the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by fulfilling which a bodhisattva mahāsattva awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti: "Subhūti, all wholesome dharmas are limbs of awakening for a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Subhūti said:
"But, Blessed One, what are those wholesome dharmas by which one fully awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:

"Subhūti, beginning from the first production of the thought of awakening, the perfection of generosity is a wholesome dharma; and therein, that non-conceptualization in which the gift does not know: 'This is the gift,' 'for whose sake it should be given,' or 'by whom it should be given.'"
And these three conceptualizations do not exist for him, by virtue of the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvaśūnyatā*).

By means of this perfection, he himself crosses over and delivers sentient beings from cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*). These are the wholesome qualities of the bodhisattva mahāsattva that constitute the path to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
it is by this path that the bodhisattva mahāsattvas of the past, future, and present have crossed over, are crossing over, and will cross over.

And they shall cross over. Likewise, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom are wholesome dharmas; and therein is that non-conceptualization which does not know wisdom as "this is wisdom," nor for whose sake it is to be cultivated, nor by whom it is to be cultivated.
Furthermore, those three conceptual constructions do not exist for him by virtue of the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) through that perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

By means of this, he himself crosses over and delivers sentient beings from cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*). These are the wholesome factors (*kuśala-dharma*) which constitute the path for a bodhisattva mahāsattva toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
it is by this path that the bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present have crossed over, are crossing over, and will cross over.

In this way, there are the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment,
the noble eightfold path, and all the emptinesses.

The eight liberations, the nine successive meditative attainments, all the gateways of the dhāraṇīs, all the samādhis, emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, the five superknowledges, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—
these are the wholesome dharmas of a bodhisattva mahāsattva; and non-conceptualization regarding those Buddha-dharmas is [the perfection of wisdom].

He does not perceive these Buddha-qualities for whose sake they are to be cultivated, nor by whom they are to be cultivated; and those three conceptualizations do not exist for him, because of their emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*). By means of these wholesome qualities, both he himself and sentient beings cross over and are delivered from saṃsāra—these are the unsurpassed [qualities] of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
This is the path to perfect enlightenment, by which the bodhisattva mahāsattvas of the past, future, and present have crossed over, are crossing over, and will cross over.

Subhūti, having fulfilled all those wholesome dharmas that constitute any paths to enlightenment whatsoever, a bodhisattva mahāsattva must attain all-aspect omniscience; and having attained all-aspect omniscience—
"The wheel of Dharma must be turned.
This concludes the activity of establishing [beings] in the factors of enlightenment.
Then, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"If, Blessed One, these dharmas are the dharmas of a bodhisattva, then what, moreover, are the dharmas of a Buddha?
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
Furthermore, as for what the Venerable Subhūti has said: "If these are the dharmas of a bodhisattva, then what are the dharmas of a Buddha?
Subhūti, these very same [dharmas] are the dharmas of a Buddha.

By means of these dharmas, one fully awakens to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). For one who has attained that knowledge of all aspects, the continuity of all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā-anusaṃdhi*) is abandoned;

the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva fully awakens to that [state] such that all dharmas have been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha through wisdom associated with a single moment. This is the distinction of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
and of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha. Subhūti, it is just as if one person were a candidate for the fruit and another were established in the fruit;

though both are indeed not non-supreme persons, even so, Subhūti, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is one who has entered the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), whereas the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has attained unobstructed knowledge regarding all phenomena.
“Subhūti, this is the distinction between a bodhisattva mahāsattva and a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One:

“Blessed One, if these dharmas are empty of their own specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇaśūnya), then how can a distinction or a differentiation be perceived among dharmas that are empty of their own specific characteristics?”

"This one belongs to the hell realms; this one belongs to the animal realm; this one belongs to the world of Yama; this one is a god; this one is a human; this one is on the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotrabhūmi*);

this one is an eighth-rank practitioner; this one is a stream-enterer; this one is a once-returner; this one is a non-returner; this one is an arhat; this one is a pratyekabuddha; this one is a bodhisattva; this one is a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."
“Blessed One, just as these persons are not apprehended, so too, Blessed One, karma is not apprehended;
and just as karma is not apprehended, so too, Blessed One, its maturation is not apprehended.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
"So it is, Subhūti, so it is, just as you say: in phenomena that are empty of their own specific characteristics, neither action nor its maturation is apprehended.
Those beings who do not directly realize phenomena that are empty of their own specific characteristics perform actions—whether misconduct or good conduct, whether with outflows or without outflows."
By means of their misconduct, they fall into the three lower realms—
whether into the hells, the animal realm, or the world of Yama;
by means of good conduct, they are reborn among gods and humans.
and they are reborn in the form realm with an indestructible body;
that is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of generosity and practices the perfection of ethical discipline.
Practicing the perfection of patience,
practicing the perfection of vigor, and practicing the perfection of meditative concentration.
Practicing in the perfection of wisdom, practicing in the perfection of skillful means,
and practicing in the perfection of aspiration;
while practicing the perfection of power, while practicing the perfection of knowledge,
and while practicing internal emptiness; (PSP_6-8:142)

Practicing while dwelling in external emptiness, practicing while dwelling in internal-external emptiness, and so on, up to practicing while dwelling in the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence.
Practicing in the applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path;
practicing in the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the liberations, the samādhis, the meditative absorptions, and the gateways of dhāraṇī;
and practicing in emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
Practicing in the five superknowledges,
practicing in the ten bodhisattva stages, and practicing in the ten powers of a Tathāgata.
Practicing in the four grounds of self-confidence,
practicing in the four analytical knowledges,
and practicing in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, he generates these flawless bodhisattva dharmas.

Having brought these to mind, he enters the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) accompanied by the retinue of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and thereby awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

Having awakened, he acts for the benefit of sentient beings; by performing that benefit, they do not again fall into ruin—that ruin through which they would fall back into the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) consisting of the five destinies.
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Furthermore, Blessed One, having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, was the cycle of existence consisting of the five destinies perceived by you?
The Blessed One replied: "No, Subhūti."
Subhūti said:
"But has any black or white karma been apprehended by the Blessed One?
The Blessed One said: "No, Subhūti."
Subhūti said:

"If nothing is apprehended, from where are the hells, the animal realm, and the world of Yama designated? From where are gods and humans designated? And from where are stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, and pratyekabuddhas designated?"
“How is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is designated as a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha?
The Blessed One said:
“Furthermore, Subhūti, do these beings know that all phenomena are empty of their own specific characteristics?”
Subhūti said: "No, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:

Subhūti, if sentient beings were to know thus: "All phenomena are empty of their own specific characteristics," then a bodhisattva would not set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening; and not having established himself in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, he would not liberate sentient beings from the three lower realms, up to and including the cycle of existence within the five destinies.

Therefore, Subhūti, because beings do not know that phenomena are empty of their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇaśūnya*), they are not liberated from the saṃsāra of the five destinies due to that ignorance.

Consequently, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having heard from those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, that all phenomena are empty of their own specific characteristics, should establish himself in unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

These phenomena do not exist in the way that foolish ordinary people are attached to them; those beings themselves conceptualize and perceive phenomena that are non-existent and unapprehendable— perceiving a self where there is no self, perceiving form where there is no form, perceiving sensation where there is no sensation, perceiving perception where there is no perception, and [perceiving] formations where there are no formations.

They perceive formations as formations, they perceive consciousness as consciousness, they perceive what are not aggregates as aggregates, they perceive elements as elements, they perceive bases as bases, they perceive dependent origination as dependent origination, they perceive dependently originated phenomena as dependently originated phenomena, and they perceive the factors of dependent origination as factors of dependent origination.

They perceive supramundane things as supramundane, and they perceive things with outflows as having outflows; they do not perceive things without outflows as being without outflows, they perceive unconditioned phenomena as conditioned phenomena,
and they perceive conditioned phenomena as unconditioned phenomena.
While these things do not exist, those with minds inverted by misconception perform karmic actions through body, speech, and mind;
they are not liberated from the saṃsāra of the five destinies.
Therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, practices the conduct of a bodhisattva after having integrated all wholesome dharmas within it.
By practicing that conduct, one awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Thus, the connection between action and its fruit consists in the activity of establishing what has been lost;
having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, [one realizes] suffering, the origin of suffering, and the cessation of suffering.
And he explains, teaches, reveals, discloses, analyzes, makes known, and establishes the path leading to the cessation of suffering.

Within these four noble truths, all wholesome qualities whatsoever are included— namely, the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma)— by means of which factors conducive to enlightenment the establishment of the Three Jewels occurs.
Which three?
The jewel of the Buddha, the jewel of the Dharma, and the jewel of the Saṅgha.
Through the appearance of these three jewels, sentient beings are completely liberated from the saṃsāra of the five destinies.
Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"But, Blessed One, do they attain parinirvāṇa through the knowledge of suffering, or do they attain parinirvāṇa through suffering?"
Or do they attain parinirvāṇa through the knowledge of origin, or rather through origin itself? Or do they attain parinirvāṇa through the knowledge of cessation?
Now, do they attain final nirvana by means of cessation,
or do they attain final nirvana by means of the knowledge of the path, or do they attain final nirvana by means of the path?
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
"Subhūti, they do not attain parinirvāṇa through the knowledge of suffering, nor through suffering; nor through the knowledge of the origin, nor through the origin."
They do not attain parinirvāṇa through the knowledge of cessation nor through cessation, nor through the knowledge of the path nor through the path;
rather, Subhūti, that which is the equality of the four noble truths— that, I have declared, is parinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, they do not attain parinirvāṇa through suffering, nor through the knowledge of suffering;
nor through the origin, nor through the knowledge of the origin;
nor through cessation, nor through the knowledge of cessation.
They do not attain parinirvāṇa by means of the path, nor by means of the knowledge of the path.
Then, the Venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, what is the equality of the four noble truths?"
The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, where there is neither suffering nor knowledge of suffering, where there is neither origination nor knowledge of origination,"
Where there is neither cessation nor knowledge of cessation,
where there is neither the path nor knowledge of the path—
but rather, Subhūti, that which is the suchness, the non-falsity, the non-other-suchness, and the true nature (dharmatā) of these four noble truths.

The realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the stability of phenomena (*dharma-sthititā*), and the fixed order of phenomena (*dharma-niyāmatā*)— whether Tathāgatas arise or whether Tathāgatas do not arise— this true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) remains constant; this realm of phenomena proceeds as a nature that is non-forgetful and a nature that does not decline.
The bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing in the perfection of wisdom, practices for the sake of awakening to the truths;
he practices in such a way as to awaken to the truths,
and in accordance with how the truths are to be awakened to.
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:

"But how, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, practice for the sake of awakening to the truths, such that by so practicing he awakens to the truths?"
Having attained full awakening, one practices for the sake of suchness;
practicing in this way, one does not fall to the level of a śrāvaka nor to the level of a pratyekabuddha, but enters the fixed course of a bodhisattva.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
There is no phenomenon whose end he perceives;
and he perceives in such a way that he does not apprehend any phenomenon whatsoever.
Not apprehending anything, he perceives that all phenomena are empty.
Whether it be included within the truth or not included within the truth, he sees all of it as empty;
seeing thus, that bodhisattva mahāsattva who has entered into the fixed course becomes established on the stage of the lineage (*gotrabhūmi*).

For one established on that stage of the lineage (gotrabhūmi), there is no falling from the summit (mūrdhavinipāta) by which one might fall into the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha;
remaining here on this stage of the lineage, he generates the four dhyānas,
the four immeasurables (apramāṇa), and the four formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti).
Abiding here on the stage of calm abiding (śamatha), he discerns all phenomena and realizes the four noble truths;
he fully understands suffering, yet he does not give rise to a mind that takes suffering as its object.
He abandons origination, yet does not give rise to a mind that has origination as its object;
he realizes cessation, yet does not give rise to a mind that has cessation as its object;
he cultivates the path, yet does not give rise to a mind that has the path as its object.
Except for a mind inclined toward awakening, entering into awakening, and leaning toward awakening, he perceives all phenomena as they truly are.
Subhūti asked:
"How, Blessed One, does he perceive all phenomena as they truly are?"
The Blessed One said:
"He perceives all phenomena as empty.
Subhūti said:
"How, Blessed One, does one see all phenomena as empty?
The Blessed One replied:
"Namely, one sees all phenomena as empty of their own specific characteristics."
Whoever, by means of this very kind of insight, perceives that all phenomena are empty and does not perceive the intrinsic nature of any phenomenon—
that intrinsic nature in which one might abide and realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Subhūti said:
"If that is so, Blessed One, then awakening has non-existence as its intrinsic nature.
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti, so it is, just as you say; awakening, Subhūti, has non-existence as its intrinsic nature."

This was not created by a Buddha, nor by a Pratyekabuddha, nor by an Arhat, nor even by those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who practice this samādhi; rather, it is that which sentient beings neither know nor see.
Therefore, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, teaches the Dharma to sentient beings through skillful means.
Thus is the activity of entering into the vision of truth.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya said this to the Blessed One:

"If, Blessed One, all phenomena have non-existence as their intrinsic nature, then, Blessed One, how should a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom— who wishes to train in the training of a Bodhisattva— train with regard to form?"
How should one train in regard to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness?

How should one train in regard to the sense-base of the eye, the sense-base of the ear, the sense-base of the nose, the sense-base of the tongue, the sense-base of the body, and the sense-base of the mind?
How should one train in regard to the sense-base of forms, the sense-base of sounds, the sense-base of odors, the sense-base of tastes, the sense-base of tangibles, and the sense-base of phenomena?
In the eye-element, the form-element, and the eye-consciousness-element; in the ear-element, the sound-element, and the ear-consciousness-element;
in the nose-element, the odor-element, and the nose-consciousness-element.

How should one train in the tongue element, the taste element, and the tongue-consciousness element; in the body element, the tangible object element, and the body-consciousness element; and in the mind element, the mental-object element, and the mind-consciousness element?
How should one train regarding the sphere of visual contact, and the spheres of auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, and mental contact?
How should one train regarding ignorance, volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age and death?
How should one train regarding the truth of suffering, the truth of the origin, the truth of cessation, and the truth of the path?

Regarding material phenomena and immaterial phenomena, visible and invisible, resistant and non-resistant, conditioned and unconditioned, with outflows and without outflows, blameworthy and blameless, inferior and sublime, internal or external, seen, heard, thought, or cognized, past, future, or present, and wholesome, unwholesome, determinate, or indeterminate.

How should one train regarding those things associated with the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm; regarding those pertaining to the stage of training (*śaikṣa*), the stage beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and that which pertains to neither training nor beyond training?
How should one train regarding attachment, aversion, pride, ignorance, views, and doubt?

How should one train in stinginess and generosity, in immorality and ethical discipline, in malice and patience, in laziness and vigor, in distraction and meditative concentration, and in faulty wisdom and true wisdom?
How should one train in conceptualization, emptiness, signs, the signless, the wrongly directed, and the rightly directed; and in wholesome and unwholesome phenomena?
"How should one train regarding afflictions, the abandonment of afflictions, defilement, purification, saṃsāra, and the realm of nirvāṇa?
How should one train in the qualities of a Buddha?
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya:

Maitreya, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom who wishes to train in the training of a bodhisattva should train thus: "Form is a mere name," and "feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are mere names," up to [the end of the aggregates].
"One should train in the thought, 'These are the Buddha-dharmas.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya said this to the Blessed One:
'Blessed One, when this designation is perceived as having a real basis (savastuka),' "

That which is called "form"—this designation is perceived as having a real basis; that which is called "feeling," "perception," "volitional formations," and "consciousness"—this designation is perceived as having a real basis; and so on, up to "the qualities of a Buddha"—this designation is perceived as having a real basis.
That is to say, based on the signs of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-nimitta*),

how then should a bodhisattva mahāsattva train in the thought that "form is merely a name," and how should they train in the thought that "feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are merely names," and so on, up to "the qualities of a Buddha are merely names"?

In that case, since it is without a real basis, even that name which is "mere name" is not applicable— namely, the mere name "this is form," the mere name "this is feeling, perception, mental formations," and so on, up to "the qualities of a Buddha. When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya:
This name "form" is an adventitious designation superimposed upon that entity which is the sign of conditioned phenomena;
this name "feeling," "perception," "volitional formations," and "consciousness" is an adventitious designation superimposed [upon them];
and this name "all factors of a Buddha" is an adventitious designation superimposed [upon them].

And because, Maitreya, by means of that sign of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-nimitta*), there arises with respect to things the conceptual cognition "this is form" (*rūpa*) regarding the name "form"— an arrival of cognition, an experiential perception— therefore, Maitreya, it should be understood through this very method.

This designation "form," this "feeling," "perception," "volitional formations," and "consciousness," and all these up to "the qualities of a Buddha"— this name has been adventitiously applied to that entity which is the sign of conditioned phenomena.
What do you think of this?

"Maitreya, in this case, for a certain person, there might be a perception, a designation, a name, a conventional expression, or an attachment toward that very object which is the sign of conditioned phenomena.
Maitreya said: "So it is, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said:
"Therefore, Maitreya, by this method also you should understand it thus:
this single adventitious designation, namely 'form,' has been superimposed upon that entity which is the sign of conditioned phenomena."
That is to say: feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; that is to say, everything up to the qualities of a Buddha.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya said this to the Blessed One:
"If this is so, Blessed One, then the intrinsic nature of form would indeed be apprehended—that thing which is the sign of conditioned phenomena."
"Based upon which there arises a name, a notion, a designation, and conventional usage— namely,
'this is form,' 'this is feeling,' 'perception,' 'formative factors,' and 'consciousness,' and so on, up to 'these are the qualities of a Buddha.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya:
Regarding things that have the conditioned as their sign, there is the name, the notion, the designation, and the conventional usage "form.
What do you think, Maitreya: is that the intrinsic nature of form, or is it merely a designation?
Maitreya said:
"O Blessed One, this which is called 'mere designation' is indeed mere designation.
The Blessed One said:
In that case, Maitreya, how is it that you think thus: "The intrinsic nature of form has been apprehended"?

For that thing which is the basis of the signs of conditioned phenomena, depending upon which there arises a name, a designation, a conceptualization, and a conventional expression, namely "this is form"—[how can its intrinsic nature be apprehended?]* *Note: The ellipsis indicates the rhetorical question implied by the context of the original text.*

"Namely, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to and including the qualities of a Buddha. What do you think, Maitreya? Is there an intrinsic nature to that feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness, and so on, up to the qualities of a Buddha, or is it merely a conceptual designation?
Maitreya replied:
“Blessed One, this which is called ‘mere designation’ is indeed mere designation.
The Blessed One said:

“Maitreya, how is it that such a thought occurs to you: that there is an apprehension of the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness, and so on, up to the qualities of a Buddha?”
Maitreya said: "Blessed One, if form is merely a name, a notion, a convention, a designation, and a worldly expression;
and if, Blessed One, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to the qualities of a Buddha, are merely names, notions, conventions, designations, and worldly expressions,"
This being so, the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is not actually perceived;
for that which is called "form" is merely a name, a notion, a convention, a designation, and a linguistic usage— and this being so, the intrinsic nature is not actually perceived.
"Regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to the qualities of a Buddha—
this is merely a matter of name, designation, convention, conceptualization, and worldly usage.
The Blessed One said:
What do you think, Maitreya? That which is called "form" is merely a name, a designation, a convention, a conceptual construct, and a worldly usage;
that which is called "feeling," "perception," or "volitional formations" [is likewise].

"From 'consciousness' up to 'the qualities of a Buddha,' is there any perception of arising or passing away, or of affliction or purification, even regarding that which is merely name, designation, convention, conceptual construction, and worldly usage? Maitreya replied:
"Certainly not, Blessed One.
[The Blessed One said:
"Maitreya, why do you think that the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—even up to the qualities of a Buddha—is indeed apprehended?"
Thus, and so forth;
Maitreya said:
"But, Blessed One, is form then entirely non-existent by way of its own characteristic?"

"But, Blessed One, is it that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do not exist at all by way of their own specific characteristics, and that even the Buddha-qualities do not exist at all?
The Blessed One said:
“Maitreya, I do not say that form does not exist at all in terms of its own characteristic;
Maitreya, I do not say that feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness, and so on, up to the qualities of a Buddha, do not exist at all in terms of their own characteristics.
Maitreya said:
“Blessed One, how does form exist?
How do feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—up to and including the qualities of a Buddha—exist?
The Blessed One replied:

“Maitreya, form exists by way of worldly convention and linguistic usage, but not in the ultimate sense. Maitreya, feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness, and so on, up to the qualities of a Buddha, exist by way of worldly convention and linguistic usage, but not in the ultimate sense. Maitreya said:
"Indeed, Blessed One, as I understand the meaning of what the Blessed One has spoken, the realm (*dhātu*) is ultimately inexpressible. If, Blessed One, the realm is ultimately inexpressible,
then how is it that with regard to that thing which is the sign of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-nimitta*), the adventitious designation 'form' (*rūpa*) is superimposed?"

How then is it that this entity which is the basis for formative forces (*saṃskāra-nimitta-vastu*)—in which feeling, perception, formations, consciousness, and so forth up to the qualities of a Buddha are superimposed as adventitious designations—is in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*) non-existent? If that is not the ultimate reality, how can the realm be inexpressible? It would be illogical to say that the entity which is the basis for formative forces is the inexpressible realm.
The Blessed One said:

"In that case, Maitreya, I shall question you on this matter; explain it exactly as it seems appropriate to you. What do you think, Maitreya: how does the activity of wisdom occur for you within the ineffable realm?"
"At that time, do you perceive any entity characterized by formative forces (*saṃskāra*) into which this adventitious designation has been superimposed—
namely, 'this is form,' 'feeling,' 'perception,' 'formative forces,' 'consciousness,' and so on, up to 'the qualities of a Buddha'?
Maitreyī said:"
"Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Therefore, Maitreya, by this very method you should understand it thus:"
That entity which is the basis for the signs of conditioned phenomena is neither different from the ineffable realm (*nirabhilāpya-dhātu*), nor is it not different.

And that ineffable realm is neither different from that entity which is the basis for the signs of conditioned phenomena, nor is it not different—wherein this adventitious designation is applied, namely: "this is form," "feeling," "perception," "formative forces," "consciousness," up to "the qualities of a Buddha."

Maitreya, if the ineffable realm were something other than the entity characterized by conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-nimitta*), then ordinary beings would attain parinirvāṇa at all times; yet they do not.

Furthermore, Maitreya, if the ineffable realm were not other than the entity characterized by conditioned formations, then even that characteristic sign (*nimitta*) would not be perceived, through which there might be a penetration of that ineffable realm. Therefore, Maitreya, by this method as well, you should understand it thus.
The ineffable realm is neither different from that entity which is the sign of conditioned phenomena,

nor is it non-different from it— that ineffable realm into which this adventitious designation is superimposed, namely: "this is form," "this is feeling," "this is perception," "these are formations," "this is consciousness," and so on,
up to "these are the qualities of a Buddha."

Maitreya said: "Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while abiding in the range of wisdom that is bound to the ineffable realm, does not perceive that basis for the signs of conditioned phenomena upon which this adventitious designation is superimposed— namely, 'this is form,' 'this is feeling,' 'this is perception,' 'these are formations,' 'this is consciousness,' up to 'these are the buddha-qualities'— "
"In that case, Blessed One, how is it that what exists is not apprehended?
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya:
"Indeed, Maitreya, for that entity characterized by conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-nimitta*), there is neither any state of existence nor any state of non-existence. For what reason? Because..."

"For at whatever time, Maitreya, you conceptualize that object which is the sign of formative forces (*saṃskāra-nimitta*), at that time that object which is the sign of formative forces comes to be grasped through conceptualization.

Or again, at that time when you abide in the movement of wisdom connected to the ineffable realm (*nirabhilāpya-dhātu*), you do not conceptualize; at that time it comes to be grasped without conceptualization.
Maitreya said:
"So it is, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"But if that is so, Maitreya, this is merely a conceptual construction—namely, the entity characterized by conditioned formations, upon which this adventitious designation has been superimposed."
Whether it be "this is form," "feeling," "perception," "formative factors," "consciousness," up to "the qualities of a Buddha"—
for one who abides either in mere conceptualization or in the non-conceptual realm where conceptualizations have ceased, what existence or non-existence can be perceived of that [reality],
wherein these adventitious designations are superimposed, namely: "this is form," "feeling," "perception," "formative factors," "consciousness," up to "the qualities of a Buddha"?
Maitreya said:

"Blessed One, by how many modes should a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, while abiding in skillfulness regarding the differentiation of phenomena, comprehend the designation for the differentiation of form?

By how many modes should he comprehend the designation for the differentiation of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to the designation for the differentiation of the qualities of a Buddha?"
The Blessed One said:

"Maitreya, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, abiding in skillfulness regarding the differentiation of phenomena, should comprehend the designation for the differentiation of form;
he should comprehend the designation for the differentiation of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to the designation for the differentiation of the qualities of a buddha."
Namely, that this is imagined form, this is discriminated form, and this is the true nature of form;

or that this is imagined feeling, this is discriminated feeling, and this is the true nature of feeling; or that this is imagined perception, this is discriminated perception, and this is the true nature of perception.

Namely: these are the conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) that are imagined (parikalpita), these are the conditioned phenomena that are conceptually constructed (vikalpita), and these are the conditioned phenomena that are the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā);
this is consciousness (vijñāna) that is imagined, this is consciousness that is conceptually constructed, and this is consciousness that is the true nature of phenomena; and so on, up to:

these are the Buddha-qualities (buddhadharma) that are imagined, these are the Buddha-qualities that are conceptually constructed, and these are the Buddha-qualities that are the true nature of phenomena.
Maitreya said:
"Blessed One, what is imagined form? What is conceptually constructed form?"
What is form as the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*)?
O Blessed One, what is imagined feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness?
What is conceptually constructed feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness?
What is the true nature (*dharmatā*) of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness?
Furthermore, Blessed One, what are the imagined Buddha-qualities? What are the conceptually constructed Buddha-qualities?
“What are the Buddha-dharmas of the nature of reality (dharmatā)?
The Blessed One said:

“Maitreya, that which, based upon the designation, name, concept, convention, and worldly usage of ‘form’ with respect to that entity characterized by conditioned phenomena, is imagined as having the intrinsic nature of form—this is the imagined [nature].”
Maitreya, regarding that basis which has the nature of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*),
whatever is designated by name, concept, convention, designation, and worldly usage as "feeling," "perception," "volitional formations," or "consciousness," up to and including the "Buddha-dharmas"—
all this is based upon the intrinsic nature of feeling, the intrinsic nature of perception, the intrinsic nature of volitional formations, and the intrinsic nature of consciousness.
To the extent that this conceptualization is conceptualized as having the nature of the Buddha-qualities—

wherein feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to these conceptualized Buddha-qualities [are included]— furthermore, the state of that thing characterized by formative factors (*saṃskāra*) abiding in the nature of mere conceptualization, and its expressibility in dependence upon conceptualization: therein lies this name, notion, convention, designation, and worldly usage.
"Form," "feeling," "perception," "formative factors," "consciousness," and so on, up to "the qualities of a Buddha."
"This is form as it is conceptually constructed; this is feeling as it is conceptually constructed; this is perception as it is conceptually constructed;

these are mental formations as they are conceptually constructed; this is consciousness as it is conceptually constructed; these are the Buddha-qualities as they are conceptually constructed. Whether Tathāgatas arise or do not arise, this nature of phenomena (dharmatā), this stability of phenomena (dharmasthititā), this realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) remains constant—by virtue of which [this is so].

In terms of its imagined nature, that discriminated form is eternally, at all times, constantly, and for all eternity, devoid of intrinsic nature; it is the selflessness of phenomena, suchness, and the limit of reality. This is the true nature of form; this is the true nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;
these, up to and including the qualities of a Buddha, are likewise.
Maitreya said: "Blessed One, among these three kinds of form, which form is to be regarded as lacking substantiality, and which is to be regarded as possessing substantiality?"

What is that which is to be seen as neither without substance nor with substance, being manifested by the ultimate truth? Blessed One, among these three feelings, three perceptions, three formations, three consciousnesses, and so on up to the Buddha-qualities— which are to be seen as without substance, and which are to be seen as with substance?
Which are those that should be seen as neither substanceless nor substantial, being manifested by the ultimate truth?
The Blessed One said:
"Maitreya, that which is imagined form (parikalpita-rūpa) should be seen as substanceless."

That form which is conceptually constructed—this conceptually constructed form should be regarded as having substantiality by way of its basis in substantiality, but not by way of independent occurrence.
That form which is the true nature (*dharmatā*) should be regarded as neither non-substantial nor substantial, but as being characterized by ultimate reality.

Maitreya, that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness which are conceptually constructed, and likewise those conceptually constructed Buddha-qualities—all these should be regarded as non-substantial.

Whatever feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are conceptually constructed, and even those Buddha-qualities that are conceptually constructed—these, by virtue of having a conceptually constructed substantiality, should be regarded as substantial, but not by way of independent existence.

As for that which is the true nature (*dharmatā*) of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, and those which are the Buddha-qualities of the true nature, Maitreya, they are neither non-substantial nor substantial; they are manifested from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
Maitreya said:

"Blessed One, as for what was said by the Blessed One— that this enumeration of the non-dual has been made, namely 'form,' and that this enumeration of the non-dual has been made, namely 'feeling,' 'perception,' 'volitional formations,' 'consciousness,' up to 'the qualities of a Buddha'— it is thus when there is the designation of the differentiation of form;
and likewise when there is the designation of the differentiation of feeling, perception, volitional formations, consciousness, up to the qualities of a Buddha."

With what intention was it taught by the Blessed One that this enumeration of non-duality has been made— namely, "form," this enumeration of non-duality having been made; "feeling," "perception," "volitional formations," "consciousness," and so on up to "the qualities of a Buddha"— this enumeration of non-duality having been made?
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Maitreya? Is that which is the lack of substantiality in conceptually constructed form itself form, or is it not?"
Maitreya said:
"Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
Furthermore, as for that which there is merely a name, a designation, a conceptual construct, and a conventional expression—namely, "form"—is that indeed form?
Maitreya replied:
"Certainly not, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said:
"Therefore, Maitreya, by this method it should be understood that whatever is imagined form is neither form nor non-form; moreover, that which is neither form nor non-form is non-dual."

And it was with this in mind that I said: "This reckoning of non-duality has been made, namely, 'this is form'. What do you think, Maitreya? Is that which is the substantiality of conceptually constructed form—that depending upon which there occurs the name, designation, conceptualization, and conventional usage 'form'—actually that very form?
Maitreya replied:
"Certainly not, Blessed One.
[The Blessed One said:
"What do you think?"
“Maitreya, is that which is the nature of imagined form— characterized by non-existence through an imagined sign— that indeed form?
Maitreya replied,
“Certainly not, Blessed One.”
The Blessed One said:
"Therefore, Maitreya, by this method you should understand it thus:
that which is conceptually constructed as form is neither form nor non-form; moreover, that which is neither form nor non-form is non-dual."

And it was with reference to this that I said: "This reckoning of non-duality has been made, namely, 'this is form. What do you think, Maitreya? Is that which is the true nature (*dharmatā*) of form—the state of being characterized by selflessness—that indeed form?
Maitreya replied:
"Certainly not, Blessed One.
[The Blessed One said:
"Furthermore, that which is suchness, the true nature of form—the true nature of form—is that indeed form?"
Maitreya said:
"Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
Therefore, Maitreya, by this method it should be understood as follows:
that which is the true nature (*dharmatā*) of form is neither form nor non-form; and that which is neither form nor non-form is non-dual.
It was with reference to this that I spoke, having established this enumeration of the non-dual, saying: "This is form," and likewise regarding feeling, perception, and mental formations.
The same should be applied in detail from consciousness up to the qualities of a Buddha.
Maitreya said:
"Blessed One, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom who is thus skilled in the characteristic of non-duality regarding form..."

Regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness, and so on up to the qualities of a Buddha— how does one who is thus skilled in the characteristic of non-duality, having abandoned the two extremes and entered upon the middle way, achieve full comprehension of characteristics?
How is the abandonment of characteristics [to be understood]?
How is the realization of characteristics [to be understood]?
How is the cultivation of characteristics to be viewed?
The Blessed One said: "Maitreya, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom— who, having avoided the two extremes, has entered upon the middle way—
that which is neither the full comprehension nor the non-comprehension of form is itself his full comprehension."

That which is neither full comprehension nor non-comprehension of feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness, and so on up to the qualities of a Buddha— this very thing is his full comprehension.
That which is neither abandonment nor non-abandonment of form— this very thing is his abandonment.
That which is neither the abandoning nor the non-abandoning of feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness, and so on up to the Buddha-qualities—this alone is their abandoning.
That which is neither the realization nor the non-realization of form—this alone is its realization.
That which is the non-realization of feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness, and so on up to the Buddha-qualities.
This very non-realization is his realization for the sake of abandoning form; it is neither the cultivation nor the non-cultivation of the path—this indeed is his cultivation.

Likewise, for the sake of abandoning feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness, and so on up to the qualities of a Buddha, it is neither the cultivation nor the non-cultivation of the path—this indeed is his cultivation.
Maitreya said:
"Blessed One, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom, who is thus endowed with full understanding, abandonment, realization, and cultivation, what is nirvāṇa?
The Blessed One replied:
"Maitreya, the nirvāṇa of bodhisattva mahāsattvas is profound, supremely profound. Maitreya asked:
"For what reason is the nirvāṇa of bodhisattva mahāsattvas so profound, supremely profound?"
The Blessed One said: "Maitreya, the nirvāṇa of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas is that nirvāṇa which is not non-nirvāṇa; for that reason, it is called profound, supremely profound.
Maitreya said:
“Blessed One, how is it that for bodhisattva mahāsattvas there is no nirvāṇa?
The Blessed One replied:
“Maitreya, because they have undertaken the welfare of others, their non-abandonment of saṃsāra is not [mere] nirvāṇa.”
"Starting from one's own welfare, not abandoning nirvāṇa does not mean [not abandoning] nirvāṇa.
Maitreya said: "Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, starting from the welfare of others, does not abandon saṃsāra, how is it that by not abandoning saṃsāra, nirvāṇa is not abandoned by him?"
“Bhagavān, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not abandon nirvāṇa by undertaking it for his own sake, then because he does not abandon nirvāṇa, how is it that saṃsāra is not abandoned by him?
The Bhagavān said:
“In this regard, Maitreya, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not even conceptualize saṃsāra as ‘saṃsāra.’”
He does not even conceptualize nirvāṇa as nirvāṇa;
for him who thus does not conceptualize, this is equal—namely, both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa. Why is that?

For in this way, just as he is not agitated by cyclic existence because he does not conceptualize cyclic existence as cyclic existence, so too he is not agitated by nirvāṇa because he does not conceptualize nirvāṇa as nirvāṇa. Thus, for one established in the realm of non-conceptuality through this reasoning, there is neither the abandonment of cyclic existence nor the abandonment of nirvāṇa.
Maitreya said:
But, Blessed One, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom is established in the realm of non-conceptualization, how is it that saṃsāra is neither abandoned nor grasped,
and thus remains unabandoned?
How is it that nirvāṇa is neither abandoned nor grasped, and thus remains unabandoned?
The Blessed One said:

"Maitreya, I do not speak of such grasping or non-grasping regarding saṃsāra, nor do I speak of such grasping or non-grasping regarding nirvāṇa; rather, Maitreya, it is for one practicing the perfection of wisdom..."
For a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has attained mastery over the mind through knowledge that takes the non-conceptual realm as its object, and who,
by means of skillful means, manifests the appearance of cyclic existence in world-systems throughout the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges—
I declare that such bodhisattva mahāsattvas do not abandon cyclic existence even though they have entered final nirvāṇa.
"Based on emptiness and the non-abiding in the realm of apprehension, I speak of the non-abandonment of nirvāṇa.
Maitreya said:
"Blessed One, how should the complete characteristic of non-conceptualization be viewed?"

The Blessed One said: "Maitreya, whatever is form, whatever is feeling, whatever is perception, whatever are mental formations, and whatever is consciousness— up to whatever are the qualities of a Buddha— and whatever is the emptiness of form, whatever is the emptiness of feeling, whatever is the emptiness of perception, and whatever is the emptiness of mental formations..."

Maitreya, that which is the emptiness of consciousness and so forth up to the Buddha-qualities, and the non-duality of existence and non-existence regarding both those phenomena and that emptiness, as well as the absence of conceptual proliferation— this, Maitreya, should be seen as the complete definition of non-conceptualization.
Maitreya said:
“Blessed One, is it the case that for all śrāvakas there is a definitive, one-sided establishment in nirvāṇa?
The Blessed One said: “Not so, Maitreya.”
For what reason?
Because, Maitreya, this world consists of various elements (*nānādhātuka*) and possesses many elements; and within those various elements, the lineages and origins of sentient beings are observed.
There exists, Maitreya, that lineage and birth of sentient beings.

There is that lineage which, from the very beginning, seeks a sublime distinction and attains a sublime distinction; there is that lineage which, from the very beginning, seeks an inferior distinction, attains an inferior distinction, and is satisfied with just that;
and there is that lineage which, from the very beginning, seeks an inferior distinction, attains an inferior distinction, yet is not satisfied with merely that.
Beyond that, he aspires for a sublime distinction and attains precisely that sublime distinction.
Maitreya said:
"Blessed One, as for the third kind of being, who is on the stage of the lineage (gotrabhūmi)..."

Having attained arhatship, while aspiring for unexcelled perfect enlightenment yet not being subject to rebirth, how does he attain it? And as for his rebirth, the Blessed One said regarding his practice:
"No, Maitreya, I do not designate his rebirth as being under the power of karma and afflictions."
"Nevertheless, I declare that even for an Arhat, rebirth is inconceivable and leads to the further shore of nirvāṇa.
Maitreya said:
"It is wonderful, Blessed One, how noble is the intention of the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, and how great is their sublime resolve!"
Since they now seek excellence that is sublime from the very beginning and attain precisely that sublime excellence,
what, Blessed One, is the magnanimity of intention of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas?
And what is the resolute intention of magnanimity?
The Blessed One said:

"Maitreya, it is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, being indifferent to the states of Śakra, a world-protector, or a universal monarch, and to all forms of worldly prosperity, [dedicates] the roots of virtue toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment."
And in those [states], this lack of attachment and lack of restraint is the noble resolve of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas.

Furthermore, desiring that happiness of non-attachment, that happiness of being unrestrained, and that happiness of cessation to be shared with all sentient beings, the bodhisattva mahāsattvas dedicate their roots of virtue toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Namely, that they do not abandon cyclic existence—this is to be seen as their resolute intention of magnanimity.
Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, the qualities of the Bodhisattvas are wonderful and marvelous."
“Blessed One, the training of a bodhisattva is wonderful and marvelous.

Blessed One, a son of good family or a daughter of good family who wishes to attain the qualities of a bodhisattva and to generate the mind set on unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening should do so because it is wonderful and marvelous.
Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
If, Blessed One, all phenomena have non-existence as their intrinsic nature, and they were not made by Buddhas, nor by Pratyekabuddhas,

nor by Arhats, nor by Non-returners, nor by Once-returners, nor by Stream-enterers, nor even by those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas— then from where is the differentiation or the establishment of these phenomena known?
"These are hell-beings; these are animals; these are those in the world of Yama; these are gods; these are humans.
By this karma they are hell-beings; by this karma they are animals; by this karma they are those in the world of Yama; by this karma they are humans;
by this karma they are gods of the desire realm."
By this karma one becomes a member of the retinue of Brahmā (Brahmapārṣadya), a minister of Brahmā (Brahmapurohita), or a Great Brahmā (Mahābrahmā);

by this karma one becomes a deity of Limited Light (Parīttābha), Immeasurable Light (Apramāṇābha), or Utmost Purity of Light (Ābhāsvara); by this karma one becomes a deity of Limited Beauty (Parīttaśubha), Immeasurable Beauty (Apramāṇaśubha), or Total Purity (Śubhakṛtsna).
By this karma, there are the Anabhrakas, Puṇyaprasavas, and Bṛhatphalas; by this karma, the Asprhas, Atapas, Sudṛśas, Sudarśanas, and Akaniṣṭhas;

and by this karma, the attainments of the sphere of infinite space, the attainments of the sphere of infinite consciousness, the attainments of the sphere of nothingness, and the attainments of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

"By this karma one becomes a stream-enterer, a once-returner, a non-returner, an arhat, or a pratyekabuddha; by this karma one becomes a bodhisattva mahāsattva; and by this karma one becomes a tathāgata, arhat, and perfectly enlightened buddha. For, Blessed One, in the case of a non-entity, there is no action whatsoever by which one might go to hell."

Whether he goes to the animal realm, the world of Yama, the realm of gods, or the realm of humans; whether he goes to the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; whether he will attain the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, or arhatship; or whether he will attain solitary enlightenment;
or whether a bodhisattva mahāsattva will practice on the bodhisattva path—[all this is known].
"Or he will attain the knowledge of all aspects,
having attained which he will liberate sentient beings from saṃsāra.
Then the Blessed One said this to the venerable Subhūti:
"So it is, Subhūti, so it is, just as you say.
For, Subhūti, that which is non-existent has no action, no activity, and no fruit.
Indeed, Subhūti, foolish common people, who are unskilled in the noble dharmas, do not know that dharmas have non-existence as their intrinsic nature."
Through conceptualizations arising from perversion, they establish various karmas; for them,

there arise corresponding personal existences, whether as denizens of hell, or as animals, or as inhabitants of the world of Yama, or among humans, or among the gods of the desire realm, or among those of the form realm.
Whether among the gods or among the gods of the formless realm, up to the point where there is no non-existence, there is neither karma, nor action, nor fruit;
moreover, that which is non-existence is simply non-existence itself. Furthermore, as Subhūti has said:

"He who is a stream-enterer, a once-returner, a non-returner, an arhat, a pratyekabuddha, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the knowledge of the path, or a Tathāgata who attains the knowledge of all aspects."

What do you think, Subhūti? Is it not the case that the path is non-existence, the fruit of stream-entry is non-existence, the fruit of once-returning is non-existence, the fruit of non-returning is non-existence, arhatship is non-existence, pratyekabuddhahood is non-existence,
and so on up to omniscience is non-existence?

Subhūti said: "O Blessed One, the path is non-existence; the fruit of stream-entry is non-existence; the fruit of once-returning is non-existence; the fruit of non-returning is non-existence; arhatship is non-existence; solitary awakening is non-existence; and so on, up to the knowledge of all aspects, which is non-existence."
The Blessed One said:
"Furthermore, Subhūti, does a non-existent dharma attain a non-existent dharma?
Subhūti replied:
"Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"For in this way, Subhūti, that which is non-existence and that which is the path—all these dharmas are neither conjoined nor disjoined."
"Subhūti, those which are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and of a single characteristic— namely, the characteristicless—

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom through skill in means, [he perceives] those beings who are attached to the four perversions regarding the five aggregates: those who perceive the impermanent as permanent, the selfless as self, and suffering as happiness."
"To those who are attached to things with the perception of beauty regarding what is beautiful, he detaches them from those various things.
This is the activity of establishing [beings] in the four perversions.
Then, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:

“Blessed One, is there a non-entity that is real, existent, suchness, and non-falsity, wherein foolish common people, by means of the adherence ‘this is an entity,’ become attached; and having become attached, they perform actions— real, existent, suchness, and non-falsity— by which action they are not liberated from the saṃsāra of the five destinies?”
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, there is not even a thing as small as the tip of a hair that exists wherein foolish ordinary people, while abiding, perform karmic formations, except through perversion."
Subhūti said:
"How, Blessed One, do foolish ordinary people perform karmic formations through perversion?
The Blessed One said:
Therefore, Subhūti, I shall provide you with a simile to further establish this very point, so that the wise may understand it.
What do you think?
“Subhūti, is there any real entity in a dream where a dreamer, being situated therein, might enjoy the five strands of sensual pleasure?
Subhūti replied:
“Blessed One, if even the dream itself does not exist, how much less could a dreamer, being situated therein, enjoy the five strands of sensual pleasure?”
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Is there any dharma—whether worldly or supramundane, with outflows or without outflows, conditioned or unconditioned—that is not like a dream?"
Subhūti said:
"Blessed One, there is no dharma whatsoever—whether conditioned or unconditioned, with outflows or without outflows, mundane or supramundane—that is not like a dream.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Does any fivefold cycle of existence exist within a dream?
Subhūti replied:
"Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think?"
“Subhūti, is there any cultivation of the path in a dream, by means of which cultivation of the path one would neither become afflicted nor purified?
Subhūti replied:
"Certainly not, Blessed One. That dream, Blessed One, is not a real entity; it is non-conceptual and cannot be designated by any words or syllables.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think?"

"Subhūti, when a reflection is seen in the surface of a mirror, does it have any real substance that could perform an action, such that by performing that action it would go to hell, or to the animal realm,
or to the world of Yama? Subhūti replied:
"Certainly not, Blessed One. That reflection, Blessed One, is not a real entity, except as a deception for foolish common people. How then could it have karma?
What karma, having been performed, would cause it to go to hell, or to the animal realm, or to the world of Yama?
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Is there any cultivation of the path for him, by means of which cultivation of the path he would neither become afflicted nor purified?
Subhūti said:
“No, Blessed One; that reflection, Blessed One, is not a real entity.
How, then, could there be cultivation of the path for it, by relying upon which cultivation of the path one would neither become defiled nor purified?
The Blessed One said:
What do you think, Subhūti? Does that echo which issues forth from the vicinity of rivers, thickets, forests, mountains, caves, open spaces,
or water have any karma such that, by performing that karma, it would go to hell?

"Would he go to the animal realm or the world of Yama, or would he go among humans, or among the gods of the desire realm, or among the gods of the form realm, or among the gods of the formless realm?
Subhūti replied:
"No, Blessed One, that echo is not a substantial entity; how could it have karma?

Having performed what karma would one go to hell, or to the animal realm, or to the world of Yama, or go among humans, or among the gods of the desire realm, or among the gods of the form realm, or among the gods of the formless realm?"
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Does that echo have any cultivation of the path, by depending upon which cultivation of the path it would neither become afflicted nor purified?"

Subhūti said: "No, Blessed One. Since that echo, Blessed One, does not exist at all, how could there be a cultivation of the path for it, by relying upon which cultivation of the path one would neither become afflicted nor purified?"
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Is that perception of water in a mirage where there is no water, or the perception of a river in what are not rivers, or the perception of a city in what are not cities?"
Is there for that perception of a mirage as a garden any karmic action— having performed which action one would go to hell, or to the animal realm, or to the world of Yama;
or whether among humans, or among the gods of the desire realm, or among the gods of the form realm, or among the gods of the formless realm— that such a destination would be reached?

Subhūti said: "No, Blessed One. Blessed One, in that mirage there is absolutely no water, nor is there any river, nor any city, nor any grove; it is nothing other than a perversion of perception and a delusion of the eye. How, then, could there be any action for it?"
Whatever karma one might perform by way of formative activity such that one would go to hell, or to the animal realm,
or to the world of Yama; or go among humans, or among the gods of the desire realm, or among the gods of the form realm, or among the gods of the formless realm— the Blessed One said:
What do you think,
Subhūti? In that perverted perception, does there occur a cultivation of the path, by relying upon which cultivation of the path one would neither become afflicted nor purified?

Subhūti said: "No, Blessed One. For when perception is inverted, Blessed One, there is no cultivation of the path; and by relying on such cultivation of the path, one would neither become afflicted nor purified.
The Blessed One said:

What do you think, Subhūti? If various illusions were produced by a magician— whether it be an army of elephants, or an army of horses, or an army of oxen, or an army of foot soldiers— what do you think?
Whether it be the body of a populace, or the form of a woman, or the form of a man— does that illusion possess any karma such that,

by performing that karma, it would go to hell, or to the animal realm, or to the world of Yama; or would it be reborn among humans, or among the gods of the desire realm, or among the gods of the form realm, or among the gods of the formless realm?

Subhūti said: "No, Blessed One. For there is not even so much as a hair-tip’s worth of a real entity in an illusion, Blessed One, wherein one might abide and perform an action, by performing which action one would go to hell or to the animal realm."
or go to the world of Yama, or be reborn among humans, or among the gods of the desire realm, or among the gods of the form realm, or among the gods of the formless realm. The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Is there any cultivation of the path for him, by relying upon which cultivation of the path he would neither become afflicted nor purified?
Subhūti said:

"No, Blessed One; there is no entity, Blessed One, of any dharma whatsoever. From where would the cultivation of the path arise, by resorting to which cultivation of the path one would neither be afflicted nor purified?
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think?"

Subhūti, furthermore, as for another emanation that a Tathāgata’s own emanation creates— does that emanation have any karma by which it might go to hell, or to the animal realm, or to the world of Yama;
or might it be reborn among humans, or among the gods of the desire realm, or among the gods of the form realm, or among the gods of the formless realm?
Subhūti said: "No, Blessed One; that emanation, Blessed One, is not a substantial entity.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Does that emanated being have any cultivation of the path, by means of which cultivation of the path he would neither become afflicted nor purified?
Subhūti said:
"No, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said: "What do you think?"
"Subhūti, is there anyone here who would be afflicted or purified?
Subhūti replied,
"No one at all, Blessed One, would be afflicted or purified."
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, just as there is neither affliction nor purification, so too there is no affliction or purification. Why is that?
Subhūti, it is because beings who abide in the notions of 'I' and 'mine' are either afflicted or purified."

"Just as one who sees reality as it is is neither afflicted nor purified, even so, Subhūti, there is neither affliction nor purification. This is the activity of establishing the knowledge that overturns [the view of] entities.
Then, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
Whether it be real, O Blessed One, it is neither afflicted nor purified; or whether it be unreal, O Blessed One, it is neither afflicted nor purified.
For all phenomena have non-existence as their intrinsic nature.
Blessed One, even for that which has non-existence as its intrinsic nature, there is neither affliction nor purification;
Blessed One, even for existence, there is neither affliction nor purification;
Blessed One, even for non-existence, there is neither affliction nor purification.

“Blessed One, even for existence and non-existence there is neither affliction nor purification. In that regard, Blessed One, as for this purification which has been taught by the Blessed One, how is it so, Blessed One?
The Blessed One said:
“Subhūti, that which is the sameness of all phenomena—that is what I have called purification.”
Subhūti said: "But what, moreover, is that equality of all dharmas?
The Blessed One replied:

Suchness, non-falsity, non-other-suchness, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the stability of phenomena (*dharma-sthititā*), and the fixed order of phenomena (*dharma-niyāmatā*)—whether Tathāgatas arise or do not arise, this nature of phenomena, this stability of phenomena, this fixed order of phenomena, and this realm of phenomena remains ever-abiding. This is what is called [the ultimate].
Furthermore, it is expressed through worldly convention, but not in the ultimate sense; for it is inexpressible, beyond verbalization, and transcends all forms of sound and speech.
Thus ends the activity of establishing purification.
Then, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"If, Blessed One, all dharmas are like a dream, like an echo, like an optical illusion, and like a reflection..."

[All things] are like a mirage, like an illusion, like a city of the Gandharvas, and like a magical creation. How then can a bodhisattva mahāsattva [be affected] by all phenomena which are like a dream, like an echo, like an optical illusion, like a reflection, like a mirage, and like an illusion?

With respect to phenomena that are like a city of the Gandharvas and like magical constructs— being without substance and lacking any real entity— one generates the mind set on unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment for the sake of fulfilling the perfection of generosity and fulfilling the perfection of ethical discipline.
for the fulfillment of the perfection of patience,
for the fulfillment of the perfection of vigor,
and for the fulfillment of the perfection of meditation;
For the fulfillment of the perfection of wisdom, for the fulfillment of the perfection of skillful means,
and for the fulfillment of the perfection of aspiration.
For the sake of fulfilling the perfection of power,
for the sake of fulfilling the perfection of gnosis,
and for the sake of fulfilling the perfection of the superknowledges.
He enters the four meditative absorptions (dhyānas),
fulfills the four immeasurables (apramāṇas) and the four formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpattis),
and fulfills the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthānas).
He fulfills the four right efforts, fulfills the four bases of psychic power, fulfills the five faculties,
and fulfills the five powers.
He fulfills the seven factors of enlightenment,
fulfills the noble eightfold path,
and fulfills the eight liberations and the nine successive meditative attainments.
He fulfills the four noble truths,
enters into the concentrations of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness,
and fulfills the five superknowledges.
He cultivates internal emptiness, he cultivates external emptiness,
and he cultivates internal-and-external emptiness.
As he cultivates the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence,
he fulfills all meditative concentrations, all doors of dhāraṇī, and the ten bodhisattva stages.
He fulfills them;
he fulfills the ten powers of a Tathāgata; he fulfills the four grounds of self-confidence.
He fulfills the four analytical knowledges;
he fulfills the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; he fulfills the thirty-two marks of a great man; he fulfills the eighty minor marks;
and he brings to perfection a radiance that illuminates the entire trichiliocosm.
He brings to perfection the quality of having a Brahma-like voice;

therein, with a single sound, throughout the world-systems in the ten directions, he teaches the Dharma to sentient beings according to their inclinations, having understood their minds with his own mind.
The Blessed One said:

What do you think, Subhūti? Are these phenomena— which have been proclaimed by you— not like a dream, not like an echo, not like an optical illusion, not like a reflection, not like a mirage, not like a magical illusion, not like a city of the Gandharvas, and not like a conjuration?

Subhūti said: "If, Blessed One, all dharmas are like a dream, like an echo, like an optical illusion, like a reflection, like a mirage, like a magical illusion, like a city of the Gandharvas, and like a created apparition, then, Blessed One, how [can there be] in things that are like a dream..."
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfection of wisdom regarding all phenomena, up to those that are like magical emanations?

For, Blessed One, a dream is not real; an echo is not real; an optical illusion is not real; a reflected image is not real; a mirage is not real; a magical illusion is not real; a city of the gandharvas is not real; and a magical emanation is not real.

Moreover, Blessed One, it is not possible to practice the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, or the perfection of wisdom through what is unreal; nor is it possible [to practice] the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditations, the formless attainments, the liberations, the concentrations, the meditative absorptions, or the gateways of the dhāraṇīs.

[to practice] in emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; in all the modes of emptiness; in the superknowledges; in the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think?"
Subhūti, it is not the perfection of giving that awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;

nor is it the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, or the perfection of wisdom that awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

It is not the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, all the modes of emptiness, the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, the formless attainments, the liberations, the concentrations, the meditative attainments, or the gateways of dhāraṇī that do so.

Subhūti, all those dharmas— the emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique buddha-dharmas— by which one awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, are all unconditioned and unproduced; it is not possible to attain omniscience by means of dharmas that are unconditioned.

Moreover, Subhūti, all these dharmas lead to the bringing forth of the path, but not to the attainment of the fruit; for that which is the non-arising, the non-manifestation, and the absence of characteristics of these dharmas is itself [the fruit].
Therefore, from the first production of the thought of awakening, the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not apprehend those wholesome dharmas—

whether it be the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, the perfection of wisdom,
or the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening.

Whether it be internal emptiness, or external emptiness, or internal-external emptiness, or up to the emptiness of the nature of non-existence; or whether it be the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the liberations, the samādhis, the meditative absorptions, or the gateways of dhāraṇī; or whether it be emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, or the unique buddha-dharmas.
He knows all of them to be like an illusion.

And without having fully perfected these dharmas—the perfection of giving, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom; nor the applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path; nor internal emptiness and external emptiness—[he does not attain awakening].
