Without having fully perfected internal and external emptiness, up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence; the noble truths, the immeasurables, the dhyānas, the formless attainments, the liberations, the meditative concentrations, the meditative absorptions, and the gateways of dhāraṇī; emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the superknowledges, the ten bodhisattva stages, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, the thirty-two marks of a great man, and the eighty minor characteristics.

It is impossible for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom to attain the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) without having fulfilled the knowledge endowed with the excellence of all modes and without having brought sentient beings to maturity;
whatever wholesome qualities (*kuśala-dharma*) he undertakes, those wholesome qualities are like a dream and like an echo.
He knows them to be like reflections, like images, like mirages, like illusions, like cities of the Gandharvas, and like magical emanations.
While practicing the perfection of wisdom, while practicing the perfection of concentration, while practicing the perfection of vigor, while practicing the perfection of patience,
while practicing the perfection of ethical discipline, while practicing the perfection of generosity, and while practicing internal emptiness and external emptiness...
Practicing while dwelling in internal-external emptiness, up to practicing while dwelling in the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature;

practicing while dwelling in the applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of awakening, and the path; [and] in the noble truths, the immeasurables, the dhyānas, the formless attainments, the liberations, the concentrations, and the meditative absorptions.
Practicing in the eight liberations, practicing in the nine successive meditative attainments,
practicing in the gateways to liberation— emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—
practicing in the five superknowledges, practicing in all samādhis, practicing in all gateways of dhāraṇīs, and [practicing] in the ten bodhisattva stages.

Practicing in the ten powers of a Tathāgata, practicing in the four grounds of self-confidence, practicing in the four analytical knowledges, practicing in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and so on, up to practicing in the knowledge of all aspects endowed with the excellence of all modes,
one knows that things are like a dream.
He knows them to be like an echo, like a reflection, like a mirror-image, like a mirage, like an illusion, like a city of the Gandharvas, and like a magical creation;

and he knows all those sentient beings as moving within a dream, knowing them as moving within an echo, a reflection, a mirror-image, a mirage, an illusion, a city of the Gandharvas, and a magical creation.
Thus, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva regards the perfection of wisdom neither as an existent nor as a non-existent.
He grasps that by which, having grasped it, he may attain the knowledge of all aspects;

having known all phenomena to be like a dream, like an echo, like an optical illusion, like a reflection, like a mirage, like a magical illusion, like a city of the Gandharvas, and like a conjuration, he does not grasp them as being existent, nor as being non-existent.
One grasps that by which, having grasped it, one may attain all-aspect omniscience; the perfection of wisdom is ungraspable,
and the perfection of meditation is ungraspable.
The perfection of vigor is ungraspable;
the perfection of patience is ungraspable;
the perfection of ethical discipline is ungraspable.
The perfection of giving is ungraspable;
the applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path are ungraspable;
internal emptiness is ungraspable.
External emptiness is ungraspable;
internal-external emptiness is ungraspable;
and so on, up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence, which is ungraspable.

The noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the liberations, the meditative absorptions, the meditative equipoises, and the gateways to the dhāraṇīs are ungraspable;

emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness are ungraspable; the superknowledges are ungraspable; the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the analytical knowledges are ungraspable; and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are ungraspable.

All dharmas are ungraspable; therefore, having understood that all dharmas are ungraspable, the bodhisattva mahāsattva establishes himself in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. Why is that?

Because all dharmas are indeed ungraspable, devoid of substance, and like a dream, like an echo, like an optical illusion, like a reflection, like a mirage, like a magical illusion, like a city of the Gandharvas, and like a phantom. And for those things that are ungraspable...
The ungraspability of phenomena is impossible to express in words;
yet, except for this, sentient beings neither know nor see these phenomena.
Therefore, the bodhisattva mahāsattva establishes himself in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening for the sake of all sentient beings.

And from the first production of the thought of enlightenment onward, whatever gift he gives, whatever ethical discipline he maintains, and whatever patience he cultivates, all that is for the sake of all sentient beings.
Whatever vigor he exerts, whatever meditative concentration he enters, and whatever wisdom he cultivates—
That is for the sake of all sentient beings, and not for his own sake.

Furthermore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not establish himself in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening for the sake of anyone else other than for the sake of all sentient beings; while practicing the perfection of wisdom, he is not a sentient being, nor does he have the perception of a sentient being toward a sentient being.
They do not abide in a self, nor do they abide in the notion of a self; they do not abide in a living being, nor do they abide in the notion of a living being.

They do not abide in the notion of a "living being" regarding a living being; they do not abide in the notion of a "nourisher" regarding a nourisher; they do not abide in the notion of a "person" regarding a person.

She does not abide in the perception of a person regarding a person, nor does she abide in the perception of a human regarding a human, nor does she abide in the perception of a youth regarding a youth.

She does not abide in the notion of an agent regarding an agent, nor does she abide in the notion of an experiencer regarding an experiencer, nor does she abide in the notion of a knower regarding a knower.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not abide in the perception of a seer regarding one who is not a seer; having separated them from perversion,
he establishes them in the deathless realm.
For those established therein, these modes of conduct do not arise:

the notion of a self, the notion of a sentient being, the notion of a soul, the notion of a creature, the notion of a nourisher, the notion of a person, the notion of an individual, the notion of a human, the notion of a youth, the notion of an agent, the notion of an experiencer, the notion of a knower.
Having discerned all these—whether they be contractions, expansions, vibrations, or conceptual proliferations—he dwells frequently, having attained and entered into one or another state of mind.

By this means, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom does not himself become attached to any phenomena, and he establishes all sentient beings in non-attachment through worldly convention, but not through the ultimate truth.
Thus ends the activity of establishing purification.
Then, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
“Blessed One, as for that dharma which has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata—is that dharma fully awakened to by way of worldly convention, or by way of the ultimate meaning?”

The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is by way of worldly convention that it is said, 'This dharma has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata,' or 'By means of this dharma, this dharma has not been fully awakened to,' or 'This dharma has been taught by the Tathāgata. Yet, therein nothing at all is apprehended."
For what reason?
Because this is a grasping at signs, namely, "by means of this dharma this dharma has been fully awakened to";
yet through duality there is no attainment whatsoever, nor is there any clear realization.
Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"If, Blessed One, realization is not by means of duality, is it then by means of non-duality?
The Blessed One replied:
Realization is not by means of duality, nor is realization by means of non-duality;
this indeed is realization here, wherein there is neither duality nor non-duality.
For what reason?

"This realization of theirs is a conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), yet there is no conceptual proliferation in the sameness of phenomena (*dharmasamatā*); the sameness of phenomena is free from conceptual proliferation. Subhūti said:
"Blessed One, what is the equality of all phenomena whose intrinsic nature is non-existence?
The Blessed One replied:
"In this context, equality is precisely that wherein neither existence nor non-existence is proclaimed."
Nor, while proclaiming the sameness of phenomena, is any other phenomenon apprehended within that sameness of phenomena;
for the sameness of phenomena is the cessation of all phenomena.
Indeed, the sameness of phenomena is neither a path nor an object for anyone, whether they be a foolish ordinary person or an arya.
Subhūti said:
"But, Blessed One, is the sameness of dharmas even beyond the range of the Tathāgata?
The Blessed One said:

Subhūti, this equality of all phenomena (sarvadharmasamatā) is not within the domain of any noble ones— whether followers by faith (śraddhānusārin), followers by dharma (dharmānusārin), those who have entered the eighth stage (aṣṭamaka), stream-enterers (srotāpanna), once-returners (sakṛdāgāmin), non-returners (anāgāmin), arhats, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or bodhisattva mahāsattvas; it is not even within the domain of the Tathāgata.
Subhūti said:
"But, Blessed One, does not the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, have mastery over the domain of all dharmas?
The Blessed One said:

Subhūti, it would be so if the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha were a master over the domain of all phenomena while the equality of phenomena were one thing and the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha another. But, Subhūti, that which is the equality of phenomena for ordinary persons, and that which is the equality of phenomena for those who follow by faith, those who follow by Dharma, and those of the eighth stage— [they are not different].

The equality of stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattva mahāsattvas, and the equality of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha— which is indeed equality itself— is the same as the equality of foolish common worldlings.
And that which is noble equality is this very single equality;
in this single equality, there is no duality.

"This is an ordinary foolish person; this is a follower by faith; this is a follower of the Dharma; this is one who has attained the eighth stage; this is a stream-enterer; this is a once-returner; this is a non-returner; this is an arhat; this is a pratyekabuddha; this is a bodhisattva mahāsattva; this is a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."
Subhūti, all these phenomena are not apprehended within equality:
"these are foolish commoners," or "this is one who follows through faith."

"This one is a follower of the Dharma; this one is an eighth-rank practitioner; this one is a stream-enterer; this one is a once-returner; this one is a non-returner; this one is an arhat; this one is a pratyekabuddha; this one is a bodhisattva mahāsattva; this one is a Tathāgata, an Arhat. Subhūti said:
If, Blessed One, within the equality of all phenomena (*sarvadharmasamatā*) none of these phenomena are apprehended—
such as "this is an ordinary person (*bālapṛthagjana*)," "this is a follower by faith (*śraddhānusārī*)," or "this is a follower of the Dharma (*dharmānusārī*)"— then...

“Blessed One, will there be no distinction between this eighth-rank person, this stream-enterer, this once-returner, this non-returner, this arhat, this pratyekabuddha, this bodhisattva mahāsattva, and this Tathāgata, Arhat; or rather, will there be no distinction between foolish commoners, those who follow by faith, those who follow by dharma, the eighth-rank persons,
the stream-enterers, the once-returners, the non-returners, the arhats, and the pratyekabuddhas?”
[This applies] to the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, and to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti; so it is."

There is no distinction in the equality of dharmas among foolish ordinary beings, followers by faith, followers by dharma, those of the eighth stage, stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas mahāsattvas, and tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly enlightened ones.

Subhūti said: "If, Blessed One, there is no distinction between foolish commoners, followers by faith, followers by dharma, those of the eighth stage, stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas..."
Of the great beings, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly awakened Buddhas— O Blessed One, from where does the appearance of these three jewels in the world arise:
the jewel of the Buddha, the jewel of the Dharma, and the jewel of the Saṅgha?
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Is the jewel of the Buddha one thing, the jewel of the Dharma another, the jewel of the Saṅgha another, and the sameness of the nature of all phenomena yet another?"
Subhūti said:
"As I understand the meaning of what the Blessed One has spoken, O Blessed One,

the Jewel of the Buddha is not other than [the Jewel of the Dharma], the Jewel of the Dharma is not other than [the Jewel of the Saṅgha], and the Jewel of the Saṅgha is not other than the sameness of the nature of all phenomena."
If, Blessed One, the Jewel of the Buddha, the Jewel of the Dharma, and the Jewel of the Saṅgha— and indeed the sameness of all phenomena—

all these dharmas are neither conjoined nor disjoined, formless, invisible, ungraspable, non-obstructive, and of a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics, then how, Blessed One, do you establish the differentiation of the fruits of these dharmas that are without characteristics?

"This is an ordinary foolish person; this is one who follows through faith; this is one who follows through the Dharma; this is an eighth-rank person; this is a stream-enterer; this is a once-returner; this is a non-returner; this is an arhat; this is a pratyekabuddha; this is a bodhisattva mahāsattva; this is a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha"? The Blessed One said:

If the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, were to attain unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, yet having attained it did not establish the classification of phenomena, then neither hell would be known, nor the animal realm, nor the world of Yama, nor gods, nor humans, nor the Cāturmahārājika gods, nor the Trayastriṃśa gods.

or the Yāmas, or the Tuṣitas, or the Nirmāṇaratis, or the Paranirmitavaśavartins; or the Brahmapārṣadyas, or the Brahmapurohitas, or the Mahābrahmans; or the Parīttābhas, or the Apramāṇābhas, or the Ābhāsvaras; or the Parīttaśubhas, or the Apramāṇaśubhas, or the Śubhakṛtsnas; or the Anabhrakas, or the Puṇyaprasavas, or the Bṛhatphalas, or the Asaṃjñisattvas.
or the gods of the Heaven of No Striving (Asprhā), the Heaven of No Heat (Atapā), the Beautifully Seeing (Sudṛśā), the Good Appearance (Sudarśanā), or the Highest (Akaniṣṭha);
or the meditative attainments of the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, or the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
or the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path.

Whether it be internal emptiness, external emptiness, or internal-external emptiness; up to and including the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence; or the noble truths, the immeasurables, the dhyānas, the formless attainments, the liberations, the meditative concentrations, the meditative absorptions, or the gateways of dhāraṇī; or emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;

or the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, or the unique qualities of a Buddha; or great loving-kindness, great compassion, the thirty-two marks of a great man, or the eighty minor characteristics.
Or the ten bodhisattva stages;
or the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, the perfection of wisdom;
or the perfection of skillful means, the perfection of aspiration, the perfection of power, or the perfection of knowledge.
Thus are the three jewels: the jewel of the Buddha, the jewel of the Dharma, and the jewel of the Saṅgha;
as well as the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the unsurpassed Mahāyāna.

In this way, why are the followers by faith, the followers by dharma, the eighth-rank practitioners, stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas mahāsattvas, tathāgatas, arhats, and perfectly enlightened buddhas, as well as the gnosis endowed with the excellence of all aspects, not perceived?
Subhūti said: "No, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:

Therefore, Subhūti, this is the personal achievement of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas: that they neither deviate from the equality of phenomena (*dharmasamatā*) nor fail to establish the distinctions among phenomena.

Subhūti said: "Blessed One, does the foolish common person, the follower by faith, the follower of the Dharma, the eighth-rank practitioner, and the stream-enterer not likewise remain unmoved from the very same dharmatā as the Tathāgata?"
The once-returner, the non-returner, the arhat, the pratyekabuddha, the bodhisattva mahāsattva, and likewise all dharmas do not move.
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti; so it is."
Subhūti, all phenomena do not move from nor deviate from the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

Subhūti, that which is the true nature, the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the stability of phenomena (*dharma-sthititā*), the fixed course of phenomena (*dharma-niyāmatā*), suchness (*tathatā*), non-falsity (*avitathatā*), and non-other-suchness (*ananyatathatā*) of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One— that very same is the true nature, the realm of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the fixed course of phenomena, suchness, non-falsity, and non-other-suchness of foolish ordinary beings.

That very same [reality] is the true nature (*dharmatā*), the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the stability of phenomena (*dharma-sthititā*), the fixed course of phenomena (*dharma-niyāmatā*), suchness (*tathatā*), non-falsity (*avitathatā*), and non-other-suchness (*ananyatathatā*) of those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*), those who follow by Dharma (*dharmānusārin*), the eighth-rank practitioners (*aṣṭamaka*), stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*), once-returners (*sakṛdāgāmin*), non-returners (*anāgāmin*), arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattva mahāsattvas.
All these phenomena do not transcend the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
Why is that?

Because this very true nature of phenomena is the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), the stability of phenomena (dharma-sthititā), the fixed order of phenomena (dharma-niyāmatā), suchness (tathatā), non-falsity (avitathatā), and non-other-suchness (ananyatathatā); there is no other conformable nature whatsoever.
Subhūti said: "If, Blessed One, that which is the true nature (dharmatā) of all phenomena is the very same true nature of foolish commoners, the very same of those who follow by faith,
the very same of those who follow by Dharma, the very same of the eighth-rank practitioners, the very same of stream-enterers, and the very same of once-returners and non-returners..."
That very same [emptiness] belongs to the Arhats, that very same to the Pratyekabuddhas, that very same to the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas,
and that very same to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas. Lord,
since these phenomena are of diverse characteristics, how can they be said to have a single characteristic?
Namely: form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;
the aggregates, elements, sense bases, dependent origination, and the factors of dependent origination.
Furthermore, Blessed One, the true nature (dharmatā) of form is distinct [from form itself].

The true nature of feeling is one thing, that of perception is another, that of mental formations is another, and that of consciousness is another; the true nature of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body is one thing,
and the true nature of the mind is another.
The true nature (*dharmatā*) of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles is one thing; the true nature of phenomena (*dharma*) is another;
and the true nature of visual consciousness is yet another.
The nature of eye-contact is one thing,
and the nature of the feeling conditioned by eye-contact is another;
likewise for the ear, nose, tongue, and body.
The nature of mental consciousness is one thing; the nature of mental contact is another;
the nature of feeling conditioned by mental contact is yet another.
The dharmatā of the earth element is one thing; the dharmatā of the water element is another;
the dharmatā of the fire element is another.
The nature of the wind element is one thing, the nature of the space element is another,
and the nature of the consciousness element is yet another.
The true nature of the aggregates is one thing, the true nature of the elements is another, and the true nature of the sense bases is yet another.
The nature of dependent origination is one thing, the nature of dependently originated phenomena is another, and the nature of ignorance is yet another.
The nature of formative forces is one thing,
the nature of consciousness is another, and the nature of name-and-form is yet another.
The nature of the six sense bases is one thing, the nature of contact is another,
and the nature of feeling is yet another.
The nature of craving is one thing,
the nature of grasping is another, and the nature of becoming is yet another.
The nature of birth is one thing; the nature of aging and death is another;
and the nature of sorrow, lamentation, suffering, dejection, and despair is yet another.
The nature of passion is one thing, the nature of hatred is another, and the nature of delusion is yet another.
The nature of the views is one thing, the nature of the meditative absorptions is another, and the nature of the immeasurables is yet another.
The true nature of the formless attainments is one thing; the true nature of the applications of mindfulness is another;
the true nature of the right efforts is yet another.
The nature of the bases of psychic power is one thing,
the nature of the faculties is another, and the nature of the powers is yet another.
The true nature of the factors of enlightenment is one thing, the true nature of the noble eightfold path is another,
and the true nature of emptiness is yet another.
The nature of the signless is one thing,
the nature of the wishless is another,
and the nature of internal emptiness is yet another.
The true nature of external emptiness is one thing;
the true nature of internal-external emptiness is another; and the true nature of everything up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature is yet another.
The nature of the eight liberations is one thing, the nature of the nine successive meditative attainments is another,
and the nature of the noble truths is yet another.
The nature of the supernormal knowledges is one thing;
the nature of the perfection of generosity is another; the nature of the perfection of ethical discipline is another.
The nature of the perfection of patience is one thing,
the nature of the perfection of vigor is another,
and the nature of the perfection of meditation is yet another.
The dharmatā of the perfection of wisdom is one thing, the dharmatā of the perfection of skillful means is another,
and the dharmatā of the perfection of aspiration is yet another.
The dharmatā of the perfection of power is one thing,
the dharmatā of the perfection of knowledge is another, and the dharmatā of the first bodhisattva stage is yet another.
The *dharmatā* of the ten stages of the bodhisattva is one thing, the *dharmatā* of the ten powers of a Tathāgata is another, and the *dharmatā* of the four grounds of self-confidence is yet another.
The true nature of the four analytical knowledges is one thing; the true nature of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha is another;
the true nature of great loving-kindness is yet another.
The true nature of great compassion is one thing;
the true nature of the thirty-two marks of a great man is another; the true nature of the eighty secondary characteristics is another; and the true nature of the conditioned realm is yet another.

The nature of reality (*dharmatā*) of the unconditioned realm (*asaṃskṛtadhātu*) is one thing; [the nature of reality] of all other phenomena is another. How then, Blessed One, is it that no such differentiation in the nature of reality of all phenomena is perceived, wherein a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), might establish the diversity of phenomena?
For without establishing the diversity of phenomena, it is not possible for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to practice the perfection of wisdom.
And how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva pass from stage to stage and enter the bodhisattva’s fixed course of certainty?
By entering that fixed course of certainty, he transcends the level of the śrāvaka or the level of the pratyekabuddha and fulfills the superknowledges;
sporting with those superknowledges, he becomes perfected in the perfection of generosity.
He is perfected in the perfection of ethical discipline,
perfected in the perfection of patience,
and perfected in the perfection of vigor.
He is perfected in the perfection of meditative concentration,
perfected in the perfection of wisdom,
and perfected in the perfection of skillful means.
He is perfected in the perfection of aspiration,
perfected in the perfection of power,
and perfected in the perfection of gnosis.
Sporting within one buddha-field, he travels from buddha-field to buddha-field; he attends upon the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and plants roots of merit under those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.
By means of those roots of merit, he brings sentient beings to maturity and takes hold of a buddha-field.
The Blessed One said:
As for what the Venerable Subhūti has said:
"If, Blessed One, that which is the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is the very same as the true nature of ordinary persons (pṛthagjana),"

That very same [nature] is the *dharmatā* of those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*), those who follow the Dharma (*dharmānusārin*), the eighth-rank practitioners (*aṣṭamaka*), stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*), once-returners (*sakṛdāgāmin*), non-returners (*anāgāmin*), arhats, and pratyekabuddhas;
that very same [nature] is the *dharmatā* of the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the Samyaksaṃbuddhas.

O Blessed One, since these phenomena (*dharma*) have distinct characteristics (*vilakṣaṇa*), how can they be of a single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*)? And how is it logical that the *dharmatā* of phenomena with distinct characteristics is of a single characteristic?
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Is that which is the true nature (*dharmatā*) of form [identical to] the true nature of all phenomena?"
That which is the true nature (*dharmatā*) of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is not empty;
why should that which is the true nature of the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields not be empty?
Is that which is the true nature (dharmatā) of dependently originated phenomena not empty?
Is it not empty?
Is that which is the dharmatā of the factors of dependent origination not empty? Is that which is the dharmatā of mundane and supramundane phenomena [not empty]?
Is that which is the true nature (dharmatā) of both contaminated and uncontaminated phenomena not empty?
Is it not empty?
Is that which is the true nature (*dharmatā*) of conditioned and unconditioned phenomena not empty? Is that which is the true nature of foolish ordinary persons [not empty]?
That which is the nature of one who follows by faith, that which is the nature of one who follows the Dharma,
that which is the nature of the eighth-rank person, and that which is the nature of one who has entered the stream;
That which is the nature of a once-returner, that which is the nature of a non-returner, and that which is the nature of an arhat.
That which is the dharmatā of the pratyekabuddhas, that which is the dharmatā of the bodhisattvas, and that which is the dharmatā of the Tathāgatas.
"Why is it not empty?
Subhūti replied:
"It is empty, Blessed One; it is empty, Sugata."
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Are distinct characteristics of phenomena perceived within emptiness?"
Whether it be the characteristic of form, or the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
or the characteristic of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases;
or the characteristic of dependent origination.
Whether it be the characteristic of dependently originated phenomena, or the characteristic of the members of dependent origination;
or the characteristic of mundane and supramundane phenomena, or the characteristic of contaminated and uncontaminated phenomena, or the characteristic of conditioned and unconditioned phenomena.
Whether it be the characteristic of foolish ordinary persons, or the characteristic of those who follow by faith,

or the characteristic of those who follow the Dharma, or the characteristic of the eighth-rank practitioners, or the characteristic of stream-enterers, or the characteristic of once-returners, or the characteristic of non-returners, or the characteristic of arhats.
...or the characteristic of Pratyekabuddhas, or the characteristic of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas,
or the characteristic of Tathāgatas.
Subhūti said:
"No, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Therefore, Subhūti, by this method it should be understood thus:"

That which is the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is neither there apart from ordinary beings, nor is it elsewhere than among ordinary beings; it is neither there apart from those who follow by faith (śraddhānusārī), nor is it elsewhere than among those who follow by faith;
it is neither there apart from those who follow the Dharma (dharmānusārī), nor is it elsewhere than among those who follow the Dharma.

Therein is no eighth-rank person, nor anyone other than eighth-rank persons; therein is no stream-enterer, nor anyone other than stream-enterers; therein is no once-returner, nor anyone other than once-returners.
Therein is no non-returner, nor is there anyone other than non-returners; therein is no arhat, nor is there anyone other than arhats;
therein is no pratyekabuddha, nor is there anyone other than pratyekabuddhas.
Therein is no bodhisattva other than the bodhisattva, nor therein is there a Tathāgata other than the Tathāgata.
Thus ends the activity of establishing the equipment for purification.
Then, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"Furthermore, Blessed One, is the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) conditioned or unconditioned?"
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
"They are neither conditioned nor unconditioned;
nor is the unconditioned perceived apart from the conditioned."
And apart from the unconditioned, the conditioned is not perceived. Why is that?

Because, Subhūti, both the conditioned realm and the unconditioned realm—these two dharmas—are neither conjoined nor disjoined; they are formless, invisible, non-resistant, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.

Furthermore, the Tathāgata conducts himself according to worldly convention (*lokavyavahāra*), but not according to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). In the ultimate truth, there is no bodily formation (*kāyasaṃskāra*), nor vocal formation (*vāksaṃskāra*), nor mental formation (*manaḥsaṃskāra*), neither apart from the bodily formation, nor apart from the vocal formation, nor apart from the mental formation. That which is the equality of all phenomena—whether conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)—is the ultimate truth. Thus, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), he does not waver from the ultimate truth.
And he performs the welfare of sentient beings.
Subhūti said:
"If, Blessed One, all phenomena are empty, then no phenomenon performs any action whatsoever toward any other phenomenon."
Since all phenomena are non-existent, devoid of anything, and lack any intrinsic essence, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom,
neither deviate from ultimate reality nor fail to perform the welfare of sentient beings through generosity, pleasant speech, purposeful action, or consistency of purpose?
The Blessed One said: "So it is, Subhūti, so it is, just as you have spoken."
That which is emptiness is nothingness, it is without anything; it performs no action, whether what is to be done or what is not to be done.
Subhūti, if these beings were to know emptiness by themselves, this would not be the preeminent power of the Tathāgata, who neither deviates from emptiness nor moves away from it.
He detaches sentient beings from the notion of a self;
having detached them from the notion of a self, he liberates them from cyclic existence by means of emptiness.
In the same way, he detaches them from the notion of a being, the notion of a soul, the notion of a creature, the notion of a nourisher, and the notion of a person.
He discriminates against the notion of a person, the notion of a human, the notion of a youth, the notion of an agent, the notion of an experiencer, the notion of a knower, and the notion of a seer;
he discriminates against the notion of form.
He detaches from the perception of feeling, he detaches from the perception of perception,
and he detaches from the perception of mental formations.
He discerns the perception of consciousness;
he discerns the perception of the eye; he discerns the perception of the ear.
He discriminates from the perception of the nose, he discriminates from the perception of the tongue,
and he discriminates from the perception of the body.
He discriminates from the perception of mind; he discriminates from the perception of eye-consciousness;
he discriminates from the perception of eye-contact.
He discriminates the perception of feeling conditioned by eye-contact;
likewise, he discriminates the perceptions of ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness;
he discriminates the perception of mind-contact.
He discriminates the perception of feeling conditioned by mental contact;
he discriminates the perception of form;
he discriminates the perception of sound, the perception of odor, the perception of taste, the perception of touch, and the perception of mental phenomena.
He detaches from the perception of the earth element, he detaches from the perception of the water element, and he detaches from the perception of the fire element.
He detaches from the perception of the wind element, he detaches from the perception of the space element, and he detaches from the perception of the consciousness element.
He detaches from the perception of the aggregates, he detaches from the perception of the elements, and he detaches from the perception of the sense bases.
He discriminates the perception of dependent origination,
he discriminates the perception of dependently originated phenomena,
and he discriminates the perception of the factors of dependent origination.
He discriminates against the notion of ignorance;

he discriminates against the notions of volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, existence, birth, and aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair.
He causes them to detach from the notion of the conditioned realm, he causes them to detach from the notion of the unconditioned realm,
and he establishes them in the unconditioned realm.
And that unconditioned realm is empty.
This is the activity of establishing the thorough knowledge of the non-differentiation between the conditioned and the unconditioned.
Then, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
“By what, Blessed One, is the unconditioned realm not empty?
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
“Subhūti, it is empty by way of the notion of a ‘being,’ up to and including the notion of the ‘unconditioned.’”
"Moreover, Subhūti, when an emanation creates another emanation,
is there any entity therein that is not emptiness?
Subhūti replied:
"No, Blessed One. For, Blessed One, there is no entity whatsoever belonging to a magical creation that is not emptiness;
and that which is emptiness is the same as that which is the magical creation."
Both these dharmas are neither conjoined nor disjoined; both are empty by virtue of emptiness.
Why, then, is this concealed—that this is emptiness and this is a magical creation? For what reason?
For both of them are not apprehended within emptiness;
this emptiness is itself an emanation.
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, there is no form, nor feeling, nor perception, nor mental formations, nor consciousness; and that which is an emanation and that which is emptiness—both of these are emptiness.
Subhūti said:
"If, Blessed One, these worldly dharmas are emanations, are these supramundane dharmas also emanations?"

Namely: the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path, the four noble truths,
and emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
Internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence;
the five superknowledges, the eight liberations, the nine successive meditative attainments, the immeasurables, the dhyānas, the formless attainments,
all samādhis, all doors of dhāraṇī, the ten perfections, the ten bodhisattva stages, and the ten powers of a Tathāgata.
The four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and great compassion;
as well as their fruit—that by which those persons are designated:
the follower by faith, the follower by dharma, the eighth-rank person, the stream-enterer, the once-returner, the non-returner, the arhat, and the pratyekabuddha.
"Blessed One, are even these—the bodhisattva mahāsattva, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—emanations?
The Blessed One said:
"Furthermore, where all phenomena are emanations, therein is there anyone who is an emanation of a śrāvaka?"
Some are emanations of a pratyekabuddha, some are emanations of a bodhisattva, some are emanations of a tathāgata,
and some are emanations of the afflictions.
"Subhūti, by this method, all dharmas are like magical emanations and are without distinction, being fashioned by karma.
Subhūti said:

"But, Blessed One, is this abandonment—the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, arhatship, or the stage of a pratyekabuddha—and the abandonment of all latent tendencies and their connections, also an emanation?"
"Are even the emanations [so]?
The Blessed One said:
'Subhūti, whatever dharmas have been produced or have ceased, all these are emanations.'"
Subhūti said:
"Blessed One, what is that dharma which is not an emanation?
The Blessed One replied:
That dharma which has neither arising nor cessation is not characterized by signs.
Subhūti said:
"But what, Blessed One, is that?"
The Blessed One said:
"That which has the nature of non-forgetfulness is not a magical creation.
Subhūti said:

Furthermore, O Blessed One, as it has been said by the Blessed One: "One does not waver from emptiness, nor is duality perceived, and there is no phenomenon whatsoever that is not empty; therefore, O Blessed One, a magical creation would be of a deceptive nature."
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti, so it is.
All dharmas, Subhūti, are empty by their own nature; they were not made by śrāvakas, nor made by pratyekabuddhas, nor made by bodhisattvas mahāsattvas, nor made by tathāgatas."
"And that which is the emptiness of intrinsic nature—that is nirvāṇa.
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Blessed One, how should a person who is a beginner be instructed?"
"How should one be instructed so that they may thoroughly understand the emptiness of intrinsic nature?
Then the Blessed One said this to the venerable Subhūti:
"Furthermore, Subhūti, could there first be an entity and later there be a non-entity?"
"Subhūti, herein there is no being, no non-being, no intrinsic nature, and no extrinsic nature;
how then could there be the emptiness of intrinsic nature? Thus is the activity of establishing [beings] in nirvāṇa."
Thus have the activities been described; thus has the realization of the Dharma-body been explained.
The Blessed One having spoken these words, the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas headed by Maitreya, as well as the venerable Subhūti, the venerable Śāriputra, and the venerable Ānanda, were uplifted in mind.

And Śakra, the lord of the gods, and the world with its gods, humans, asuras, and gandharvas, rejoiced in what the Blessed One had spoken. Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Chapter on Training," concerning the Dharmakāya, in the Noble *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Bhagavatī Prajñāpāramitā*, as edited in accordance with the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*.

Of those phenomena that arise from causes, the Tathāgata has declared their cause, as well as their cessation; such is the teaching of the Great Śramaṇa. Oṃ gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā.
